days.title: Event-Driven Messaging: Delivery Guarantees, Ordering, Idempotency, and Cross-Account Event Buses

concepts.heading: At-Least-Once Delivery and Why Duplicates Happen
concepts.body: Almost every AWS messaging service promises at-least-once delivery, not exactly-once delivery. An SQS standard queue can occasionally hand the same message to two consumers, EventBridge retries a failed target delivery for up to 24 hours by default, SNS retries Lambda and HTTP subscribers, and a Kinesis producer that times out and retries can write the same record twice. Consumers also cause duplicates: if a Lambda function processing an SQS message runs longer than the queue's visibility timeout, the message becomes visible again and a second invocation picks it up, which is why AWS recommends a visibility timeout of at least six times the function timeout. The design consequence is that consumers must tolerate duplicates rather than assume they never happen. On the exam, a requirement such as never charge a customer twice is answered by making the consumer idempotent, not by searching for a transport that claims to remove all duplicates.

concepts.heading: Designing Idempotent Consumers
concepts.body: An idempotent operation gives the same result no matter how many times it runs. The common pattern records an idempotency key before or together with the side effect. For example, a payment consumer writes the order ID to a DynamoDB table with PutItem and the condition expression attribute_not_exists(pk); if the write fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException, the order was already processed and the consumer simply acknowledges the message. A TTL attribute on the table removes old keys after, say, seven days. The key must come from the business data (order ID, payment request ID) rather than from the transport message ID, because a producer retry creates a new message ID for the same business event. Powertools for AWS Lambda ships an idempotency utility that implements this pattern. Exam scenarios that mention retries, replays, or duplicate side effects are testing whether you add this layer.

concepts.heading: Ordering: SQS FIFO, SNS FIFO, and Kinesis Partition Keys
concepts.body: Ordering is always scoped, never global at scale. In an SQS FIFO queue, order is guaranteed within a message group ID, and different groups are processed in parallel; deduplication uses a MessageDeduplicationId or content-based deduplication within a 5-minute interval. SNS FIFO topics deliver to SQS FIFO queues while keeping that order, which gives ordered fan-out. In Kinesis Data Streams the partition key is hashed to a shard, and records are ordered within a shard, so all events for one customer stay in sequence when customer ID is the partition key. The design choice is the scope key: use a high-cardinality value such as account ID or device ID so work spreads across many groups or shards. A single message group ID or a constant partition key forces everything through one sequence and caps throughput, a classic distractor when a question asks for per-entity ordering at high volume.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and Kinesis
concepts.body: Each service answers a different integration question. SQS is a queue: consumers pull work at their own pace, which levels load and isolates a slow consumer. SNS pushes one message to many subscribers (queues, Lambda, HTTP, email) and can filter by message attributes or body. EventBridge routes events by content with rules that match event patterns, receives events from AWS services and SaaS partners, can reshape payloads with input transformers, and offers archive and replay. Kinesis Data Streams is an ordered, replayable stream where several applications read the same records independently, with retention from the default 24 hours up to 365 days. Example: an OrderPlaced event goes to an EventBridge bus, one rule sends orders with detail.amount greater than 1000 to a fraud-check queue, and another sends every order to analytics. Exam questions pair keywords with services: buffering means SQS, fan-out means SNS, content routing means EventBridge, replayable ordered streams mean Kinesis.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account and Cross-Region Event Routing
concepts.body: EventBridge forwards events natively: a rule on one event bus can target another event bus, including one in a different account and a different Region, and rules on the receiving bus then process the event as usual. Two permissions are involved. The receiving bus needs a resource-based policy that allows events:PutEvents, and a statement with the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition authorizes every current and future account in the organization. The sending rule uses an IAM role allowed to call events:PutEvents on the target bus ARN. To place the forwarding rule in every account and Region, including accounts created later, deploy it with a service-managed CloudFormation StackSet with automatic deployment. Event buses are not shared through AWS RAM, and archive replay only sends events back to the bus that archived them. For publisher-side Regional failover, an EventBridge global endpoint fronts two same-named buses in two Regions with a Route 53 health check and optional event replication.

examPoints: A question that requires per-customer or per-device ordering at high throughput is testing whether you choose a high-cardinality message group ID or partition key instead of one global sequence.

A question that mentions retries, replays, or a side effect that must not happen twice is testing idempotent consumers (for example a DynamoDB conditional write on a business key), because SQS, SNS, EventBridge, and Kinesis all deliver at least once.

A question that aggregates events from many accounts and Regions into one bus without code is testing an organization-wide bus policy plus forwarding rules deployed by StackSets, not RAM sharing or archive replay.

quiz.q: A bank posts card transactions to customer accounts. Transactions for the same account must be applied in the order they arrive, the system handles thousands of accounts at once, and a transaction must never be posted twice even if a consumer retries. Which design meets these requirements?
choices: Use one SQS FIFO queue with a single message group ID for all accounts so that every transaction is processed in one global sequence
Use an SQS standard queue and sort the messages by timestamp inside each consumer before applying them to the account balances
Use an SQS FIFO queue with the account ID as the message group ID, and record each transaction ID with a DynamoDB conditional write before posting it
Use an SNS standard topic with one subscription filter per account so that each account's transactions reach a dedicated Lambda function
quiz.explain: Grouping by account ID keeps order per account while thousands of groups run in parallel, and the conditional write on the transaction ID makes posting idempotent. Choice A preserves order but forces every account through one message group, which throttles throughput to a single sequence.

quiz.q: A company has 120 accounts in AWS Organizations in two Regions and creates new accounts every month. Every workload publishes AuditEvent events to its default event bus. The security team needs all AuditEvent events delivered continuously to one custom event bus in a central account, including events from future accounts, without writing forwarding code. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Allow the organization with an aws:PrincipalOrgID condition on the central bus policy, and deploy a rule that targets the central bus ARN to every account and Region with a service-managed StackSet
Share the central event bus with the organization through AWS Resource Access Manager so that each member account can publish to it as if it were a local event bus
Create an EventBridge archive on each account's default bus and schedule an hourly replay that sends the archived AuditEvent events to the central account's bus
Subscribe a Lambda function in each account to the default bus and have it call PutEvents on the central bus with credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager
quiz.explain: A bus rule can target a bus in another account and Region, the PrincipalOrgID policy covers new accounts automatically, and StackSets with automatic deployment place the rule everywhere. Choice B fails because event buses are not shared through AWS RAM; cross-account delivery is authorized by the receiving bus's resource policy.

days.recap: Assume at-least-once delivery everywhere and make consumers idempotent with business keys, scope ordering with message group IDs or partition keys, pick SQS, SNS, EventBridge, or Kinesis by the integration pattern, and route events across accounts and Regions with bus-to-bus rules, an organization-wide bus policy, and StackSets.

days.title: Stateless Services, Serverless Data Pipelines, and Durable Workflows

concepts.heading: Externalizing State So Compute Becomes Disposable
concepts.body: A stateless service keeps nothing between requests that another copy of the service could not serve. Session data, shopping carts, uploaded files, and workflow progress move out of instance memory and local disks into managed stores. Once state is external, Auto Scaling can terminate any instance during scale-in, Spot interruptions lose no user data, deployments can replace the whole fleet, and the load balancer no longer needs sticky sessions. Example: an ALB fleet stores each cart in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID with a TTL attribute named expiresAt set 24 hours ahead, so abandoned carts disappear on their own and any instance can answer any request. Large user uploads go straight to S3 with presigned URLs instead of passing through the web tier. On the exam, symptoms such as users losing their session when an instance is replaced, or a fleet that cannot scale in, point to externalizing state rather than lengthening stickiness.

concepts.heading: Choosing the External State Store
concepts.body: The right store depends on latency, durability, and object size. Amazon ElastiCache (Valkey, Redis OSS, or Memcached) keeps data in memory with sub-millisecond latency; with replication and Multi-AZ failover it suits sessions, rate-limit counters, and leaderboards, but capacity is sized by memory. Amazon DynamoDB is durable and serverless with single-digit millisecond latency, scales without clusters, and expires items with TTL, which makes it a strong default for session and idempotency records. Amazon S3 stores large objects and files durably and cheaply but is not meant for tiny, frequent updates. Local options do not count as shared state: Lambda's /tmp directory belongs to one execution environment and an instance store disappears with the instance. A useful exam heuristic is ElastiCache when microsecond-to-sub-millisecond reads dominate, DynamoDB when durability and zero cluster management matter, and S3 for files and blobs.

concepts.heading: Serverless Analytics Pipelines with Kinesis, Firehose, Glue, and Athena
concepts.body: A common serverless pipeline ingests events into Kinesis Data Streams, lands them in S3, and queries them with Athena. Athena charges by data scanned, so the storage layout matters. Amazon Data Firehose can read an existing Kinesis stream as one more consumer, buffer records for up to 900 seconds, convert JSON to Parquet or ORC using a table schema in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and use dynamic partitioning to write prefixes such as dt=2026-10-27/country=DE, all without servers or code. AWS Glue adds serverless Spark jobs for heavier transformations and crawlers that catalog new data. When a table has millions of predictable partitions, Athena partition projection computes partition locations from table properties, which removes slow catalog lookups and makes new prefixes queryable immediately. On the exam, answers that keep raw JSON, run long-lived EMR clusters, or rewrite the full history on a schedule lose to Firehose conversion plus partitioning.

concepts.heading: Lambda as a Kinesis Stream Consumer
concepts.body: An event source mapping polls each shard and, by default, processes one batch per shard at a time, in order. A failing batch is retried until it succeeds or the records expire, so one malformed record can stall its shard. Failure settings contain this: BisectBatchOnFunctionError splits a failing batch to isolate the bad record, MaximumRetryAttempts and MaximumRecordAgeInSeconds bound retries, and an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue receives details of skipped records for later replay. Throughput settings fix lag: ParallelizationFactor (1 to 10) lets Lambda process several batches from one shard at once while keeping records with the same partition key in order, so 20 shards with a factor of 5 allow up to 100 concurrent invocations. Raising reserved concurrency does nothing while the mapping allows only one batch per shard. Enhanced fan-out gives a consumer its own read throughput per shard but does not fix slow serial processing.

concepts.heading: Step Functions Standard versus Express Workflows
concepts.body: AWS Step Functions orchestrates multi-step work with retries, catch blocks, parallel branches, and direct integrations with more than 200 AWS services. Standard workflows run for up to one year, execute each step exactly once, keep a full visual execution history, support the .waitForTaskToken callback pattern for human approvals or external systems, and are priced per state transition. Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes, are built for high-volume event processing, are priced by request count and duration, offer at-least-once execution when started asynchronously and at-most-once when called synchronously, and do not support .waitForTaskToken. Example: an order saga that reserves stock, charges a card, and books shipping uses a Standard workflow whose Catch states run compensating steps such as releasing stock when payment fails. A Distributed Map state fans out over millions of S3 objects. Exam signal: long waits or approvals mean Standard; millions of short executions mean Express.

concepts.heading: Durable Execution with Lambda Durable Functions
concepts.body: Lambda durable functions let developers write a multi-step, long-running workflow as ordinary Lambda code instead of a state machine definition. A durable execution SDK checkpoints the result of each named step. When the function waits, fails, or is interrupted, it later resumes by replaying the code and skipping steps that already completed, using their saved results, so work is not repeated. Waits and callbacks suspend the execution without paying for compute while it waits, which lets one workflow span far longer than the 15-minute limit of a single invocation. Example: an order function runs a step to reserve stock, a step to charge the card, then waits for a warehouse callback before a final shipping step. Code inside steps should still be idempotent, because a step that fails mid-way can run again. Choose durable functions when the team wants workflow logic in its application code; choose Step Functions for visual orchestration and code-free service integrations.

examPoints: A question where users lose sessions or carts when instances are replaced is testing externalized state (DynamoDB, ElastiCache, S3), not longer sticky sessions or bigger instances.

A question about cheap Athena queries over streaming data without servers is testing Firehose record format conversion to Parquet with dynamic partitioning, and partition projection when partitions are numerous.

A question that contrasts long waits or human approval with millions of short executions is testing Step Functions Standard versus Express, while workflow logic kept in function code with checkpointed steps points to Lambda durable functions.

quiz.q: A web application runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions. Shopping carts are kept in each instance's memory. Customers lose their carts whenever the group scales in or a Spot Instance is interrupted. The company wants any instance to serve any request. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Increase the ALB stickiness duration to 7 days so that each customer stays on the same instance for the whole lifetime of the cart
Store carts on an EBS volume of each instance and take hourly snapshots that a replacement instance restores when it launches
Replace the Auto Scaling group with a fixed number of Reserved Instances so that instances are never removed by scale-in events
Store carts in a DynamoDB table keyed by session ID with a TTL attribute, and turn off stickiness so any instance can serve any request
quiz.explain: Moving carts to DynamoDB makes the instances stateless, so scale-in and Spot interruptions lose nothing and TTL cleans up abandoned carts. Choice A still loses every cart held on an instance the moment that instance is terminated, however long stickiness lasts.

quiz.q: A company processes 20 million IoT events per day. Each event passes through four short steps that finish in under 30 seconds, and every step is idempotent, so an occasional duplicate execution is harmless. The company wants managed orchestration with retries at the lowest cost. Which solution should a solutions architect choose?
choices: Step Functions Standard workflows, because exactly-once step execution and a full execution history are required for each event
Step Functions Express workflows started asynchronously, because they are priced by requests and duration and suit short, high-volume runs
A Lambda function per step chained through SQS queues, with a DynamoDB table that tracks which steps each event has completed
An EC2 Auto Scaling group running an open-source workflow engine that keeps execution state in an Amazon RDS database
quiz.explain: Express workflows are built for high-volume executions under 5 minutes, and at-least-once semantics are acceptable because the steps are idempotent. Choice A works functionally, but Standard workflows are priced per state transition, which is far more expensive for at least 80 million transitions a day.

days.recap: Keep compute stateless by moving sessions and files to DynamoDB, ElastiCache, or S3; build serverless pipelines with Kinesis, Firehose Parquet conversion, Glue, and Athena; tune Lambda stream consumers with bisect, on-failure destinations, and ParallelizationFactor; and choose Step Functions Standard, Express, or Lambda durable functions by duration, volume, and where the workflow logic should live.

days.title: Containers for Microservices: ECS, EKS, Fargate, Service Networking, ECR, and Scaling

concepts.heading: Choosing Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, and AWS Fargate
concepts.body: Amazon ECS is the AWS-native orchestrator: task definitions and services are simple to operate and integrate tightly with IAM, load balancers, and CloudWatch, which suits teams without Kubernetes requirements. Amazon EKS runs upstream Kubernetes, so it fits teams that already have manifests, Helm charts, operators, and Kubernetes skills, or that need the Kubernetes API for portability. Both run on two kinds of capacity. AWS Fargate removes nodes entirely: each task or pod gets its own isolated compute, you pay for the vCPU and memory requested, and there is nothing to patch. EC2 capacity is needed for GPUs, specific instance types, or very high, steady utilization where Reserved Instances or Savings Plans on nodes are cheaper. Example: a team with 40 existing Helm charts moves to EKS with Fargate profiles for stateless services and a GPU node group for inference. On the exam, existing Kubernetes investment points to EKS, least operations points to Fargate.

concepts.heading: ECS Service Connect for Service-to-Service Calls
concepts.body: ECS Service Connect gives ECS services a simple service mesh without application changes. You define an AWS Cloud Map namespace, and each ECS service in it gets a short client alias such as http://orders:8080. ECS injects a managed proxy into every task; the proxy resolves the alias, load balances across healthy tasks on the client side, retries failed connections on a different task, ejects unhealthy endpoints through outlier detection, and sends traffic to new tasks only after they pass their health checks. It also publishes request counts, error rates, and latency for each service to CloudWatch, which gives traffic observability without instrumenting the code. Because the proxy is managed by ECS, there is no sidecar to configure or upgrade yourself. Service Connect applies to ECS services that share a namespace; it does not cover Lambda functions or EKS pods. On the exam, ECS microservices that need service discovery, retries, and traffic metrics with minimal effort point to Service Connect rather than an internal load balancer per service.

concepts.heading: Amazon VPC Lattice for Cross-VPC and Cross-Account Services
concepts.body: Amazon VPC Lattice is an application networking service for service-to-service traffic across VPCs and accounts. A Lattice service has listeners, rules, and target groups that can point at EC2 instances, IP addresses, Lambda functions, ECS tasks, Application Load Balancers, or Kubernetes pods through the AWS Gateway API Controller. Services are grouped into a service network, VPCs are associated with it, and the service network is shared with other accounts through AWS RAM. Clients call services by DNS name, and Lattice handles connectivity without VPC peering or transit gateway routes, even with overlapping CIDRs. Auth policies with the AWS_IAM auth type check each SigV4-signed request against the caller's IAM principal, for example allowing only the checkout role to call GET /orders. Access logs can go to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Firehose. Exam signal: mixed compute types across many accounts that need identity-based authorization per request point to VPC Lattice.

concepts.heading: Managing Images in Amazon ECR
concepts.body: Amazon ECR stores container images and enforces image hygiene. Basic scanning checks images for operating system vulnerabilities on push or on demand. Enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector to scan operating system and programming language packages and to rescan images continuously when new vulnerabilities are published, sending findings to Inspector and EventBridge, where a rule can alert or block promotion. Lifecycle policies keep repositories small with ordered rules, for example expire untagged images 14 days after push and keep only the most recent 30 images whose tags start with release. Tag immutability stops a tag such as v1.4.2 from being overwritten, so a deployment always pulls exactly the image that was tested. Replication copies images to other Regions or accounts so each Region pulls locally, which matters for multi-Region disaster recovery. On the exam, continuous rescanning means enhanced scanning, and storage growth from CI builds means lifecycle policies rather than custom cleanup scripts.

concepts.heading: Scaling Lambda with Concurrency Controls
concepts.body: Lambda scales by running more concurrent execution environments, drawing on a Regional account concurrency quota (1,000 by default and raisable). Reserved concurrency sets aside part of that quota for one function and also caps it, which protects a downstream database from being flooded and prevents one function from starving others. Provisioned concurrency keeps a chosen number of environments initialized ahead of time, removing cold starts for latency-sensitive APIs; it is billed while configured. Application Auto Scaling can manage provisioned concurrency on an alias with a schedule, for example 200 environments from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays, or with target tracking on the LambdaProvisionedConcurrencyUtilization predefined metric. For queue consumers, the maximum concurrency setting on an SQS event source mapping limits how many invocations one queue can drive. Exam signal: protect a downstream system means reserved or maximum concurrency; predictable latency at known peaks means scheduled provisioned concurrency.

concepts.heading: Two-Layer Scaling for ECS and EKS
concepts.body: Containers scale at two layers: the number of tasks or pods, and the capacity they run on. In ECS, service auto scaling uses Application Auto Scaling with target tracking (for example ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization at 60 percent or ALBRequestCountPerTarget), step scaling on a custom metric such as SQS backlog per task, or scheduled scaling. On EC2 capacity, a capacity provider with managed scaling adds and removes instances so new tasks can be placed; on Fargate there is no capacity layer to manage. In EKS, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the replica count from CPU, memory, or custom metrics, and when new pods cannot be scheduled, the Cluster Autoscaler grows the node group's Auto Scaling group, or Karpenter launches right-sized nodes directly. Exam traps include scaling pods with nothing to add nodes, which leaves pods pending, and scaling on CPU when the real signal is queue depth.

examPoints: A question about ECS services needing service discovery, retries, and traffic metrics without code is testing ECS Service Connect, while mixed compute across accounts with IAM authorization per request is testing VPC Lattice.
A question about rescanning stored images when new CVEs appear, or about repositories filling up with CI builds, is testing ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector and lifecycle policies.

A question about scaling is testing which layer is missing: reserved or provisioned concurrency for Lambda, Application Auto Scaling for ECS tasks, HPA for pods, and Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, or capacity providers for nodes.

quiz.q: A company runs microservices on Amazon EKS, Amazon ECS, and AWS Lambda in 40 accounts. Many VPCs use overlapping CIDR ranges. Services must call each other over HTTPS, and each call must be authorized by the calling service's IAM role. The network team does not want to manage peering or transit gateway routes. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Create an Amazon VPC Lattice service network shared through AWS RAM, register each service's targets, associate the client VPCs, and attach IAM auth policies
Enable ECS Service Connect in every account with one shared AWS Cloud Map namespace, and register the EKS pods and Lambda functions in that namespace
Peer every client VPC with every service VPC, and use security group rules that reference the caller's security group ID to authorize each request
Put each service behind an internet-facing ALB, and use AWS WAF rules that allow only the NAT gateway IP addresses of the client accounts
quiz.explain: VPC Lattice connects services across VPCs and accounts without routing, works with overlapping CIDRs, supports EKS, ECS, and Lambda targets, and checks each request against IAM auth policies. Choice B fails because Service Connect works only for ECS services, so EKS pods and Lambda functions cannot join it.

quiz.q: A platform team's CI pipeline pushes about 200 images per day to Amazon ECR, and storage costs keep rising. Security also requires that images already stored in ECR are re-evaluated automatically whenever a new vulnerability is published, not only when they are pushed. Which solution meets both requirements with the least custom code?
choices: Turn on basic scanning with scan on push, and schedule a nightly Lambda function that deletes every image pushed more than 30 days ago
Turn on tag immutability, and have the CI pipeline call DescribeImageScanFindings once after each push before it promotes the image
Turn on enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector for continuous rescanning, and add a lifecycle policy that expires untagged images and keeps the last 30 release images
Replicate every repository to a second Region, and run Amazon Inspector scans every week on the EC2 build hosts that produced each image
quiz.explain: Enhanced scanning rescans stored images continuously as new vulnerabilities are published, and a lifecycle policy removes old images without code. Choice A scans only at push time, and deleting by age with a custom function can remove images that are still deployed.

days.recap: Pick ECS for AWS-native simplicity, EKS for Kubernetes investment, and Fargate to drop node management; connect ECS services with Service Connect and mixed services across accounts with VPC Lattice; keep ECR clean and safe with enhanced scanning, lifecycle policies, and immutable tags; and scale both the workload (concurrency, tasks, pods) and the capacity under it.

days.title: Ingress, Edge Compute, Real-Time Push, and Multi-Tenant Isolation

concepts.heading: Choosing the Front Door: ALB, NLB, or API Gateway
concepts.body: An Application Load Balancer works at layer 7 for HTTP, HTTPS, and gRPC: it routes by host, path, and header, terminates TLS with ACM certificates, supports AWS WAF and OIDC authentication, and can invoke Lambda targets. A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 for TCP, UDP, and TLS: it passes TLS through untouched so targets can do mutual TLS, preserves client source IPs, handles long-lived connections and very high request rates, and offers one static IP per Availability Zone, including your own Elastic IPs. It is also the front of a PrivateLink endpoint service. Amazon API Gateway adds API management: authorizers, request validation, usage plans with throttling and quotas per API key, mapping templates, and pay-per-request pricing with no idle cost. Example: MQTT sensors on TCP 8883 with firewall allowlists need an NLB with Elastic IPs. Exam signal: WAF and path routing mean ALB, static IPs or raw TCP mean NLB, per-client quotas mean API Gateway.

concepts.heading: Ingress on Amazon EKS with the AWS Load Balancer Controller
concepts.body: The AWS Load Balancer Controller watches Kubernetes objects and creates AWS load balancers for them: a Service of type LoadBalancer gets a Network Load Balancer, and an Ingress gets an Application Load Balancer with host and path rules. By default each Ingress creates its own ALB, which multiplies cost when dozens of services are exposed. The annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/group.name creates an IngressGroup that merges every Ingress with the same group name into one ALB, while each team still owns its own manifest. The annotation alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip registers pod IPs directly, which is required for pods on Fargate because there is no node to forward to. Another annotation, wafv2-acl-arn, attaches an AWS WAF web ACL, and ACM certificates terminate TLS on the HTTPS listener. On the exam, 35 services each with its own load balancer is the cue for an IngressGroup, and NGINX behind an NLB fails any WAF requirement.

concepts.heading: CloudFront Functions versus Lambda@Edge
concepts.body: Both run code at the edge, but they fit different jobs. CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript only on viewer request and viewer response events, at every edge location, with sub-millisecond execution, very high scale, and the lowest cost. They suit header manipulation, URL rewrites and redirects, cache key normalization, and simple token validation; they cannot make network calls or read the request body, and CloudFront KeyValueStore supplies small lookup data. Lambda@Edge runs Node.js or Python functions on viewer and origin request and response events, with longer execution time, network access, and the option to read the body, so it suits calling an external service, generating responses, or heavier authentication. Origin events run only on cache misses. Example: normalizing the Accept-Language header on every viewer request at 400,000 requests per second belongs in a CloudFront Function. On the exam, choose the lighter option unless the logic needs network calls, the body, or origin events.

concepts.heading: Real-Time Push with API Gateway WebSocket APIs
concepts.body: An API Gateway WebSocket API keeps a persistent two-way connection between each client and API Gateway, so the backend stays stateless and serverless. The $connect route runs when a client connects; a Lambda function can authenticate the user and store the connection ID with the user ID or the topics the user follows, for example in DynamoDB. The $disconnect route cleans up the mapping on a best-effort basis. To push a message, any backend with IAM permission calls the @connections management API with the connection ID; a 410 Gone response means the client has left. This gives a publish-subscribe pattern: producers publish to SQS, SNS, or EventBridge, and a Lambda consumer looks up subscribers and posts to each connection. Connections close after 10 idle minutes and after 2 hours in any case, so clients send heartbeat messages and reconnect and resynchronize automatically. Exam signal: push to specific browser users without servers means WebSocket API plus a connection table.

concepts.heading: Tenant Isolation Models: Silo, Pool, and Bridge
concepts.body: Multi-tenant SaaS designs place each resource on a spectrum. In the silo model each tenant gets dedicated resources, sometimes a whole account or stack; isolation, per-tenant cost tracking, and noisy-neighbor protection are strong, but onboarding and operations grow with the tenant count. In the pool model tenants share the same compute and data stores, and every item carries a tenant ID; cost per tenant is low and operations are uniform, but isolation must be enforced in code and policy, and one heavy tenant can affect others. The bridge model mixes both, for example a pooled web tier with siloed databases, or premium tenants in silos and basic tenants in the pool. Noisy neighbors in the pool are contained with per-tenant throttling such as API Gateway usage plans by tier. On the exam, strict regulatory isolation or per-tenant customization points toward silo, while thousands of small tenants and cost pressure point toward pool.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Tenant Context: Cognito Claims, Row-Level Security, and Per-Tenant Keys
concepts.body: In a pooled design, the tenant ID must come from a trusted token, never from the request body. Amazon Cognito can carry it as a custom attribute such as custom:tenant_id, or a pre token generation trigger can add it to tokens; the authorizer then passes the verified value to the service. That context drives isolation at each layer. For DynamoDB, the service assumes a role with a session tag for the tenant, and a policy condition on dynamodb:LeadingKeys limits access to items whose partition key equals that tag. For relational data, PostgreSQL row-level security attaches a policy such as tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id') to each table, so a forgotten WHERE clause cannot leak rows. For encryption, a per-tenant KMS key, or an encryption context containing the tenant ID, separates data cryptographically, and disabling or deleting a tenant's key supports offboarding. Exam signal: isolation that a code bug cannot break.

examPoints: A question listing WAF, path routing, static IPs, raw TCP, or per-client quotas is testing the choice between ALB, NLB, and API Gateway; on EKS, many services behind one ALB means an IngressGroup.
A question about edge logic is testing CloudFront Functions for simple viewer-side header and URL work versus Lambda@Edge for network calls, body access, or origin events.

A question about pooled SaaS data leaking between tenants is testing enforcement from a verified tenant claim, such as row-level security, dynamodb:LeadingKeys with session tags, or per-tenant keys, rather than application-only filtering.

quiz.q: A news site behind Amazon CloudFront must normalize the Accept-Language header to three values and rewrite URLs into A/B test paths on every viewer request, so that cache keys stay consistent. Peak traffic is about 400,000 requests per second, added latency must be well under a millisecond, and the logic needs no network calls. Which solution is most cost-effective?
choices: A Lambda@Edge function on the origin request event that rewrites the URL and header after the cache lookup and before forwarding to the origin
A CloudFront Function on the viewer request event that normalizes the header and rewrites the URL before CloudFront performs the cache lookup
An Application Load Balancer listener rule at the origin that rewrites URLs and sets the Accept-Language header for each A/B test bucket
A Lambda@Edge function on the viewer request event that reads each user's A/B bucket from a DynamoDB table in us-east-1 before rewriting
quiz.explain: CloudFront Functions run on viewer request before the cache lookup, with sub-millisecond execution at the lowest cost, and the logic needs no network access. Choice A runs only on cache misses after the cache key is already chosen, so it cannot improve cache consistency, and Lambda@Edge costs more per request.

quiz.q: A SaaS provider stores all tenants' orders in one Aurora PostgreSQL database. Last month a missing filter in one query returned another tenant's rows. The provider wants the database itself to enforce tenant isolation without creating a database per tenant. Users sign in with Amazon Cognito, and tokens carry a verified tenant_id claim. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?
choices: Create a separate Aurora cluster for every tenant and route each request to the right cluster through a tenant-to-cluster map in DynamoDB
Add a tenant_id filter to a shared data access library, and require a security code review for every query that touches tenant tables
Encrypt each tenant's rows with a separate AWS KMS key and decrypt in the application only the rows whose key the caller can use
Enable PostgreSQL row-level security with policies that compare tenant_id to a session setting the application sets from the verified claim
quiz.explain: Row-level security makes the database return only the current tenant's rows, so a query without a filter cannot leak data, and the tenant value comes from a verified token. Choice A is the silo model, which the provider explicitly wants to avoid and which multiplies cost and operations.

days.recap: Match the front door to the traffic (ALB for HTTP routing and WAF, NLB for TCP, static IPs, and pass-through TLS, API Gateway for API management), share one ALB on EKS with an IngressGroup, use CloudFront Functions for light viewer logic and Lambda@Edge for heavier work, push real-time updates with WebSocket APIs and @connections, and isolate tenants with silo, pool, or bridge models enforced from verified tenant context.

days.title: Generative AI Integration and RAG with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases

concepts.heading: Calling Foundation Models from Applications
concepts.body: Applications call Amazon Bedrock models through the bedrock-runtime API. InvokeModel takes a request body in each provider's native format, so Anthropic, Amazon Nova, and Meta models need different code. The Converse API (Converse and ConverseStream) uses one format for messages, system prompts, inference parameters such as maxTokens and temperature, and tool definitions in toolConfig, so changing models is mostly a change to the modelId value. When a model's quota is exhausted, Bedrock returns a ThrottlingException; nothing in Bedrock automatically retries on another provider's model, so the application retries with backoff and then calls a fallback model. Keeping model IDs in a runtime configuration store such as AWS AppConfig lets operators switch models without a deployment. Intelligent prompt routing chooses among models of the same family by predicted quality and cost, which is not cross-provider failover. For documents, images, and audio that must become structured JSON, Bedrock Data Automation projects with blueprints extract fields without per-layout code.

concepts.heading: Private and Governed Access to Bedrock
concepts.body: Bedrock traffic can stay off the internet through interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink), for example com.amazonaws.eu-west-1.bedrock-runtime for inference; there is no gateway endpoint for Bedrock. With private DNS enabled, the standard Regional hostname resolves to the endpoint inside the VPC, and on-premises clients reach it over Direct Connect when on-premises DNS conditionally forwards the name to a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint. To make the endpoint the only path, an IAM policy or SCP denies bedrock:InvokeModel and related actions when aws:SourceVpce does not equal the endpoint ID; an endpoint policy alone only filters traffic that already uses the endpoint. SCPs can also allow only approved model IDs across the organization. Model invocation logging records prompts and responses to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for audit. On the exam, private on-premises access with standard SDK endpoints is solved by an interface endpoint, private DNS, a Resolver inbound endpoint, and an aws:SourceVpce deny.

concepts.heading: Multi-Account Patterns for Generative AI
concepts.body: Large organizations choose how workload accounts reach models. In direct access, each account calls Bedrock itself, governed by SCPs that allow only approved models and by logging in each account; this is simple but gives no per-team budget and ties code to model IDs. In the gateway pattern, a shared services account hosts a private API Gateway API with usage plans that set rate limits and monthly quotas per team, a Lambda function that calls the approved model through the Converse API, and central prompt and response logging; teams see a stable internal API, and the platform team can change models or providers without touching application code. When a custom or fine-tuned model runs on Provisioned Throughput in a central AI account, a narrowly scoped role in that account allows bedrock:InvokeModel on the provisioned model ARN and trusts the whole OU with aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, so new accounts get access automatically and share capacity already paid for.

concepts.heading: How a Bedrock Knowledge Base Implements RAG
concepts.body: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds a model's answer in your documents instead of relying on what the model memorized. An Amazon Bedrock knowledge base automates the pipeline. During ingestion it reads files from a data source such as S3, parses them into text, splits the text into chunks, converts each chunk into a vector with an embedding model, and stores the vectors with their text and metadata in a vector store. At query time it embeds the question, finds the most similar chunks, and either returns them through the Retrieve API or passes them to a model with RetrieveAndGenerate, which returns an answer with citations. A sync started with StartIngestionJob is incremental: it processes new and changed files and removes deleted ones. The embedding model is fixed for an index, so changing it means a new index and re-ingestion. On the exam, frequently changing documents point to RAG with re-syncs rather than fine-tuning.

concepts.heading: Ingestion Strategy: Parsing and Chunking
concepts.body: Answer quality is often decided before any query runs. The default parser extracts plain text and loses text in scanned images and the structure of tables and charts; advanced parsing with Bedrock Data Automation or a foundation model as the parser reads visually rich documents and describes tables and figures so they can be retrieved. Chunking then trades precision for context. Fixed-size chunking with overlap and default chunking split by token count; semantic chunking splits where meaning changes; hierarchical chunking stores small child chunks inside larger parent chunks, searches on the children, and returns the parent, so the model gets the precise hit plus the surrounding section; no chunking treats each file as one chunk. Example: 200-token chunks find the right step in an equipment manual but omit nearby warnings, which hierarchical chunking fixes. The chunking strategy is set when the data source is created, so changing it means a new data source and a fresh sync.

concepts.heading: Retrieval Strategy and Vector Store Choice
concepts.body: Several retrieval settings change what reaches the model. Hybrid search, chosen with overrideSearchType set to HYBRID on stores that keep a text field such as OpenSearch Serverless, combines keyword and semantic matching, which fixes exact identifiers such as part number XK-4471 that embeddings confuse with similar strings. A reranking model retrieves a larger candidate set and reorders it by relevance. Metadata filters restrict results; in a pooled multi-tenant knowledge base, each document's .metadata.json file carries a tenant_id, and the backend adds an equals filter from the verified token claim to every Retrieve call, which a prompt cannot override. The vector store sets cost and features: OpenSearch Serverless gives high query rates, low latency, and hybrid search but bills compute units continuously; Amazon S3 Vectors stores very large, rarely queried vector sets cheaply with sub-second queries and no capacity to manage; Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector keeps vectors beside relational data; Neptune Analytics supports GraphRAG.

examPoints: A question about switching models or providers without code changes is testing the Converse API with model IDs in runtime configuration, and per-team quotas across many accounts point to a central gateway with API Gateway usage plans.

A question where retrieval finds the right passage but answers lack surrounding context is testing hierarchical chunking; exact codes and part numbers that semantic search misses point to hybrid search and reranking.

A question about tenant isolation in a shared knowledge base is testing server-side metadata filters from a verified identity, and a huge, rarely queried vector set at the lowest cost points to S3 Vectors.

quiz.q: A bank has 30 application teams in separate accounts that want to use foundation models. The platform team must enforce a monthly request quota and rate limit per team, log every prompt and response in one account, and be able to change the approved model to another provider later without application teams changing code. Which architecture meets these requirements?
choices: Let every account call Bedrock through its own interface endpoint, restrict model IDs with an SCP, and enable model invocation logging in each account
Create one IAM role in a central account that every team assumes to call Bedrock, and raise that account's Bedrock quotas to the sum of the team budgets
Build a private API Gateway API with per-team usage plans in a shared account, backed by a Lambda function that calls the approved model through the Converse API
Give each team an application inference profile for the approved model, and have each team call the profile ARN directly within its own account quotas
quiz.explain: Usage plans enforce per-team rate limits and quotas, the gateway logs centrally, and the Converse API behind a stable internal API lets the platform team change providers without application changes. Choice A keeps traffic private and restricts models, but nothing enforces per-team budgets and every team still codes against model IDs.

quiz.q: An engineering firm built a Bedrock knowledge base over 5,000 long equipment manuals with 200-token fixed-size chunks. Evaluations show that retrieval reliably finds the correct passage, but generated answers often miss the surrounding steps, warnings, and table headers in the same section. Which change fixes answer completeness without losing retrieval precision?
choices: Recreate the data source with hierarchical chunking so that small child chunks are matched during search and their larger parent chunks are returned as context
Recreate the data source with 2,000-token fixed-size chunks and no overlap so that every chunk always holds an entire section of a manual
Keep the current chunks and raise the generation model's temperature so that the model fills in the steps that the retrieved passages leave out
Keep the current chunks and switch the knowledge base to a larger embedding model without re-ingesting the documents already in the index
quiz.explain: Hierarchical chunking searches on small child chunks, keeping precision, and returns the parent chunk with the surrounding section, fixing completeness. Choice B adds context but each large embedding mixes many topics, so retrieval precision drops.

days.recap: Integrate Bedrock with the Converse API and application-side fallback, keep traffic private with interface endpoints and aws:SourceVpce denies, govern many accounts with SCPs, central roles, or a gateway with usage plans, and build RAG with knowledge bases whose parsing, chunking, retrieval settings, metadata filters, and vector store are chosen deliberately.

days.title: AI Agent Architectures with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and SageMaker AI Inference

concepts.heading: What an Agent Architecture Needs
concepts.body: An AI agent runs a loop: the model plans, calls a tool, reads the result, and plans again until the task is done. One user task can take minutes or hours and holds sensitive context in memory while it runs. A production agent therefore needs a runtime that allows long sessions and isolates users, a way to expose tools such as APIs and functions, memory that survives across sessions, identity for both the caller and the services the agent touches, and access to shared knowledge. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides these as separate managed building blocks: Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Identity, and tools such as Code Interpreter, which can be combined with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The older Amazon Bedrock Agents, now called Agents Classic, closed to new customers on 2026-07-30, so new agent designs use AgentCore. On the exam, map each requirement in the stem to one building block rather than looking for a single service that does everything.

concepts.heading: AgentCore Runtime and Code Interpreter
concepts.body: AgentCore Runtime is a serverless host for agents and tools. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic, so existing code written with LangGraph, CrewAI, Strands Agents, or custom logic runs unchanged, with models in or outside Bedrock. Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and file system that is cleaned up when the session ends, so one session cannot see another's data, and sessions can run for up to 8 hours. Runtime also authenticates inbound callers with IAM or OAuth tokens. When an agent writes code at run time, that code is untrusted because a prompt injection hidden in user data could steer it. AgentCore Code Interpreter runs such code in a separate, managed sandbox with its own files, where network access can be disabled, so the code never runs with the agent's credentials. Exam signal: multi-hour, isolated agent sessions without servers mean Runtime; model-generated code means Code Interpreter, never exec inside the agent.

concepts.heading: AgentCore Gateway: Turning Existing APIs into Tools
concepts.body: Agents act through tools, each with a name, description, and input schema. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for listing and calling tools, but exposing existing APIs over MCP usually means writing and hosting an MCP server for each one. AgentCore Gateway removes that work. Its targets can be OpenAPI specifications, Smithy models, Lambda functions, and existing MCP servers, and it exposes them all as one MCP endpoint. Inbound authorization checks the agent's OAuth token, for example one issued by Amazon Cognito, and outbound credentials for each target are handled through AgentCore Identity. Semantic tool search lets an agent ask for tools that match its task instead of loading hundreds of tool definitions into every prompt, which saves tokens and improves tool choice. Example: 30 REST APIs with OpenAPI specs and 12 Lambda functions become tools behind one gateway. Exam signal: many APIs as MCP tools with OAuth and no per-API servers means AgentCore Gateway.

concepts.heading: AgentCore Memory, AgentCore Identity, and Knowledge Bases as Tools
concepts.body: Agents need two kinds of knowledge. Shared domain knowledge, such as 40,000 policy documents, belongs in an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base that the agent calls as a retrieval tool through the Retrieve API, so it reads only the relevant passages and stays current through re-syncs. Per-user context belongs in AgentCore Memory: short-term memory keeps events within a session, and long-term memory strategies (user preferences, semantic facts, summaries) extract durable facts and store them per user namespace, so a session days later retrieves a few facts instead of replaying whole transcripts. When the agent acts in third-party services for a person, AgentCore Identity holds OAuth credential providers for services such as Google or Salesforce; the user consents once, a token vault stores and refreshes the user's tokens, and the agent receives a per-user access token at call time without storing refresh tokens. On the exam, full histories pasted into prompts and shared admin API keys are the wrong answers.

concepts.heading: SageMaker AI Endpoint Types
concepts.body: Amazon SageMaker AI offers four main ways to serve a model, and the request shape decides. Real-time endpoints run chosen instances, give the lowest and most consistent latency, and bill per instance-hour even when idle. Serverless inference provisions compute per request from a memory size and maximum concurrency you set, scales to zero, and bills for compute time used; it runs on CPU only and the first request after idle can see a cold start. Asynchronous inference queues requests whose input and output live in S3, supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing times up to one hour, notifies through Amazon SNS, and can scale to zero instances on a backlog metric. Batch transform scores whole datasets in S3 offline. Example: a CPU fraud model with hours of idle time and a synchronous API fits serverless; 800 MB scans taking 20 minutes on a GPU fit asynchronous. Exam signal: payload size, duration, GPU need, and idle time.

concepts.heading: Hosting Many Models and Releasing Safely
concepts.body: When many models share a framework, multi-model endpoints put thousands of small artifacts behind one endpoint: each model loads from S3 on first use (the TargetModel parameter), is cached, and is evicted when memory is needed, at the cost of a cold load on first call. Multi-container endpoints host a small number of different containers, up to 15, on one endpoint. For several large models on GPUs, inference components let each model declare the accelerators and memory it needs, share instances, and scale its own copy count independently, down to zero. Releases have two separate risks. A shadow test sends a copy of live requests to a new version as a shadow variant while callers receive only production answers, which measures real latency and errors. Deployment guardrails then perform blue/green updates with canary or linear traffic shifting, a baking period, and automatic rollback when CloudWatch alarms fire. Exam signal: compare on live traffic, then release gradually with alarm-based rollback.

examPoints: A question about hosting existing agent code with per-session isolation and multi-hour runs is testing AgentCore Runtime, and exposing many APIs or Lambda functions as MCP tools with OAuth is testing AgentCore Gateway.

A question where an agent must remember a user across sessions or act in SaaS tools as that user is testing AgentCore Memory long-term strategies and AgentCore Identity token vaults, with a knowledge base as the shared-knowledge tool.

A question about SageMaker AI hosting is testing the match between request shape and endpoint type: real-time, serverless (CPU, idle-heavy), asynchronous (large, long, notify), batch transform, multi-model endpoints, or inference components.

quiz.q: A consulting firm is building an assistant on AgentCore Runtime that books meetings in each consultant's own Google Calendar. Every action must use the individual user's consent and permissions, the agent code must never store or refresh OAuth refresh tokens, and users must not sign in again for each request. Which design meets these requirements?
choices: Store one Google Workspace administrator API key in AWS Secrets Manager and have the agent filter calendar results by the signed-in user's email address
Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to exchange each user's token for temporary AWS credentials and sign the calendar API calls with those credentials
Run the OAuth flow inside the agent, encrypt each user's refresh token with AWS KMS, and keep the tokens in a DynamoDB table keyed by user ID
Configure AgentCore Identity with an OAuth credential provider so that user-consented tokens are kept in its token vault and supplied to the agent per call
quiz.explain: AgentCore Identity stores and refreshes each user's consented tokens in its vault and hands the agent a per-user access token, so the agent never handles refresh tokens. Choice B fails because identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials, which Google's APIs do not accept.

quiz.q: A medical imaging startup runs a GPU segmentation model on 3D scans of 300 to 800 MB that take 8 to 20 minutes each. Hospitals upload scans in bursts with long quiet periods. Hospitals must be notified when results are ready, and the startup wants to pay nothing for GPU instances when there is no work. Which SageMaker AI option meets these requirements?
choices: A serverless inference endpoint with the largest memory size and provisioned concurrency so that bursts of scans start without cold starts
An asynchronous inference endpoint with S3 input and output, SNS notifications, and auto scaling on backlog with a minimum of zero instances
A real-time endpoint on GPU instances with target tracking auto scaling, and clients that hold the connection open until each result returns
A multi-model endpoint on GPU instances that loads the model from S3 on first use and unloads it after a period with no invocations
quiz.explain: Asynchronous inference accepts large S3 payloads and long processing, queues bursts, notifies through SNS, and can scale GPU instances to zero between bursts. Choice A fails because serverless inference has no GPUs and its payload and timeout limits are far below 800 MB and 20 minutes.

days.recap: Build agents from AgentCore parts (Runtime for isolated long sessions, Gateway for MCP tools, Memory for cross-session context, Identity for per-user OAuth, Code Interpreter for untrusted code) plus knowledge bases as tools, and serve ML models on the SageMaker AI option that matches latency, payload, duration, GPU, and idle-time needs, releasing with shadow tests and guarded canaries.

days.title: Hybrid Connectivity and DNS: Redundant Direct Connect, VPN, Transit Gateway, and Route 53 Resolver

concepts.heading: Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN Trade-offs
concepts.body: AWS Site-to-Site VPN builds IPsec tunnels over the internet between a customer gateway and a virtual private gateway, transit gateway, or Cloud WAN. It can be set up in hours and costs little, but bandwidth and latency vary with internet conditions, and a standard tunnel carries only about 1.25 Gbps. AWS Direct Connect is a private physical connection from a Direct Connect location into AWS, giving consistent bandwidth and predictable latency, but a new connection usually takes weeks to provision. Traffic over Direct Connect is not encrypted by default; MACsec on supported dedicated connections or a VPN running over the Direct Connect link adds encryption when policy requires it. A Direct Connect gateway lets one connection reach VPCs and transit gateways in many Regions and accounts. On the exam, fast or temporary connectivity points to VPN, sustained high-throughput or latency-sensitive traffic points to Direct Connect, and encryption over Direct Connect points to MACsec or VPN over Direct Connect.

concepts.heading: Designing Redundancy and Failover
concepts.body: A single Direct Connect connection is a single point of failure: the circuit, the device, or the whole Direct Connect location can fail. AWS resiliency guidance scales with need: a Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN as backup is the low-cost option; two connections at two different Direct Connect locations give high resiliency; and two connections at each of two locations give maximum resiliency, surviving the loss of a location plus a device. Failover is driven by BGP. When the same prefix is learned over both Direct Connect and VPN, AWS prefers the Direct Connect path, and Bidirectional Forwarding Detection speeds up failure detection. To steer active and standby links, prepend AS_PATH on routes advertised over the backup so AWS prefers the primary for return traffic, and raise local preference on premises for outbound traffic. On the exam, surviving the loss of a whole location with consistent bandwidth requires connections at two locations, not two ports in one.

concepts.heading: Transit Gateway as the Hybrid Hub
concepts.body: AWS Transit Gateway connects many VPCs and on-premises networks through one Regional hub with transitive routing. On-premises networks attach through a Direct Connect gateway with a transit virtual interface associated with the transit gateway, or through VPN attachments. With equal-cost multi-path routing enabled, several VPN tunnels can be used together to add bandwidth beyond one tunnel. Transit gateway route tables segment traffic: for example, production VPCs and the on-premises attachment share one route table, while development VPCs use another that has no route to production. For several Regions, one Direct Connect gateway can associate transit gateways in multiple Regions, and transit gateways can be peered across Regions. Example: a data center reaches 80 VPCs in two Regions through two Direct Connect connections into one Direct Connect gateway, with a VPN backup attached to each transit gateway. Exam signal: many VPCs plus on-premises with segmentation means Transit Gateway, with Cloud WAN when the network is global and policy-driven.

concepts.heading: Route 53 Resolver Endpoints and Conditional Forwarding
concepts.body: Every VPC has a built-in Route 53 Resolver, but on-premises DNS servers cannot query it directly, and it does not know on-premises zones. Resolver endpoints bridge the two. An inbound endpoint places network interfaces in your VPC so on-premises DNS servers can conditionally forward queries, for example for app.internal or for AWS service names that resolve to interface endpoints, to resolve private AWS names. An outbound endpoint plus a forwarding rule sends queries for on-premises domains, such as corp.example.com, from VPCs to on-premises DNS servers. Endpoints should have interfaces in at least two Availability Zones. Forwarding rules can be shared with other accounts through AWS RAM and associated with their VPCs, so one central DNS VPC serves the whole organization over Direct Connect or Transit Gateway. On the exam, remember the direction: inbound endpoints answer questions coming from on premises, and outbound endpoints with rules send questions to on premises.

concepts.heading: Private Hosted Zones, Split-Horizon DNS, and Route 53 Profiles
concepts.body: A Route 53 private hosted zone answers queries only from the VPCs associated with it. Associating a VPC from another account needs an authorization from the zone's account. Split-horizon DNS uses a public hosted zone and a private hosted zone with the same name, such as example.com: clients on the internet get public answers, while resources in associated VPCs get private answers such as internal load balancer addresses. On-premises clients see the private answers only when their DNS forwards the domain to a Resolver inbound endpoint. At scale, a Route 53 Profile bundles private hosted zones, Resolver rules, and DNS Firewall rule groups, is shared through AWS RAM, and is associated with VPCs, so adding a zone to the Profile updates every associated VPC. Exam signal: same name, different answers inside and outside means split-horizon; many VPCs needing the same DNS setup means Profiles.

examPoints: A question demanding consistent bandwidth that survives the loss of a Direct Connect location is testing connections at two locations, while a low-cost backup path is testing VPN behind Direct Connect with BGP preference.

A question about on-premises servers resolving private AWS names is testing a Resolver inbound endpoint with conditional forwarding; AWS workloads resolving on-premises names is testing an outbound endpoint with forwarding rules shared through RAM.
A question where one domain must return internal addresses inside VPCs and public addresses outside is testing split-horizon DNS with same-named public and private hosted zones.

quiz.q: A company connects its data center to a shared services VPC over Direct Connect and Transit Gateway. On-premises servers must resolve records in the private hosted zone app.internal, and EC2 instances in 50 VPCs across several accounts must resolve names in the on-premises domain corp.example.com. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Create a Resolver inbound endpoint for on-premises queries about app.internal and an outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.example.com, shared to the VPCs with AWS RAM
Associate the app.internal private hosted zone with the on-premises network through the Direct Connect gateway and create a public hosted zone for corp.example.com
Run BIND servers on EC2 instances in each VPC, point each VPC's DHCP options set at them, and copy the on-premises zone files to them every night
Create a Resolver outbound endpoint for on-premises queries about app.internal and an inbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.example.com, shared with AWS RAM
quiz.explain: On-premises DNS forwards app.internal to the inbound endpoint, and the outbound endpoint with a RAM-shared forwarding rule sends corp.example.com queries from every VPC to on-premises servers. Choice D has the endpoint directions reversed: forwarding rules work only with outbound endpoints, and on-premises queries arrive at inbound endpoints.

quiz.q: A trading firm needs consistent, high-bandwidth connectivity from its data center to AWS. The connection must keep the same bandwidth even if an entire Direct Connect location becomes unavailable, and the firm reaches VPCs in two Regions through transit gateways. Which design meets these requirements?
choices: One Direct Connect connection at one location, plus a second connection that terminates on a different AWS device in that same location
Two Site-to-Site VPN connections to each transit gateway with equal-cost multi-path routing across all tunnels and no Direct Connect
Direct Connect connections at two different Direct Connect locations, with BGP sessions to a Direct Connect gateway associated with both transit gateways
One Direct Connect connection with a link aggregation group of four ports so that a failed port moves traffic to the remaining ports
quiz.explain: Connections at two separate locations survive the loss of one location with dedicated bandwidth, and one Direct Connect gateway reaches transit gateways in both Regions. Choice A protects against a device failure but not against the whole location going down, which is the stated requirement.

days.recap: Use VPN for speed and backup and Direct Connect for consistent bandwidth, build redundancy across Direct Connect locations with BGP steering, hub hybrid routing on Transit Gateway with a Direct Connect gateway, and solve hybrid DNS with Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints, RAM-shared rules, private hosted zones, split-horizon zones, and Route 53 Profiles.

days.title: Hybrid Data Sync, Legacy Integration, and Hybrid Compute

concepts.heading: Synchronizing Files with AWS DataSync
concepts.body: AWS DataSync moves and synchronizes file and object data between on-premises storage, other clouds, and AWS storage. An agent deployed near the source reads NFS or SMB shares, HDFS, or object storage, and DataSync writes to Amazon S3, Amazon EFS, or Amazon FSx. Each task can run on a schedule and copies only data that changed since the last run, verifies data integrity, encrypts data in transit, and can be limited to a bandwidth cap so business traffic is not starved. Over Direct Connect, a VPC endpoint keeps traffic private. Example: a nightly task copies new lab results from an on-premises NFS share to an S3 bucket for analytics, capped at 500 Mbps during working hours. DataSync is a transfer service, not a mount point: applications do not read files through it. On the exam, recurring or one-time bulk copies with verification and scheduling point to DataSync, while ongoing low-latency file access from on premises points to Storage Gateway.

concepts.heading: Ongoing Hybrid Storage with AWS Storage Gateway
concepts.body: AWS Storage Gateway is a virtual or hardware appliance on premises that presents standard storage protocols while keeping data in AWS. Amazon S3 File Gateway exposes NFS or SMB file shares; each file is stored as an S3 object, and a local cache keeps recently used data close to applications for low-latency reads. When other systems change objects directly in S3, a cache refresh makes them visible on the share. Volume Gateway presents iSCSI block volumes, either cached with the primary data in AWS or stored with the full copy on premises, backed up as EBS snapshots. Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library to existing backup software and archives tapes to S3 Glacier storage classes. Example: an imaging application keeps writing to an SMB share, while the files land in S3 for analytics and lifecycle tiering. On the exam, an application that cannot change protocols but should use cloud storage with a local cache points to Storage Gateway.

concepts.heading: Partner File Exchange with AWS Transfer Family
concepts.body: Many businesses still exchange files with partners over SFTP, FTPS, FTP, or AS2. AWS Transfer Family provides fully managed endpoints for these protocols, storing files directly in Amazon S3 or Amazon EFS, so partners keep their existing clients and scripts. Users can be service managed with SSH keys, or authenticated through a custom identity provider (for example a Lambda function) or Active Directory, and each user is mapped to an IAM role and a home directory. Managed workflows run steps after upload, such as copying, tagging, decrypting, or calling a Lambda function to validate the file. A VPC-hosted endpoint with Elastic IP addresses gives fixed addresses that partners can allowlist. Example: 300 suppliers upload invoices over SFTP to s3://invoices/<supplier>/, and a workflow tags each file for downstream processing. On the exam, partners who must keep using SFTP while the company wants no servers to run points to Transfer Family rather than EC2-based SFTP servers or DataSync.

concepts.heading: Modernizing Legacy Integrations with Transformations
concepts.body: Legacy systems often speak formats and protocols that new services do not. API Gateway REST APIs translate HTTP payloads with mapping templates written in Velocity Template Language on non-proxy integrations: a template reads JSON fields and emits a SOAP envelope, and a response template turns the XML reply back into JSON. A private integration reaches an on-premises service through a VPC link to a load balancer whose targets are on-premises IP addresses over Direct Connect. HTTP APIs are cheaper but cannot rewrite request bodies. For messaging, Amazon MQ runs managed Apache ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ with the same protocols and JMS APIs, so legacy clients change only the broker URL; a Lambda event source mapping on an Amazon MQ queue can parse each message into JSON and publish it to EventBridge for new microservices. On the exam, configuration-only JSON to SOAP translation means REST API mapping templates, and JMS clients means Amazon MQ.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Compute: Outposts, Local Zones, and Wavelength
concepts.body: AWS Outposts installs AWS-owned, AWS-managed racks or servers in your own data center. Outposts subnets extend a VPC from the parent Region, and you run EC2, EBS, and services such as Amazon RDS, Amazon ECS, and Amazon EKS on them, while AWS monitors and replaces the hardware. An Outpost needs a service link back to its parent Region and is ordered for a multi-year term. AWS Local Zones are AWS facilities in large metro areas; you opt in, add a Local Zone subnet to a VPC in the parent Region, and run supported resources with pay-as-you-go pricing for single-digit millisecond latency to local users. AWS Wavelength places compute inside telecom carriers' 5G networks for mobile devices. Example: artists in Los Angeles who need single-digit latency for a few weeks use the Los Angeles Local Zone. Exam signal: data must stay in your building means Outposts; low latency in a metro with no hardware means Local Zones.

concepts.heading: Containers on Your Own Hardware: EKS Anywhere, ECS Anywhere, and EKS Hybrid Nodes
concepts.body: Three options run AWS-managed container orchestration on hardware you own, and the deciding factor is how much they depend on a Region. Amazon EKS Anywhere is software that creates and operates complete Kubernetes clusters, control plane included, on VMware vSphere, bare metal, Nutanix, or CloudStack using EKS Distro, the same distribution as Amazon EKS; it supports air-gapped installs from a local registry, and paid support comes from an EKS Anywhere Enterprise Subscription. Amazon EKS Hybrid Nodes attach on-premises machines as worker nodes to an EKS cluster whose control plane stays in a Region, so they need continuous private connectivity. Amazon ECS Anywhere registers external servers as ECS capacity; their agents connect outbound to Regional ECS and Systems Manager endpoints. None of these provides managed AWS databases or EBS on premises. On the exam, a site with no path to any Region means EKS Anywhere, and Kubernetes on premises managed from a Regional control plane means Hybrid Nodes.

examPoints: A question about recurring bulk copies with verification is testing DataSync, ongoing low-latency file access from unchanged on-premises applications is testing S3 File Gateway, and partners who must keep SFTP is testing Transfer Family.

A question about putting a modern JSON API or event bus in front of a legacy SOAP or JMS system with configuration rather than code is testing API Gateway REST mapping templates or Amazon MQ with a Lambda event source mapping.

A question about hybrid compute is testing the constraint: data in your own building with AWS services means Outposts, metro latency without hardware means Local Zones, and an air-gapped site means EKS Anywhere.

quiz.q: A manufacturer exchanges files with 300 suppliers who use their own SFTP scripts and will not change them. Files must land in Amazon S3, each upload must be tagged for downstream processing, and the company does not want to run or patch servers. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Run an SFTP server on an EC2 Auto Scaling group behind a Network Load Balancer, and copy each uploaded file to S3 with a cron job on every instance
Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that stores files in S3, with service-managed supplier users and a managed workflow that tags each upload
Deploy an S3 File Gateway at each supplier site so that suppliers copy files to a local SMB share that writes the files to the company's bucket
Schedule an AWS DataSync task at each supplier site that copies new files from the supplier's outbound folder to the company's bucket every hour
quiz.explain: Transfer Family provides a managed SFTP endpoint backed by S3 that the suppliers' scripts can use unchanged, and a managed workflow tags each file after upload. Choice C fails because it requires installing gateways at 300 supplier sites and switches the suppliers from SFTP to SMB.

quiz.q: A hospital's imaging application writes studies to an SMB file share and frequently re-reads recent studies, so reads must stay low latency on premises. The hospital wants to stop buying file server capacity, the files must be stored as objects in Amazon S3 for analytics, and the application cannot be changed. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Run an AWS DataSync task every 15 minutes from the existing file server to S3, and keep the application writing to the existing file server
Mount an Amazon EFS file system on premises over Direct Connect, and run a nightly job that copies the EFS contents into the S3 bucket
Create an AWS Transfer Family FTPS server so that the application uploads each study to S3 as soon as it finishes writing it locally
Deploy an Amazon S3 File Gateway on premises that exposes an SMB share with a local cache and stores each file as an object in S3
quiz.explain: S3 File Gateway presents the same SMB protocol, keeps recent files in a local cache for fast reads, and stores every file as an S3 object, so local capacity no longer grows. Choice A copies data to S3 but the hospital keeps buying file server capacity, because the existing server still holds every file.

days.recap: Copy and sync data with DataSync, keep unchanged applications on cloud storage with Storage Gateway, exchange partner files with Transfer Family, wrap legacy systems with API Gateway mapping templates and Amazon MQ plus Lambda, and choose Outposts, Local Zones, Wavelength, EKS Anywhere, EKS Hybrid Nodes, or ECS Anywhere by where data must live and how much the site can depend on a Region.

days.title: Network Architectures: Multi-VPC Connectivity, IPAM, Inspection, IPv6, and Global Routing

concepts.heading: Peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, and Cloud WAN
concepts.body: VPC peering is a direct, non-transitive link between two VPCs; it is simple, but a full mesh grows with the square of the VPC count and peering does not work with overlapping CIDRs. AWS Transit Gateway is a Regional hub with transitive routing and route tables for segmentation, the default for dozens or hundreds of VPCs plus on-premises networks. AWS PrivateLink exposes one service, not a network: a provider puts a Network Load Balancer behind an endpoint service, and consumers create interface endpoints in their own VPCs, which also works across overlapping CIDRs. AWS Cloud WAN builds a global network from a JSON core network policy: segments such as prod, dev, and shared span Regions, attachment policies place new VPCs into segments by tag, and routes propagate between Regions automatically. Exam signal: a few VPCs means peering, many VPCs in a Region means Transit Gateway, one service means PrivateLink, many Regions with policy segments means Cloud WAN.

concepts.heading: IP Address Planning with IPAM and Subnet Strategy
concepts.body: Overlapping CIDRs block peering and routing later, so large organizations plan address space centrally with Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM). You build a pool hierarchy, for example a top-level pool 10.0.0.0/8, Regional pools such as 10.16.0.0/12 for eu-west-1, and prod and dev pools beneath them. Pools are shared with accounts through AWS RAM, and allocation rules set allowed netmask lengths and required tags. When a team creates a VPC with an IPAM pool ID, IPAM hands out the next free, non-overlapping block; it also monitors CIDRs created by hand and flags overlapping or unmanaged ones.
