Inside each VPC, a common subnet strategy uses one public, one private, and one isolated subnet per Availability Zone: public for load balancers and NAT gateways, private for application tiers, isolated with no internet route for databases. On the exam, preventing overlap across hundreds of accounts points to IPAM pools, not spreadsheets or Config checks after the fact.

concepts.heading: Centralized Traffic Inspection
concepts.body: Many organizations route traffic between VPCs, to the internet, and to on premises through a central inspection VPC. With AWS Network Firewall, the inspection VPC holds firewall endpoints in each Availability Zone, and transit gateway route tables send spoke traffic through them; stateful rules can match domains, protocols, and Suricata-compatible signatures. Appliance mode must be enabled on the inspection VPC's transit gateway attachment so that both directions of a flow use the same Availability Zone; without it, return traffic can hit a different firewall endpoint and stateful inspection drops the connection. For third-party firewalls, a Gateway Load Balancer distributes traffic to a fleet of appliances using GENEVE encapsulation, and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in spoke or inspection VPCs act as route targets. A centralized egress VPC with NAT gateways can share the same path. On the exam, asymmetric drops through a stateful firewall behind a transit gateway point to appliance mode.

concepts.heading: Layered Filtering: AWS WAF, Security Groups, Network ACLs, and Flow Logs
concepts.body: Each control works at a different layer. AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests on CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway, and other supported resources, using managed rule groups (for example against SQL injection), custom rules, and rate-based rules that block clients exceeding a request count. Security groups are stateful, allow-only rules attached to network interfaces, and can reference other security groups, so an app tier can accept traffic only from the load balancer's group. Network ACLs are stateless allow and deny rules at the subnet boundary, evaluated in rule-number order, so return traffic on ephemeral ports must be allowed explicitly; they are useful for blocking a specific CIDR. VPC Flow Logs record metadata about accepted and rejected flows (addresses, ports, action, bytes) to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Firehose for troubleshooting and audit; they never contain packet payloads. On the exam, deny a known bad IP range means NACL, application attacks mean WAF, and who talked to whom means Flow Logs.

concepts.heading: IPv6 Adoption and Dual-Stack Migration
concepts.body: IPv6 removes address exhaustion and overlapping-CIDR pain and avoids charges for public IPv4 addresses. A dual-stack VPC adds an IPv6 block (Amazon-provided or from IPAM) alongside IPv4, and each subnet gets its own IPv6 block, usually a /64 (netmasks from /44 to /64 are allowed); resources then hold both address types, so migration can be gradual. IPv6 addresses are globally unique, so private subnets use an egress-only internet gateway, which allows outbound IPv6 connections and blocks inbound ones, the IPv6 equivalent of a NAT gateway's role. IPv6-only subnets are possible for new workloads; to reach IPv4-only services, enable DNS64 on the subnet so Resolver synthesizes IPv6 addresses, and route the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96 to a NAT gateway, which performs NAT64. Load balancers, security groups, NACLs, and route tables all need IPv6 entries. Example: a dual-stack ALB accepts IPv6 clients while targets remain IPv4. On the exam, outbound-only IPv6 means egress-only internet gateway, and IPv6-only workloads calling IPv4 services means DNS64 plus NAT64.

concepts.heading: Global Traffic Routing: Route 53 Policies and Global Accelerator
concepts.body: Route 53 routing policies decide which answer DNS returns. Failover sends traffic to a secondary record when a health check fails; weighted splits traffic by percentage for gradual rollouts; latency-based returns the Region with the lowest measured latency; geolocation answers by the user's country or continent, useful for residency and localization; geoproximity routes by distance with an adjustable bias; multivalue answer returns several healthy records; IP-based routing maps client CIDR blocks to endpoints. Health checks can probe endpoints or follow CloudWatch alarms. All DNS-based answers depend on client caching and TTLs. AWS Global Accelerator instead gives two static anycast IPv4 addresses announced from edge locations; traffic enters the nearest edge, rides the AWS backbone, and goes to the closest healthy endpoint group. Failover happens within seconds without DNS changes, traffic dials drain a Region, and it handles TCP and UDP. Exam signal: fast failover independent of DNS caching or fixed IPs for allowlisting means Global Accelerator.

examPoints: A question about connecting many VPCs, one shared service, or a multi-Region segmented network is testing Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, or Cloud WAN respectively, and preventing CIDR overlap across accounts is testing IPAM pools.

A question about inspecting east-west or egress traffic is testing Network Firewall or Gateway Load Balancer in an inspection VPC with transit gateway appliance mode, layered with WAF, security groups, NACLs, and Flow Logs.

A question about IPv6 is testing dual-stack subnets, egress-only internet gateways, and DNS64 with NAT64, while global routing questions test Route 53 policies versus Global Accelerator's DNS-independent failover.

quiz.q: A company has 300 VPCs in 90 accounts. Acquisitions left several overlapping CIDR ranges, and the network team now wants every new VPC to receive a non-overlapping CIDR automatically, with Regional and environment boundaries enforced, and wants to see which existing ranges overlap. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Keep a list of assigned CIDRs in a shared S3 bucket, and add an AWS Config rule that flags any VPC whose CIDR appears twice in the list
Create every new VPC with the same 10.0.0.0/16 range, and connect all VPCs to each other only through AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints
Create Amazon VPC IPAM pools per Region and environment under a top-level pool, share them through AWS RAM, and have new VPCs allocate CIDRs from them
Use static routes in transit gateway route tables for each new VPC, and have the network team reject any attachment whose CIDR conflicts
quiz.explain: IPAM pools hand out free, non-overlapping blocks within Regional and environment boundaries, RAM sharing makes them available to every account, and IPAM monitoring flags existing overlaps. Choice B fails because PrivateLink exposes individual services, not general network routing between VPCs.

quiz.q: A company sends traffic between spoke VPCs through an inspection VPC that holds AWS Network Firewall endpoints in two Availability Zones and is attached to a transit gateway. Some connections between spokes in different Availability Zones time out because return traffic passes through the firewall endpoint in the other zone. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's transit gateway attachment so that both directions of each flow use the same Availability Zone
Replace the Network Firewall stateful rule groups with stateless rule groups so that the firewall no longer needs to track each connection
Add network ACL rules to the inspection VPC subnets that allow all ephemeral ports so that return traffic is accepted in either zone
Create VPC peering connections between each pair of spoke VPCs so that traffic across Availability Zones avoids the inspection VPC
quiz.explain: Appliance mode makes the transit gateway keep both directions of a flow on the same network interface, so the stateful firewall sees the whole connection. Choice D removes the timeouts only by bypassing inspection, which defeats the purpose of the design.

days.recap: Pick peering, Transit Gateway, PrivateLink, or Cloud WAN by scale and scope, plan addresses with IPAM pools and tiered subnets, inspect traffic centrally with Network Firewall or Gateway Load Balancer and appliance mode, layer WAF, security groups, NACLs, and Flow Logs, adopt IPv6 with dual-stack, egress-only gateways, and DNS64/NAT64, and route globally with Route 53 policies or Global Accelerator.

days.title: Data, Storage, and Database Architectures: Lakehouse, Pipelines, Sharing, Databases, Storage, and Caching

concepts.heading: Lakehouse Architecture: S3, Iceberg, Lake Formation, and Redshift Spectrum
concepts.body: A data lake keeps raw and curated data in Amazon S3 in open formats such as Parquet, cataloged in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Plain Parquet files are immutable, so deleting one person's rows means rewriting files yourself. Apache Iceberg tables add a metadata layer that turns the lake into a lakehouse: DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE INTO with ACID guarantees, time travel to query a table as of a past timestamp, and schema and partition evolution without rewriting data. Spark on EMR, Athena, and Amazon Redshift can all work on the same Iceberg tables. Redshift Spectrum lets Redshift query S3 data through an external schema backed by the Glue Data Catalog, joining it with warehouse tables. AWS Lake Formation adds table, column, row, and cell permissions: LF-Tags grant access by tag expression, and data filters restrict rows such as region = 'emea'. Exam signal: privacy deletes, audit time travel, and several engines on one copy mean Iceberg.

concepts.heading: Real-Time and Batch Analytics Pipelines
concepts.body: Pick pipeline services by latency and by how much infrastructure the team wants to run. Amazon MSK provides managed Apache Kafka for event streaming when producers and consumers already speak Kafka. Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion reads Kinesis Data Streams or MSK topics directly into a materialized view with auto refresh, reaching dashboards within seconds with no S3 staging and only SQL. Amazon EMR runs Spark, Hive, and other frameworks; EMR Serverless runs a job without a cluster and bills only while the job runs, which suits a nightly 90-minute Spark job. Amazon AppFlow pulls data from SaaS applications such as Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zendesk into S3 or Redshift on a schedule, on demand, or on an event, with no integration code. AWS DMS replicates databases and cannot read Kafka or SaaS sources. Exam signal: SaaS data without code means AppFlow, occasional Spark means EMR Serverless, Kafka or Kinesis into Redshift in seconds means streaming ingestion.

concepts.heading: Data Cataloging and Cross-Account Sharing
concepts.body: The AWS Glue Data Catalog is the shared metadata layer for S3 data, used by Athena, EMR, Redshift Spectrum, and Glue jobs. To share a governed lake across accounts without copying data, the producer account grants Lake Formation permissions on databases, tables, or columns, by name or by LF-Tags, to consumer accounts, an OU, or the organization; behind the scenes this uses AWS RAM. In each consumer account, the data lake administrator creates resource links that point to the shared databases and grants local roles access, and queries read the producer's S3 data through Lake Formation credentials. When two companies must analyze combined data and neither may see the other's rows, AWS Clean Rooms keeps each party's data in its own account: configured tables join a collaboration, and analysis rules such as aggregation with minimum thresholds limit queries to approved aggregates. Exam signal: same organization, no copies means Lake Formation sharing; different companies, no row access means Clean Rooms.

concepts.heading: Selecting a Database by Workload
concepts.body: Start from access patterns, consistency needs, and scale, not from familiarity. Amazon RDS runs managed open-source and commercial engines for relational workloads that need joins and transactions, especially when engine compatibility matters. Amazon Aurora is a MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine with storage replicated across three Availability Zones, fast failover, and up to 15 low-latency replicas; Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine increments for variable load. Amazon DynamoDB is a serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, but access patterns must be designed up front around partition and sort keys and secondary indexes, since it has no ad hoc joins. Amazon Redshift is a columnar data warehouse for analytical queries over large data sets, not for high-rate single-row transactions. Example: a shopping cart at millions of requests per second fits DynamoDB; order reporting across years fits Redshift. On the exam, joins and transactions mean relational, known key lookups at extreme scale mean DynamoDB.

concepts.heading: Database High Availability and Scaling
concepts.body: Different features solve different problems. An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance deployment keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone for automatic failover; that standby does not serve reads. Read replicas are asynchronous copies that scale reads and can be promoted, including across Regions. Aurora replicas share the cluster storage, serve reads through the reader endpoint, and act as failover targets. Aurora Global Database replicates a cluster from one primary Region to secondary Regions with typical lag under one second; secondaries serve local reads and can be promoted to primary with a recovery time typically measured in minutes, but only the primary accepts writes. DynamoDB global tables replicate every item to every replica Region and accept writes in all of them, with eventual consistency between Regions. Example: a reporting tool overloads an RDS primary that must also survive an AZ failure, so Multi-AZ handles failover and a read replica takes the reports. Exam signal: availability means Multi-AZ, read scale means replicas, global writes mean global tables.

concepts.heading: Storage Choices and Caching Strategies
concepts.body: Match storage to access pattern. Amazon S3 is object storage for any scale. Amazon EBS gives block volumes to one instance: gp3 sets IOPS and throughput independently of size, and io2 serves the most demanding databases. Amazon EFS is elastic NFS shared by many instances, containers, and Lambda functions across Availability Zones. Amazon FSx provides FSx for Windows File Server (SMB, Active Directory), FSx for Lustre (high-throughput HPC and ML, linked to S3), FSx for NetApp ONTAP (multiprotocol, snapshots, replication), and FSx for OpenZFS. Caching removes repeated reads: ElastiCache (Valkey, Redis OSS, or Memcached) is a general in-memory cache, used with lazy loading (fill on miss, set a TTL) or write-through (update cache on every write). DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an API-compatible, write-through cache only for DynamoDB that delivers microsecond reads for eventually consistent requests. Exam signal: shared Linux files mean EFS, Windows SMB means FSx for Windows, microsecond DynamoDB reads with little code change mean DAX.

examPoints: A question combining row-level deletes, time travel, schema changes, and several engines on S3 data is testing Apache Iceberg in the Glue Data Catalog, governed by Lake Formation LF-Tags and data filters.

A question about sharing data across accounts without copies is testing Lake Formation grants with resource links, while joint analysis between companies without row access is testing AWS Clean Rooms analysis rules.

A question about database resilience is testing the difference between Multi-AZ (availability), read replicas (read scaling), Aurora Global Database (one write Region, fast promotion), and DynamoDB global tables (multi-Region writes).

quiz.q: A media company keeps 400 TB of viewing data in S3 as partitioned Parquet tables used by Spark on Amazon EMR, Amazon Athena, and Amazon Redshift. A new privacy law requires deleting a viewer's rows within 72 hours, auditors want to query tables as they were on past dates, and engineers want to add columns without rewriting data. Which approach meets these requirements with the least custom code?
choices: Keep the Parquet layout and run a nightly EMR job that rewrites each partition containing requested viewers, keeping a dated copy of every table for audits
Load all viewing data into Amazon Redshift tables, delete rows there, and restore Redshift snapshots to new clusters whenever auditors need historic views
Store each viewer's events as separate S3 objects under a viewer ID prefix and use S3 Lifecycle rules to expire the prefixes named in deletion requests
Convert the tables to Apache Iceberg tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog, run DELETE statements for requests, and use time travel queries for audits
quiz.explain: Iceberg adds row-level deletes, snapshot-based time travel, and schema evolution on the same S3 data, and EMR, Athena, and Redshift can all use the tables. Choice C fails because billions of tiny objects make analytics slow, and Lifecycle rules expire objects by age, not by a list of requested viewers.

quiz.q: An RDS for MySQL database must fail over automatically if its Availability Zone fails. A reporting tool also runs heavy queries that slow down the application during business hours. Which solution addresses both problems?
choices: Add two read replicas in other Availability Zones, and point the reporting tool at the primary so that the replicas stay idle for failover
Enable a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment for automatic failover, and add a read replica that the reporting tool connects to for its queries
Enable a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and point the reporting tool at the standby instance so that its reports never touch the primary
Move the data to DynamoDB global tables so that reporting queries run in a second Region while application writes stay in the first one
quiz.explain: Multi-AZ provides synchronous standby and automatic failover, and a read replica offloads the reporting queries. Choice C fails because the standby in a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment cannot serve read traffic; it exists only for failover.

days.recap: Build lakehouses with S3, Iceberg, the Glue Data Catalog, Lake Formation, and Redshift Spectrum; choose MSK, Redshift streaming ingestion, EMR Serverless, or AppFlow by latency and effort; share data with Lake Formation grants or Clean Rooms; select databases by access pattern and scale them with Multi-AZ, replicas, Aurora Global Database, or global tables; and match S3, EBS, EFS, FSx, ElastiCache, and DAX to the access pattern.

days.title: Domain 1 Review: Architecture Design and Implementation Built for the Cloud

concepts.heading: Events, State, and Workflows
concepts.body: Domain 1 starts with cloud-native application design. Messaging services deliver at least once, so consumers must be idempotent with business keys, and ordering is scoped by SQS FIFO message group IDs or Kinesis partition keys chosen with high cardinality. SQS buffers, SNS fans out, EventBridge routes by content and forwards between buses across accounts and Regions with an organization-wide bus policy and StackSet-deployed rules, and global endpoints give publishers Regional failover. Stateless compute keeps sessions and files in DynamoDB, ElastiCache, or S3. Serverless pipelines land Kinesis data through Firehose as partitioned Parquet for Athena, and Lambda stream consumers are tuned with bisect, on-failure destinations, and ParallelizationFactor. Step Functions Standard handles long waits and approvals, Express handles millions of short runs, and Lambda durable functions keep checkpointed workflow logic in code. When a stem lists duplicates, ordering, waits, or volume, translate each word into one of these settings.

concepts.heading: Containers, Ingress, Edge, and Tenancy
concepts.body: For microservices, ECS fits AWS-native simplicity, EKS fits existing Kubernetes investment, and Fargate removes nodes. ECS Service Connect adds discovery, retries, and metrics among ECS services, while VPC Lattice connects mixed compute across VPCs and accounts with IAM auth policies. ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector rescans stored images, and lifecycle policies and immutable tags keep repositories clean and deployments reproducible. Scaling must cover the workload (Lambda concurrency, ECS service auto scaling, HPA) and the capacity (capacity providers, Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter). At the front door, ALB means layer-7 routing and WAF, NLB means TCP, static IPs, and pass-through TLS, API Gateway means API management, and an IngressGroup shares one ALB on EKS. CloudFront Functions handle light viewer logic, Lambda@Edge heavier logic. WebSocket APIs push updates through @connections with heartbeats and reconnects. Multi-tenant designs choose silo, pool, or bridge, and enforce isolation from verified tenant claims.

concepts.heading: Generative AI, Agents, and ML Inference
concepts.body: AI integration is new in this exam version. Bedrock calls should use the Converse API for a provider-neutral format, with fallback logic and model IDs in runtime configuration. Private access uses interface endpoints, private DNS, Resolver inbound endpoints for on-premises callers, and aws:SourceVpce denies. Many accounts use SCP model allowlists, a central role trusted by the OU with aws:PrincipalOrgPaths, or a gateway with API Gateway usage plans. Knowledge bases implement RAG: choose advanced parsing for scans and tables, hierarchical chunking for context, hybrid search and reranking for identifiers, server-side metadata filters for tenants, and a vector store by cost and query rate. AgentCore supplies Runtime, Gateway, Memory, Identity, and Code Interpreter, while Agents Classic is closed to new customers. SageMaker AI endpoints are chosen by request shape, many models share hosting through multi-model endpoints or inference components, and releases use shadow tests and guarded canaries.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Connectivity, Data, and Compute
concepts.body: Hybrid questions combine links, DNS, data movement, and compute placement. Direct Connect gives consistent bandwidth, VPN gives quick setup and backup, connections at two locations survive the loss of a location, and BGP AS_PATH prepending and local preference steer traffic. A Direct Connect gateway with Transit Gateway connects many VPCs in several Regions. DNS uses Resolver inbound endpoints for queries from on premises, outbound endpoints with RAM-shared forwarding rules for queries to on premises, private hosted zones, split-horizon zones, and Route 53 Profiles. Data moves with DataSync for scheduled copies, Storage Gateway for unchanged applications needing a local cache, and Transfer Family for partners on SFTP. Legacy systems gain modern interfaces through API Gateway REST mapping templates and Amazon MQ with a Lambda bridge to EventBridge. Compute lands on Outposts when data must stay in your building, Local Zones for metro latency, and EKS Anywhere for air-gapped Kubernetes.

concepts.heading: Network Architecture
concepts.body: Network design questions reward matching scope to tool. Peering suits a few VPCs, Transit Gateway many VPCs in a Region with segmentation, PrivateLink a single service across accounts or overlapping CIDRs, and Cloud WAN a global network with policy-driven segments. IPAM pools shared through RAM prevent overlapping CIDRs, and subnets are tiered into public, private, and isolated per Availability Zone. Central inspection uses Network Firewall or Gateway Load Balancer appliances in an inspection VPC, with appliance mode on the transit gateway attachment to keep flows symmetric. WAF protects HTTP applications, security groups are stateful and allow-only, NACLs are stateless with explicit denies, and Flow Logs record metadata, never payloads. IPv6 adoption uses dual-stack subnets, egress-only internet gateways, and DNS64 with NAT64 for IPv6-only workloads. Route 53 policies steer DNS answers for failover, weights, latency, and geography, and Global Accelerator gives static anycast IPs with fast, DNS-independent failover.

concepts.heading: Data, Storage, and Databases
concepts.body: Data questions start with the access pattern. Lakehouses keep data in S3 with Apache Iceberg tables in the Glue Data Catalog for row-level changes, time travel, and schema evolution, governed by Lake Formation LF-Tags and data filters, with Redshift Spectrum joining lake and warehouse data. Pipelines use MSK for Kafka, Redshift streaming ingestion for second-level dashboards, EMR or EMR Serverless for Spark, and AppFlow for SaaS sources. Lake Formation grants plus resource links share data across accounts without copies, and Clean Rooms lets companies analyze joint data through aggregation rules. Databases are chosen by joins and transactions (RDS, Aurora), key-based scale (DynamoDB), or analytics (Redshift), and made resilient with Multi-AZ for availability, replicas for reads, Aurora Global Database for fast cross-Region promotion, and DynamoDB global tables for multi-Region writes. Storage maps to EBS, EFS, FSx, or S3, and caching to ElastiCache or DAX.

examPoints: Domain 1 is the largest domain (25 percent), and most of its questions list several requirements at once; underline each requirement and eliminate any choice that misses even one, because distractors usually satisfy all but one.

Watch for the new AI topics (Bedrock integration, RAG, AgentCore, SageMaker AI endpoints) alongside classic networking and data design, and remember that closed services such as Bedrock Agents Classic are not the answer for new designs.

quiz.q: A company runs an HTTPS API on Application Load Balancers in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Clients are corporate systems that cache DNS answers for long periods and allowlist destination IP addresses. If one Region fails, traffic must move to the other within seconds. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Create an AWS Global Accelerator with both ALBs as endpoints, because its static anycast IPs move traffic between Regions without waiting for DNS caches
Create Route 53 latency-based records for both ALBs with a 300-second TTL, because client resolvers will choose the healthy Region at their next lookup
Create a CloudFront distribution with a CloudFront Function that picks a Region for each request from a health flag stored in the function code
Create an EventBridge global endpoint in front of both ALBs, because its Route 53 health check moves requests to the secondary Region automatically
quiz.explain: Global Accelerator provides fixed anycast IPs for allowlisting and shifts traffic to the healthy endpoint group within seconds without any DNS change. Choice D fails because EventBridge global endpoints route events published with PutEvents, not HTTPS requests to load balancers.

quiz.q: A company serves a CPU-based scikit-learn model that takes about 200 ms per request. Traffic is unpredictable: hours with no requests, then a few hundred per minute during campaigns. Callers wait for a synchronous response, and a few seconds of extra latency on the first request after idle time is acceptable. The company wants to minimize cost and avoid managing instances. Which SageMaker AI option fits best?
choices: A real-time endpoint on one small instance with target tracking auto scaling from one to four instances based on invocations per instance
An asynchronous inference endpoint that scales to zero when idle and writes each prediction to S3 for the caller to fetch later
A serverless inference endpoint with enough memory for the model and a maximum concurrency that covers the campaign peaks
A batch transform job started every five minutes by an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that scores all requests collected in S3
quiz.explain: Serverless inference keeps the synchronous API, scales to zero during idle hours, bills only for compute used, and runs CPU models; the cold start is acceptable here. Choice B also scales to zero, but callers no longer get a synchronous response, which breaks the API contract.

days.recap: Domain 1 asks you to design cloud-native applications, integrate AI and ML, connect hybrid environments, build network architectures, and choose data, storage, and database designs; success comes from mapping each stated requirement to the specific feature that satisfies it and rejecting choices that miss any one requirement.

days.title: Identity Federation and Application Auth: IAM Identity Center, SAML, OIDC, SCIM, Cognito, and EKS Pod Identity

concepts.heading: IAM Identity Center as the Workforce Front Door
concepts.body: AWS IAM Identity Center is the standard way to give a company's employees single sign-on into every account of an AWS Organization. You connect one identity source (the built-in directory, Active Directory, or an external identity provider such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID), define permission sets that describe what a job role may do, and assign a group plus a permission set to one or more accounts. Behind the scenes Identity Center creates an IAM role in each assigned account, and users receive short-lived credentials for the role they pick in the access portal or through aws sso login in the CLI. For example, a group named NetworkAdmins can receive a NetworkAdmin permission set in 40 network accounts with one assignment. A scenario with many accounts, an existing corporate directory, and a ban on IAM users points to Identity Center.

concepts.heading: SAML 2.0 Versus OpenID Connect
concepts.body: Both protocols let an identity provider vouch for a user so AWS never stores the password. SAML 2.0 exchanges signed XML assertions through the browser and is the usual protocol between a corporate IdP and IAM Identity Center or an IAM SAML provider (AssumeRoleWithSAML). OpenID Connect is a JSON layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that issues signed JWT ID tokens, and it is common for modern apps and for workloads. A frequent workload example is a CI system such as GitHub Actions: you create an IAM OIDC identity provider for its token issuer, and the pipeline calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity. The role trust policy must check the audience and the sub claim, for example a specific repository and branch, otherwise any pipeline from that issuer could assume the role. On the exam, removing long-lived access keys from an external pipeline signals OIDC federation.

concepts.heading: SCIM for Automatic Provisioning and Deprovisioning
concepts.body: Federation proves who a user is at sign-in, but Identity Center also needs to know which users and groups exist so it can hold assignments. System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) is the protocol that keeps those records in sync. When you enable automatic provisioning in Identity Center, it gives you a SCIM endpoint and an access token that you enter in the external IdP, which then pushes creates, updates, group membership changes and deactivations. Without SCIM, an administrator must create matching users and groups by hand before they can be assigned. The deprovisioning half is what auditors care about: when HR disables an employee in Entra ID, SCIM removes the user from Identity Center and their access to every account ends. A requirement such as access removed automatically within minutes of offboarding is answered by SAML for sign-in plus SCIM for lifecycle.

concepts.heading: Cognito User Pools Versus Identity Pools
concepts.body: Amazon Cognito has two parts that solve different problems. A user pool is a user directory and OAuth 2.0 authorization server for customer-facing applications: it handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA, and federation with social, SAML or OIDC providers, and it issues JWTs (ID, access and refresh tokens). An API Gateway Cognito authorizer validates those tokens directly, and an ALB authenticate action can run the sign-in against the user pool. An identity pool exchanges a token from a user pool or another provider for temporary AWS credentials through STS, mapping users to an authenticated or unauthenticated IAM role, or to roles chosen by rules on token claims. For example, a mobile app that uploads photos straight to Amazon S3 uses a user pool to sign in and an identity pool to get credentials whose policy limits writes to a prefix such as the user's cognito-identity sub. Tokens for your API mean user pool; AWS credentials for the device mean identity pool.

concepts.heading: OAuth 2.0 Flows for Users and Machines
concepts.body: OAuth 2.0 defines grant types, and choosing the right one is a common design question. The authorization code grant with PKCE is the recommended flow for web, single-page and mobile apps: the user signs in at the authorization server, the app receives a short code, and it exchanges the code plus a code verifier for tokens, so no client secret has to live in a browser or phone. The implicit grant, which returned tokens in the URL, is discouraged. The client credentials grant serves machine-to-machine calls with no user present: a backend authenticates with its client ID and secret and receives an access token with custom scopes, such as orders.read, that a Cognito user pool resource server defines. APIs should authorize with access token scopes, not with the ID token, which only describes the user. When a scenario says no user is involved, think client credentials.

concepts.heading: EKS Pod Identity for Kubernetes Workloads
concepts.body: Pods on Amazon EKS should never share the broad IAM role of the worker node. EKS Pod Identity gives each Kubernetes service account its own IAM role: you install the EKS Pod Identity Agent add-on, create a pod identity association that links a cluster, namespace and service account to a role, and the role trusts the service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com. The SDK in the pod then receives temporary credentials for that role only. Compared with the older IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA), Pod Identity needs no per-cluster OIDC provider in IAM and no cluster-specific trust policy, so one role can be reused across many clusters, and it adds session tags such as the cluster name and namespace that ABAC policies can test. For example, the payments service account in the prod namespace maps to a role that may read only one DynamoDB table. Per-pod least privilege on EKS points to Pod Identity.

examPoints: A question that describes thousands of employees in an external directory who need SSO across many accounts and automatic removal when they leave is testing IAM Identity Center with SAML federation plus SCIM provisioning.
A question that contrasts JWTs for an API with temporary AWS credentials for a mobile device is testing the difference between Cognito user pools and identity pools.
A question in which pods on a shared node need different AWS permissions is testing EKS Pod Identity (or IRSA), not the node instance role.

quiz.q: A company with 120 AWS accounts manages 6,000 employees in Microsoft Entra ID. Security requires single sign-on to the AWS accounts with existing corporate credentials, no IAM users, and removal of all AWS access within minutes when HR disables an employee in Entra ID. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
choices: Create an IAM SAML identity provider for Entra ID in every account, map Entra ID groups to roles in each account, and run a nightly script that deletes roles of users who have left
Deploy AWS Directory Service for Microsoft AD, set up a one-way trust to the corporate forest, and connect it to IAM Identity Center so that users are read from the directory on each sign-in
Connect IAM Identity Center to Entra ID as an external identity provider with SAML 2.0, enable SCIM automatic provisioning, and assign Entra ID groups to permission sets on the accounts
Create IAM users for each employee in a central identity account, require MFA, and let users switch roles into the 120 accounts, disabling the IAM user when HR offboards the employee
quiz.explain: Identity Center with SAML handles sign-in across all accounts from one place, and SCIM pushes disables and group changes from Entra ID, so access ends automatically. Choice A needs a provider and role mappings in all 120 accounts plus a custom cleanup script, which is far more effort and not near real time.

quiz.q: A photo-sharing mobile app signs users in with an Amazon Cognito user pool. The app must upload images directly to an Amazon S3 bucket, and each user may write only under a prefix that belongs to that user. The company does not want to embed AWS access keys in the app or proxy uploads through its own servers. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Add a Cognito identity pool that trusts the user pool and maps signed-in users to a role allowing s3:PutObject only under a prefix named with the cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub variable
Add a custom scope for S3 uploads to a user pool resource server, and have the app send the access token as a bearer token in the Authorization header of each S3 PutObject request
Create one IAM user per app user during sign-up with a Lambda trigger, store its access keys in the user pool as a custom attribute, and sign S3 requests with them
Enable an ALB authenticate action with the user pool in front of the bucket, and use the ID token's email claim in the bucket policy to restrict each user to a prefix
quiz.explain: An identity pool exchanges the user pool token for temporary AWS credentials, and the identity ID policy variable limits each user to its own prefix. Choice B fails because S3 does not accept Cognito access tokens; S3 requests must be signed with AWS credentials (SigV4).

days.recap: IAM Identity Center with SAML and SCIM serves the workforce across accounts, OIDC federation removes keys from external workloads, Cognito user pools issue app tokens while identity pools hand out AWS credentials, and EKS Pod Identity gives each pod its own role.

days.title: Least Privilege and Data Perimeters: Cross-Account Roles, Boundaries, ABAC, Access Analyzer, Verified Access, and IAM Roles Anywhere

concepts.heading: Cross-Account Roles, External IDs, and Session Policies
concepts.body: Cross-account access should always use an IAM role that the other account assumes through STS, which returns credentials that expire, instead of shared access keys. The role's trust policy names who may assume it, and the caller's own identity policy must allow sts:AssumeRole on that role. When a third-party SaaS vendor assumes roles in many customers' accounts, require an external ID with the sts:ExternalId condition so that another customer of the same vendor cannot trick it into using your role (the confused deputy problem). A session policy is an optional policy passed in the AssumeRole call; the session gets only the intersection of the role's permissions and the session policy, so a broker can hand a job credentials narrowed to one bucket. Session duration can also be kept short. Source identity, which persists through role chaining, ties every session to a person in CloudTrail.

concepts.heading: Permissions Boundaries for Safe Delegation
concepts.body: A permissions boundary is a managed policy attached to an IAM user or role that sets the most it can ever do; effective permissions are the intersection of its identity policies and the boundary, and any explicit deny still wins. Boundaries solve delegation: a platform team lets developers create roles for their Lambda functions, but only if each new role carries the approved boundary. You enforce that with a condition on iam:CreateRole and iam:PutRolePolicy such as iam:PermissionsBoundary equal to the boundary ARN, and you deny changes to the boundary policy itself, so nobody can escalate by creating an unbounded role. A boundary differs from an SCP, which caps every principal in an account or OU, and from a session policy, which narrows one session. When a question says teams may create roles but must not exceed a ceiling, think boundary.

concepts.heading: Attribute-Based Access Control with Tags
concepts.body: Role-based policies list resource ARNs and must be rewritten as resources grow. Attribute-based access control (ABAC) instead compares tags at request time, so one policy scales to every team or tenant. A typical statement allows actions when aws:ResourceTag/project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/project}. Principal tags can come from the role, from session tags passed during AssumeRole (the trust policy must allow sts:TagSession), or from attributes sent by Identity Center or a SAML IdP. For example, a SaaS backend assumes one role with the session tag TenantId taken from a verified Cognito token, and the policy allows DynamoDB access only when dynamodb:LeadingKeys matches that tag, so one tenant can never read another tenant's items. ABAC only works if tags are protected: deny tag changes on resources and principals except for an automation role, using aws:TagKeys and aws:RequestTag conditions.

concepts.heading: Data Perimeters with Policies and VPC Endpoints
concepts.body: A data perimeter ensures that only trusted identities access trusted resources from expected networks. Each side uses specific condition keys. The identity perimeter, set in resource policies or RCPs, allows only principals where aws:PrincipalOrgID is your organization, plus AWS service principals through aws:PrincipalIsAWSService. The resource perimeter, set in SCPs or VPC endpoint policies, lets your principals reach only resources where aws:ResourceOrgID is your organization, which blocks copying data to a personal bucket. The network perimeter requires calls to come through your VPC endpoints with aws:SourceVpce or from corporate ranges with aws:SourceIp. For example, an S3 gateway endpoint policy that allows access only to buckets in your organization stops exfiltration from private subnets. For people reaching private web applications, AWS Verified Access replaces a VPN: it evaluates every request against Cedar policies using identity and device posture trust providers.

concepts.heading: Validating Access with IAM Access Analyzer
concepts.body: IAM Access Analyzer answers who outside the boundary can reach what. An external access analyzer, created with the account or the whole organization as its zone of trust, uses automated reasoning on resource policies for S3 buckets, KMS keys, IAM role trust policies, Lambda functions, SQS queues, Secrets Manager secrets and more, and creates a finding for every grant to a principal outside that zone. An unused access analyzer reports roles, access keys, passwords and permissions that have not been used, which feeds least-privilege cleanups. Policy validation checks grammar and best practices, and custom policy checks such as CheckNoNewAccess or CheckAccessNotGranted can run in a CI/CD pipeline to block a change that would widen access. Access Analyzer can also generate a least-privilege policy from CloudTrail activity. A question that asks how to find every resource shared outside the organization points to an organization-level external access analyzer.

concepts.heading: Workload Identities Outside AWS with IAM Roles Anywhere
concepts.body: Servers on premises or in another cloud often hold long-lived access keys, which leak and rarely rotate. IAM Roles Anywhere lets those workloads exchange an X.509 certificate for temporary credentials. You create a trust anchor that holds your CA (AWS Private CA or your own CA bundle), a profile that lists which roles sessions may use and optional session policies, and roles that trust rolesanywhere.amazonaws.com. The workload's credential helper signs a CreateSession request with its private key. Certificate fields become session tags, so a trust policy can require aws:PrincipalTag/x509Subject/OU to equal Payments and only those certificates can assume the payments role. Roles Anywhere does not query OCSP; to revoke a stolen certificate you import the updated CRL, and you can deny its already issued credentials with a condition on its subject CN tag. Keys removed from a factory or another cloud means Roles Anywhere.

examPoints: A question that describes a SaaS vendor assuming roles in many customer accounts is testing the external ID condition that prevents the confused deputy problem.

A question that lets developers create their own IAM roles under a fixed ceiling is testing permissions boundaries enforced with the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition, while one about a policy that must scale to every new tenant or project is testing ABAC with session tags.

A question about removing access keys from on-premises or multi-cloud servers is testing IAM Roles Anywhere, and one about blocking data movement to buckets outside the organization is testing data perimeter conditions such as aws:ResourceOrgID in VPC endpoint policies.

quiz.q: A manufacturer runs 300 Linux servers in two factories and in another cloud provider. The servers upload telemetry to Amazon S3 using IAM user access keys stored in configuration files. Security requires that long-term AWS credentials are eliminated, that each server's identity can be revoked individually, and that the company's existing private CA is reused. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Store the access keys in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 30 days, and have each server retrieve the current key at startup by using a bootstrap key with read access to the secret
Install the SSM Agent on every server with a hybrid activation, and have the telemetry process read the instance role credentials from the managed node's local credential file
Federate the servers through IAM Identity Center with a SAML application, and have each server request credentials for a permission set by signing in with a service account
Configure IAM Roles Anywhere with a trust anchor for the private CA, issue a certificate to each server, and import the CA's CRL so that single certificates can be revoked
quiz.explain: Roles Anywhere exchanges each server's certificate for temporary credentials, reuses the existing CA through the trust anchor, and supports per-certificate revocation through an imported CRL. Choice A still depends on long-term access keys, including a bootstrap key, which is exactly what must be removed.

quiz.q: A company's security team must ensure that workloads in private subnets can write only to Amazon S3 buckets that belong to the company's AWS Organization, even if a developer's IAM policy allows s3:PutObject on all resources. The workloads reach S3 through a gateway VPC endpoint. What is the most direct control?
choices: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the organization level, so that objects written by the workloads can never be made readable by principals outside the organization
Attach an endpoint policy to the S3 gateway endpoint that allows S3 actions only when aws:ResourceOrgID equals the organization ID, so requests to other buckets are denied
Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer for the organization, so that any bucket outside the organization that receives objects generates a finding
Add a bucket policy to every company bucket that denies s3:PutObject unless aws:PrincipalOrgID equals the organization ID, and enable default encryption with SSE-KMS
quiz.explain: An endpoint policy sits on the network path the workloads must use and, with aws:ResourceOrgID, refuses requests to buckets owned outside the organization, regardless of IAM allows. Choice D protects the company's own buckets from outside principals, which is the identity perimeter, but does nothing to stop writes to a bucket the company does not own.

days.recap: Cross-account roles with external IDs and session policies, permissions boundaries for delegation, and ABAC with session tags implement least privilege; data perimeters, Access Analyzer and Verified Access control and verify external access; and Roles Anywhere replaces keys on servers outside AWS.

days.title: Encryption and Key Management: KMS Keys and Rotation, ACM and Private CA, CloudHSM, and Post-Quantum Cryptography

concepts.heading: Customer Managed Keys and Key Policies
concepts.body: AWS KMS offers AWS managed keys, which a service creates for you, and customer managed keys, which you create and control. Customer managed keys are the exam default for regulated data because you write the key policy, can grant access to other accounts, can disable or schedule deletion, and see every use in CloudTrail. The key policy is the primary control: unless it allows the account to use IAM policies, IAM alone cannot grant access. Cross-account use needs both the key policy in the key's account and an IAM policy in the caller's account. Services such as S3, EBS and RDS use envelope encryption: KMS generates a data key, the service encrypts data with it, and stores only the encrypted data key, so large data never travels to KMS. Grants give temporary, narrow permissions to services. A requirement for separate control and audit of keys points to customer managed keys.

concepts.heading: Automatic Key Rotation and Key Material Options
concepts.body: For a symmetric customer managed key, automatic rotation creates new key material on a schedule while keeping all older material, so existing ciphertext still decrypts and the key ID and ARN never change. The rotation period is configurable (one year by default), and on-demand rotation is available for urgent cases. Rotation for a multi-Region key is set on the primary and propagates to the replicas. Imported-material keys support only on-demand rotation; asymmetric, HMAC and custom key store keys are rotated by creating a new key and moving an alias. Where key material lives is a separate decision: KMS HSMs by default, imported material (BYOK) that you can expire or delete, a CloudHSM key store in a cluster you own, or an external key store (XKS) that keeps the root key in your own HSM outside AWS, which you must keep highly available. Compliance that demands keys outside AWS means XKS.

concepts.heading: Encryption in Transit with ACM, Private CA, and TLS 1.3
concepts.body: AWS Certificate Manager issues public TLS certificates at no charge and renews them automatically when they are deployed on integrated services such as Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront and API Gateway; a CloudFront certificate must be requested in us-east-1. AWS Private CA runs private root and subordinate CAs for internal names, mutual TLS and devices; its short-lived certificate mode issues certificates valid for at most 7 days at a lower price, which suits service meshes where expiry replaces revocation. The protocol version is chosen where TLS terminates: on an Application Load Balancer the listener security policy decides, so ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-3-2021-06 accepts only TLS 1.3 regardless of the target's settings. An ALB can also verify client certificates in mTLS verify mode against a trust store with CRLs and pass the subject to the application in headers. A TLS 1.3-only rule means changing the listener policy.

concepts.heading: AWS CloudHSM for Regulated Workloads
concepts.body: AWS CloudHSM provides single-tenant hardware security modules validated at FIPS 140 Level 3 inside your VPC. You initialize the cluster and create the crypto officer and crypto user accounts yourself; AWS maintains the hardware but has no access to your keys or HSM users. Applications use standard interfaces, PKCS#11, JCE, OpenSSL and the Microsoft KSP and CNG providers, which is why CloudHSM fits Oracle Transparent Data Encryption, custom signing services and SSL offload. For availability run at least two HSMs in different Availability Zones; the cluster synchronizes keys and the client fails over. Backups are encrypted so they can only be restored into CloudHSM, and you can copy a backup to another Region and create a cluster from it for disaster recovery. Choose CloudHSM when a regulation requires exclusive, single-tenant control or an application needs PKCS#11; choose KMS for everything that just needs service integration.

concepts.heading: Post-Quantum Threats: Harvest Now, Decrypt Later
concepts.body: A large quantum computer would break today's public-key algorithms (RSA, Diffie-Hellman and elliptic curves), whatever their key size. It does not exist yet, but an adversary can record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it later, so data that must stay secret for decades is already exposed if its session keys were agreed with classical key exchange. Symmetric encryption is far less affected: AES-256, used by KMS symmetric keys and S3 encryption, is considered quantum-resistant. The urgent fix is therefore key exchange in transit. ML-KEM (FIPS 203) is the NIST post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism, and TLS 1.3 can use a hybrid group such as X25519MLKEM768 that derives the session key from both secrets, so a session stays safe unless both fall. Endpoints such as KMS, ACM and Secrets Manager support it, but the client must offer the hybrid key share, so the SDK's TLS stack has to support it.

concepts.heading: Post-Quantum Signatures and Crypto Agility
concepts.body: Signatures need a different algorithm. ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is the NIST post-quantum signature scheme, and AWS KMS supports asymmetric keys with the key specs ML_DSA_44, ML_DSA_65 and ML_DSA_87 and key usage SIGN_VERIFY. The private key never leaves KMS HSMs; you call Sign and distribute the public key from GetPublicKey, so devices can verify offline. This suits long-lived products such as medical devices or firmware that must stay trustworthy for 15 years. Do not mix the roles: ML-KEM establishes keys and cannot sign, and an HMAC key would place a signing secret in every device. A post-quantum program starts with a cryptographic inventory ranked by data lifetime, then crypto agility: algorithm choices live in shared libraries and configuration, and applications reference KMS keys by alias so a new key type can be swapped in. Transitions run in hybrid mode so older clients keep working.

examPoints: A question that warns about adversaries recording traffic today for data that must stay secret for decades is testing hybrid ML-KEM key exchange in TLS 1.3, not re-encryption of data at rest with AES-256.

A question about post-quantum code or firmware signing is testing KMS asymmetric keys with an ML-DSA key spec, while one about single-tenant HSMs, exclusive control or a PKCS#11 application is testing AWS CloudHSM.
A question in which a backend's TLS settings were changed but scans still show old protocol versions is testing where TLS terminates: the load balancer listener security policy decides.

quiz.q: A government contractor sends engineering data that must stay confidential for 30 years between its sites and AWS service endpoints over TLS 1.3 with classical ECDHE key exchange. The data at rest in Amazon S3 is encrypted with KMS symmetric keys. A security review warns that an adversary may be recording traffic now. Which action addresses the most urgent risk?
choices: Re-encrypt every S3 object with new KMS keys and shorten the key rotation period, because the AES-256 keys protecting data at rest are the first target of a quantum computer
Configure the clients with a TLS stack that offers hybrid post-quantum key exchange (X25519 combined with ML-KEM-768) so that new sessions resist decryption of recorded traffic
Replace the RSA keys in the TLS certificates with the largest RSA key size that ACM supports, so that recorded sessions can no longer be decrypted with quantum algorithms
Create KMS keys with an ML-DSA key spec and use them to sign each file before transfer, so that recorded files cannot be decrypted by an adversary in the future
quiz.explain: Recorded traffic is threatened through its classical key exchange, and a hybrid ML-KEM group protects new sessions against later quantum decryption while keeping ECDHE as a safety net. Choice D confuses signatures with confidentiality: ML-DSA proves integrity and origin but does not stop anyone from decrypting recorded traffic.

quiz.q: A bank is moving a self-managed Oracle Database to Amazon EC2. Oracle Transparent Data Encryption stores its master key in an on-premises HSM through PKCS#11. The regulator requires single-tenant HSMs validated at FIPS 140 Level 3 in which only the bank's crypto officers can manage users and keys, and the database must survive the loss of an Availability Zone. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Create an AWS KMS customer managed key with automatic rotation for the EBS volumes, and turn off Oracle TDE because the KMS HSMs are validated at FIPS 140 Level 3
Create a KMS key in a CloudHSM custom key store, and point the Oracle wallet at the KMS key ARN so that TDE wraps its tablespace keys through the KMS API
Deploy an AWS CloudHSM cluster with HSMs in two Availability Zones, and have Oracle TDE keep its master key there through the CloudHSM PKCS#11 library
Import the master key into KMS as external key material with a one-year expiration, and configure Oracle TDE to request data keys from KMS with GenerateDataKey
quiz.explain: CloudHSM gives single-tenant FIPS Level 3 HSMs under the bank's exclusive control, Oracle TDE keeps using PKCS#11, and two HSMs in different AZs keep the keys available. Choice B fails because KMS exposes no PKCS#11 interface, so Oracle TDE cannot use a KMS key even when its material sits in a CloudHSM key store.

days.recap: Use customer managed KMS keys with automatic rotation for data at rest, ACM and Private CA plus listener TLS policies for data in transit, CloudHSM when regulations demand single-tenant HSMs or PKCS#11, hybrid ML-KEM TLS against harvest-now-decrypt-later, and ML-DSA KMS keys for post-quantum signatures.

days.title: Multi-Account Structure and Policy Guardrails: Organizations, Control Tower, SCPs, RCPs, and AWS RAM

concepts.heading: Designing the OU Structure and Landing Zone
concepts.body: A landing zone is the baseline multi-account environment that every workload lands in. AWS Organizations groups accounts into organizational units, and policies attach at the OU so they apply to every account below it. A common structure has a Security OU with a log archive account and an audit (security tooling) account, an Infrastructure OU for shared networking, Workloads OUs split into prod and non-prod, a Sandbox OU with looser rules, and a Suspended OU for closed accounts. Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary: they separate blast radius, quotas, billing and regulatory scope, so a PCI workload belongs in its own account rather than behind IAM conditions in a shared one. Delegated administrator accounts let security services such as GuardDuty or Config be run from the audit account instead of the management account, which should hold no workloads. Many teams with different rules signals an OU design, not more IAM policies.

concepts.heading: Control Tower and Account Factory
concepts.body: AWS Control Tower sets up and governs a landing zone on top of Organizations. It creates the Security OU with log archive and audit accounts, an organization CloudTrail trail and AWS Config recording, and IAM Identity Center access. Controls come in three behaviors: preventive controls implemented as SCPs, RCPs or declarative policies, detective controls implemented as Config rules, and proactive controls implemented as CloudFormation hooks that check resources before they are created. Each control is mandatory, strongly recommended or elective and is enabled per OU. Account Factory provisions new accounts that are enrolled with the baseline from the start, through the console or Service Catalog, and Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) runs the same vending through a GitOps pipeline with account customizations. A scenario of frequent, standardized account creation with logging and guardrails in place on day one is answered by Control Tower Account Factory, not by scripts calling CreateAccount.

concepts.heading: Service Control Policies as the Identity Ceiling
concepts.body: A service control policy limits the maximum permissions of IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the account root user. It never grants anything; a principal still needs an identity or resource policy allow below the SCP. SCPs do not affect the management account or service-linked roles, which is one reason the management account holds no workloads. Most organizations use a deny-list strategy: keep FullAWSAccess and add deny statements. Typical examples are denying actions outside approved Regions with aws:RequestedRegion while exempting global services in a NotAction list, preventing member accounts from leaving the organization, protecting CloudTrail and Config from being stopped, and blocking Bedrock inference on unapproved model ARNs. A break-glass role can be exempted with an aws:PrincipalArn condition. Because an explicit deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by account administrators, SCPs are the preventive answer when member account admins must not bypass a rule.

concepts.heading: Resource Control Policies as the Resource Ceiling
concepts.body: Resource control policies are the resource-side counterpart of SCPs. An RCP sets the maximum permissions for resources in member accounts, whoever the caller is, including principals from outside the organization that an SCP can never reach. RCPs support services such as Amazon S3, AWS STS, AWS KMS, Amazon SQS and AWS Secrets Manager, and like SCPs they only restrict. The classic use is an identity perimeter at scale: deny s3:* unless aws:PrincipalOrgID equals your organization ID, so a misconfigured bucket policy that allows Principal * still cannot expose data. AWS service principals that deliver logs must be exempted with aws:PrincipalIsAWSService, or CloudTrail and Config delivery breaks. A second common RCP requires secure transport for all S3 requests. The rule of thumb: SCPs stop your principals from doing things anywhere, RCPs stop anyone from doing things to your resources.

concepts.heading: Sharing Resources Across Accounts with AWS RAM
concepts.body: AWS Resource Access Manager shares a resource owned by one account with other accounts, OUs or the whole organization, so it is created once instead of in every account. When sharing with AWS Organizations is enabled, shares inside the organization need no invitation. Commonly shared resources include Transit Gateways, VPC subnets, Route 53 Resolver rules, AWS Network Firewall policies, IPAM pools, AWS Private CA certificate authorities and License Manager configurations. In a hub design, a network account owns the Transit Gateway and shares it with the Workloads OU; each workload account then creates its own attachment, which the owner accepts automatically or reviews depending on the auto-accept setting, and route tables in the network account control who can reach whom. VPC sharing goes further: participants launch resources into subnets of a VPC that the network team owns and manages, which reduces the number of VPCs and Transit Gateway attachments.

examPoints: A question that must stop principals outside the organization from reaching S3 buckets or KMS keys in every account, even with a misconfigured resource policy, is testing RCPs; a question that must stop member account principals from using a Region or service is testing SCPs.
A question about creating many new accounts that already have logging, guardrails and network baselines is testing Control Tower Account Factory (or AFT for a Terraform pipeline).
A question about one Transit Gateway, subnet or Resolver rule used by dozens of accounts is testing AWS RAM sharing with the organization or an OU.

quiz.q: A company with 250 accounts in AWS Organizations found an S3 bucket whose policy accidentally allowed access to any AWS principal. Security wants a preventive control that guarantees no principal outside the organization can access S3 data in any member account, even if a bucket policy is misconfigured, without breaking log delivery by AWS services. What should a solutions architect implement?
choices: An RCP attached to the root that denies S3 actions unless aws:PrincipalOrgID equals the organization ID, with an exemption when aws:PrincipalIsAWSService is true
An SCP attached to the root that denies S3 actions unless aws:PrincipalOrgID equals the organization ID, with an exemption for the organization's break-glass administrator role
An AWS Config organization rule that detects bucket policies with Principal set to all and runs an SSM Automation runbook that removes the offending statement from the policy
S3 Block Public Access settings enabled at the account level in every member account through a Control Tower detective control that alerts when the setting is disabled
quiz.explain: An RCP limits what can be done to resources in member accounts by any caller, including outside principals, and the service principal exemption keeps CloudTrail and Config delivery working. Choice B fails because SCPs apply only to principals in the organization's member accounts, so they never restrict an outside principal calling the bucket.

quiz.q: A network team owns an AWS Transit Gateway in a central network account. Sixty workload accounts in the Workloads OU must attach their VPCs to it, and new accounts added to the OU must be able to attach without the network team running per-account steps. Which approach meets these requirements?
choices: Create a Transit Gateway in each workload account and peer every one of them with the central Transit Gateway, using a StackSet so that new accounts receive the peering automatically
Grant each workload account's administrator role permission in the network account to call ec2:CreateTransitGatewayVpcAttachment through a cross-account IAM role that the network team manages
Create VPC peering connections from the central inspection VPC to every workload VPC, and add peering routes in each workload VPC route table with a Lambda function on account creation
Share the Transit Gateway with the Workloads OU through AWS RAM with organization sharing enabled, so that each workload account, including new ones, can create its own attachment
quiz.explain: A RAM share to the OU is inherited by new accounts in that OU, and each account creates its attachment against the shared Transit Gateway while the network account keeps control of routing. Choice A multiplies Transit Gateways and peering attachments, which adds cost and complexity for something RAM solves with one share.

days.recap: Design OUs so policies attach once, let Control Tower and Account Factory vend governed accounts, cap principals with SCPs and resources with RCPs, and share Transit Gateways and other network resources through AWS RAM.

days.title: Centralized Logging, Compliance Monitoring, and Vulnerability Management: CloudTrail, Config, GuardDuty, Security Lake, Security Hub CSPM, Inspector, and Patch Manager

concepts.heading: Organization Trails and the Log Archive Account
concepts.body: AWS CloudTrail records API activity. Management events (control plane calls such as CreateBucket or PutBucketPolicy) are recorded by default; data events (high-volume calls such as S3 GetObject or Lambda Invoke) must be enabled and are charged per event, so advanced event selectors should scope them to the resources that matter. An organization trail, created in the management account or by a delegated administrator, logs every member account automatically, and member accounts can see it but cannot change or stop it. Deliver it to an S3 bucket in a separate log archive account, enable log file integrity validation so hourly digest files prove nothing was altered or deleted, and add S3 Object Lock for tamper-resistant retention. The console's event history keeps only 90 days of management events per account and Region, so it is not an archive. CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers, so new designs use trails and S3.

concepts.heading: AWS Config Recording, Aggregators, and History
concepts.body: AWS Config records a configuration item every time a recorded resource changes, building a timeline of what each resource looked like, with retention you can set up to seven years. The delivery channel in every account and Region can write configuration history and snapshots to one central bucket, typically in the log archive account, where Amazon Athena can query any date across the organization. An aggregator in the audit account collects configuration and compliance data from all accounts and Regions into one view, and its advanced queries search current state, not history. Organization Config rules and conformance packs are deployed once from a delegated administrator and apply to new accounts automatically. Recording the resource type AWS::Config::ResourceCompliance adds compliance history, showing when a resource became non-compliant and when it was fixed. An auditor asking what a security group looked like on a past date is answered from Config history, not from CloudTrail or Flow Logs.

concepts.heading: Threat Detection and Security Data: GuardDuty, Security Hub CSPM, and Security Lake
concepts.body: Amazon GuardDuty analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs, plus optional protection plans such as S3, EKS and runtime monitoring, to detect threats like credential misuse or crypto mining, with no agents for the foundational sources; enable it for the organization from a delegated administrator with auto-enable for new accounts. AWS Security Hub CSPM aggregates findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partners, and runs security standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS and PCI DSS; central configuration and cross-Region aggregation give one view. Security Hub CSPM is a working view: it removes findings about 90 days after their last update. For long-term evidence, Amazon Security Lake collects CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver logs and Security Hub CSPM findings from all accounts into S3 in the OCSF schema, with retention you choose and queries through Athena or subscribers.

concepts.heading: Logging AI Model Invocations and Centralizing CloudWatch Logs
concepts.body: Generative AI adds a new audit need: what was asked and what was answered. CloudTrail records who called Bedrock InvokeModel or Converse and when, as management events, but never the prompt or response body. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging captures the input and output data plus metadata such as the model and caller identity; it is off by default and configured per account and per Region, delivering to S3, CloudWatch Logs or both. Because prompts often contain personal data, encrypt the destination with a customer managed KMS key and restrict reads. For application and service logs, CloudWatch Logs can be centralized by cross-account subscription filters to a Data Firehose stream in the log archive account, or viewed across accounts with CloudWatch cross-account observability. A requirement to keep full prompts and responses for every Region the company uses means invocation logging in each of those Regions.

concepts.heading: Automated Compliance Monitoring and Remediation
concepts.body: Continuous compliance means every resource is evaluated against rules automatically, not reviewed by hand before an audit. AWS Config rules come as AWS managed rules (for example restricted-ssh, s3-bucket-server-side-encryption-enabled or required-tags), custom rules written as Lambda functions, and custom policy rules written in Guard syntax. Rules run on configuration changes or on a schedule, and remediation actions can run an SSM Automation runbook automatically, such as removing a public ingress rule. Conformance packs bundle many rules with remediations, for example a HIPAA operational best practices pack, and deploy organization-wide. Security Hub CSPM controls are backed by Config rules and produce scored findings per standard. EventBridge receives Config and Security Hub CSPM events, so a finding can trigger a Lambda function or a Step Functions workflow. The exam signal is detect plus auto-remediate across all accounts: organization Config rules with SSM Automation remediation.

concepts.heading: Vulnerability Scanning and Patch Management
concepts.body: Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2 instances (through the SSM Agent, or agentless scanning of EBS snapshots), container images in Amazon ECR, and Lambda functions and their code for known software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure. It rescans automatically when a new CVE is published, scores each finding by severity and exploitability, and can be enabled for the whole organization from a delegated administrator. Findings flow to Security Hub CSPM and EventBridge. Finding a vulnerability is half the job; AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager fixes the operating system side. Patch baselines define which patches are approved, for example critical security updates auto-approved seven days after release, and patch policies created through Quick Setup apply scanning and installation schedules across accounts and Regions of the organization, with maintenance windows controlling when reboots happen. Compliance reports show which nodes are missing patches.

examPoints: A question that needs audit logs no workload administrator can disable, with proof the files were not altered, is testing an organization trail with log file validation delivered to an Object Lock bucket in a log archive account.

A question about point-in-time configuration evidence is testing AWS Config recording with central history files, while one about keeping Security Hub CSPM findings longer than about 90 days is testing Amazon Security Lake.

A question about continuous CVE detection for EC2, ECR images and Lambda functions plus scheduled OS patching across the organization is testing Amazon Inspector together with Systems Manager Patch Manager patch policies.

quiz.q: A retailer runs Security Hub CSPM with central configuration across 90 accounts and aggregates findings into one Region. Its PCI assessor asks for control status evidence covering the full previous 12 months, stored where application teams cannot change it. The security team discovers that findings older than about three months no longer exist. What should a solutions architect do for future assessments?
choices: Increase the finding retention setting in the Security Hub CSPM administrator account to 13 months, and use an SCP to deny member accounts the ability to update findings
Deploy an AWS Config aggregator in the audit account so that Security Hub CSPM findings are copied into Config compliance history, and set the Config retention period to 7 years
Enable Amazon Security Lake with a delegated administrator in the log archive account, add Security Hub CSPM findings as a source for all accounts, and set a 13-month retention
Schedule a monthly Lambda function in each member account that exports the Security Hub CSPM summary dashboard as a CSV file to a versioned S3 bucket in the same account
quiz.explain: Security Lake continuously collects findings from every account into a separate account with the retention the assessor needs, queryable with Athena. Choice A fails because the roughly 90-day finding retention in Security Hub CSPM is fixed and has no setting to extend it.

quiz.q: A company with 80 accounts must detect known software vulnerabilities in its EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR and Lambda functions within hours of a new CVE being published, and must install critical operating system patches on all EC2 instances within 7 days of release. Teams should not run their own scanners. Which combination meets these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
choices: Enable Amazon GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring for the organization to detect vulnerable packages, and use EC2 Image Builder to rebuild every AMI weekly with the latest operating system patches
Enable Amazon Inspector for the organization from a delegated administrator, and use a Systems Manager Quick Setup patch policy whose baseline auto-approves critical patches
Enable the CIS standard in Security Hub CSPM across all accounts, and create an AWS Config rule that marks instances non-compliant when they have not been rebooted for 7 days
Run an open-source scanner in AWS CodeBuild against every image and AMI each night, and have each team schedule its own cron job on its instances that installs all available updates
quiz.explain: Inspector rescans EC2, ECR images and Lambda functions automatically when new CVEs appear, and a Patch Manager patch policy applies approved critical patches across accounts on a schedule. Choice A fails because GuardDuty detects threats and suspicious behavior, not vulnerable software packages, and weekly AMI rebuilds do not patch running instances.

days.recap: Centralize audit and configuration evidence with an organization trail and Config history in a log archive account, aggregate detections in Security Hub CSPM and archive them in Security Lake, log Bedrock invocations per Region, automate compliance with Config rules, and close vulnerabilities with Inspector and Patch Manager.

days.title: Compliance Architectures: Data Protection, Sovereignty and Residency, Audit Trails, AWS Artifact Evidence, and Threat Modeling

concepts.heading: Data Protection Requirements: At Rest, In Transit, and In Use
concepts.body: A data protection requirement is met by layering controls, and the exam expects you to match each layer to its threat. Classify first: Amazon Macie finds sensitive data such as PII in S3 so you know which buckets are in scope. Encrypt at rest with customer managed KMS keys whose key policies separate key administrators from key users, and encrypt in transit with TLS. Restrict access with least-privilege IAM, data perimeter conditions and resource policies, and record access with CloudTrail data events for the sensitive buckets. Data in use needs more: when a regulation says even OS administrators of the instance must not see plaintext, process the data in an AWS Nitro Enclave, an isolated VM with no storage, interactive access or external network, and allow kms:Decrypt only when the request carries matching enclave attestation measurements, for example with the kms:RecipientAttestation:ImageSha384 condition.

concepts.heading: Sovereignty Controls: Region Choice and Key Control
concepts.body: Data sovereignty means data stays under the legal control of a specific jurisdiction. On AWS that starts with Region choice: you decide where data is stored, and AWS does not move it unless you configure a feature that does. Make the choice enforceable with an SCP that denies requests outside approved Regions using aws:RequestedRegion, exempting global services in a NotAction list. Keys are part of sovereignty too. A regulation that says the root key must never be stored in the cloud provider's infrastructure, yet services must keep native SSE-KMS, is met by a KMS external key store (XKS), which sends each cryptographic operation to an XKS proxy and HSM you run outside AWS; disconnecting the proxy cuts off decryption. Where no AWS Region exists in the country, AWS Outposts or Local Zones can keep compute and primary data in-country, but check where copies go.

concepts.heading: Residency Controls: Every Copy Counts
concepts.body: A residency rule is satisfied only if every copy stays in approved Regions: replicas, backups, caches, logs and key material. Several features copy data by design. DynamoDB global tables replicate every item to every replica Region with no item-level filter, so different jurisdictions need separate cells with a tenant-to-cell routing map. S3 Cross-Region Replication and AWS Backup copy actions must target only approved Regions.
