A multi-Region KMS key shares the same key material across all its replicas, so EU data needs its own key with replicas only in EU Regions, guarded by an SCP that denies kms:ReplicateKey unless kms:ReplicaRegion is approved. Bedrock cross-Region inference processes prompts in destination Regions, so choose a geographic profile such as the EU profile, not the global one. On Outposts, EBS snapshots and RDS backups go to the parent Region by default unless you use EBS local snapshots and the RDS backup target of the Outpost.

concepts.heading: Audit Trails for Regulated and AI Workloads
concepts.body: Regulated workloads need audit records that are complete, attributable and tamper-resistant. Complete means the right sources: an organization trail with management events plus scoped S3 data events for in-scope buckets, AWS Config history for configuration state, and, for generative AI, Bedrock model invocation logging in every Region used, because only invocation logs contain the prompts and responses. Attributable means every action maps to a person: when operators share or chain roles, require an STS source identity set by the identity provider, which cannot be changed and follows every chained role into CloudTrail. Tamper-resistant means a separate log archive account, log file integrity validation, SSE-KMS with a customer managed key, and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode for the retention period, for example seven years; S3 Replication can copy invocation logs into an Object Lock bucket. Least-privilege read access matters because prompts may contain personal data.

concepts.heading: Compliance Evidence with AWS Artifact
concepts.body: Auditors need evidence for both halves of the shared responsibility model. AWS's half (data centers, hardware, hypervisor and managed service operations) is attested by third-party auditors, and AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for those reports: SOC 1, SOC 2 and SOC 3 reports, the PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance, ISO certifications and others. Many are confidential, so you accept the Artifact terms before downloading and sharing them with your auditor. Artifact also holds agreements such as the HIPAA Business Associate Addendum; from the management account of an organization with all features enabled you can accept it as an organization agreement that covers every current and future member account. Your half, the configuration of your own accounts and workloads, needs your own evidence from AWS Config history, conformance packs, Security Hub CSPM standards and CloudTrail. Neither a Config conformance pack nor a Security Hub CSPM standard is a legal agreement or an AWS attestation.

concepts.heading: Threat Modeling and Risk Assessment
concepts.body: Threat modeling is a design-time practice that asks what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, and did we do a good job. Diagram components, data stores, actors and data flows, and mark trust boundaries such as internet to API Gateway or application to foundation model. Walk each element with STRIDE (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege), adding AI threats such as prompt injection and sensitive data in prompts. Record each threat with a mitigation and an owner, store the model with the code, for example in AWS Threat Composer, and revisit it when the design changes. Then map threats to controls: credential stuffing to AWS WAF account takeover prevention, layer 7 floods to rate-based rules and AWS Shield Advanced, repudiation to source identity. Scanners such as Inspector or GuardDuty are mitigations, not a threat model.

examPoints: A question that requires root key material to stay outside AWS while S3, EBS and RDS keep native SSE-KMS is testing a KMS external key store, while one that hides plaintext from the instance's own administrators is testing Nitro Enclaves with attestation conditions in the key policy.

A question about data residency with global tables, multi-Region keys, cross-Region inference or Outposts backups is testing whether every copy stays in approved Regions, not just where users are routed.

A question asking for AWS's SOC or PCI reports, or a BAA covering all accounts, is testing AWS Artifact; a question that asks for a design-time, repeatable risk practice is testing threat modeling with STRIDE and Threat Composer.

quiz.q: A national bank is moving analytics to Amazon S3, Amazon EBS and Amazon RDS. The regulator requires that root key material is never stored in the cloud provider's infrastructure and that the bank can stop AWS services from decrypting data by acting only on infrastructure it controls. The bank wants native SSE-KMS integration and no application code changes. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Create KMS keys in a custom key store backed by an AWS CloudHSM cluster in the bank's VPC, and delete the cluster if access must be cut off
Create KMS keys with imported key material generated in the bank's on-premises HSM, and delete the imported material from KMS if access must be cut off
Encrypt all data on the client side with keys from the on-premises HSMs before upload, and revoke the HSM credentials if access must be cut off
Create KMS keys in an external key store that uses an XKS proxy in front of the bank's on-premises HSMs, and disconnect the proxy if access must be cut off
quiz.explain: An external key store keeps the root key in the bank's own HSMs outside AWS while S3, EBS and RDS use normal SSE-KMS, and disconnecting the proxy stops KMS from decrypting data keys. Choice A keeps the material in a single-tenant cluster that still runs in an AWS data center, so the first condition fails.

quiz.q: A bank uses Amazon Bedrock in two Regions for a customer-facing assistant. Regulators require the bank to retain the full text of every prompt and response for seven years in tamper-resistant storage, encrypted with a bank-managed key, together with who invoked the model. An organization trail already exists. What additional configuration meets the requirement?
choices: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging in both Regions to S3 buckets encrypted with a customer managed key, replicated to an Object Lock bucket with seven-year compliance retention
Add CloudTrail data event selectors for Amazon Bedrock to the organization trail so that the request and response bodies of every InvokeModel call are written to the trail's log files
Enable guardrail tracing on every Bedrock request and forward the traces to CloudWatch Logs log groups with a seven-year retention policy and a customer managed key
Turn on CloudWatch Logs data protection for the assistant's log group and have the application log each prompt and response there with a seven-year retention setting
quiz.explain: Model invocation logging is the only source that records the prompt and response text with caller identity, it is set per Region, and Object Lock plus a customer managed key meet the tamper-resistance and encryption rules. Choice B fails because no CloudTrail event carries the prompt or response payload; CloudTrail only records who called the API.

days.recap: Layer encryption, access control and logging for data protection, use Region choice, SCPs and key placement for sovereignty, check every copy for residency, build attributable tamper-resistant audit trails including AI invocation logs, get AWS's evidence from Artifact, and run threat modeling at design time.

days.title: Security and Responsible AI Controls: Bedrock Guardrails, AgentCore Identity, and Human Approval with Step Functions

concepts.heading: Bedrock Guardrails Policies
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails applies a reusable policy to user inputs and model outputs, independent of which model produced the text, so it is a model-agnostic control that a system prompt is not. A guardrail combines several policies. Denied topics describe subjects in natural language with sample phrases, such as personalized investment advice, and block them by meaning. Content filters score categories such as hate, insults, sexual, violence and misconduct, and the prompt attack filter catches jailbreaks and prompt injection in user input, each with a strength setting. Sensitive information filters detect built-in PII types and custom regular expressions, each with an action: Block replaces the whole response with your blocked message, while Mask replaces only the match with a tag such as {NAME} and returns the rest. Word filters match exact words plus a managed profanity list. Choose Mask when the answer must still be useful without specific values.

concepts.heading: Contextual Grounding for RAG Answers
concepts.body: Content filters judge whether text is harmful, so a confident but invented fact passes them. The contextual grounding check in Bedrock Guardrails targets that failure in retrieval-augmented generation. You supply the grounding source, such as the passages the retriever returned, and the query, the user's question. The guardrail scores the response from 0 to 1 for grounding (is it supported by the source) and relevance (does it answer the question), and blocks responses below the thresholds you set, replacing them with a message such as I could not find that in your policy documents. For example, a grounding threshold of 0.8 stops an answer that cites a coverage limit that appears nowhere in the retrieved passages. Lowering temperature, adding word lists of real values or raising content filter strength does not solve this. On the exam, hallucinated numbers or drifting answers in a RAG assistant point to contextual grounding.

concepts.heading: Operating Guardrails Across Applications
concepts.body: Treat a guardrail like code. Every guardrail has a mutable working draft and immutable numbered versions created with CreateGuardrailVersion; production should reference a tested version, never the draft, so behavior changes only through an approved release and auditors can tell which version was in force on any date. A request names the guardrail and version and cannot switch off one of its policies, so applications that need different rules get separate guardrails, built from one infrastructure-as-code template to keep shared parts such as PII masking identical. For models outside Bedrock, such as a SageMaker AI endpoint or a third-party API, call the ApplyGuardrail API on the prompt and again on the response, so one guardrail governs every path. Guardrail traces and CloudWatch intervention metrics give compliance evidence. To control which foundation models may be used at all, an SCP can deny Bedrock inference actions unless the resource is an approved model or inference profile ARN.

concepts.heading: AgentCore Identity for Inbound and Outbound Access
concepts.body: AI agents act on behalf of users or of themselves, and both directions need managed identity. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity gives each agent a workload identity. Inbound, the agent runtime can require a valid OAuth token or JWT from an identity provider such as Amazon Cognito, so only authenticated callers can invoke it. Outbound, credential providers manage the secrets the agent needs to call other systems: an OAuth client credentials provider for machine-to-machine calls when no user is present, an OAuth authorization code provider for user-delegated access where tokens are kept per agent and per user in the token vault after the user consents, and API key providers for services that only accept keys. Agent code asks for a token at run time and never reads the client secret, so secrets stay out of code, images and environment variables. A nightly agent calling a partner API with scoped tokens points to the client credentials flow.

concepts.heading: Least Privilege for Agent Tools
concepts.body: Treat the model as untrusted: prompt injection in a user message, document or tool result can steer which tool it calls and with which arguments. Hard limits therefore sit outside the model. Give each agent its own execution role rather than one shared role, scope its identity policy to the tool ARNs it is approved to call, and, across accounts, name that exact role ARN in each Lambda function's resource-based policy. Expose each tool as a separate AgentCore Gateway target backed by a function with its own minimal role, so a tricked status tool cannot issue refunds. Enforce business rules deterministically in the tool backend, such as a refund limit and order ownership checked against the authenticated customer bound to the session, never against IDs the model supplies. For multi-tenant data, assume a role with a tenant session tag from the verified token and use conditions such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys. System prompt rules lower risk but bound nothing.

concepts.heading: Human Oversight with Step Functions
concepts.body: High-impact AI actions need a human decision that the model cannot skip. AWS Step Functions Standard workflows can run for up to a year and keep full execution history, so they host approvals with the callback pattern: a task state uses the .waitForTaskToken integration to send the proposal and task token to reviewers, the execution pauses without consuming compute, and the review backend calls SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure with the token and the reviewer's identity. Set TimeoutSeconds to the real business deadline and catch States.Timeout to escalate; an expired token cannot be revived. Express workflows (5-minute limit) do not support this pattern, Lambda stops at 15 minutes and SQS delay tops out at 15 minutes. Avoid approval fatigue by putting a deterministic Choice state before the callback so only high-risk actions, such as deletes, IAM changes or production database targets, wait for a human. Model promotion can use SageMaker Model Registry approval status the same way.

examPoints: A question that needs the same content, topic and PII rules for several models, including models outside Bedrock, is testing one versioned guardrail applied on every call or through the ApplyGuardrail API.

A question about RAG answers that invent facts or drift off topic is testing the contextual grounding check, and one about agents calling third-party APIs without secrets in code is testing AgentCore Identity credential providers.

A question that requires a named person to approve an AI-proposed action, possibly days later, is testing a Step Functions Standard workflow with .waitForTaskToken, ideally behind a deterministic risk rule.

quiz.q: An insurer's RAG assistant on Amazon Bedrock answers questions from policy documents retrieved from a knowledge base. A guardrail with content filters set to High is attached. Auditors found answers that quote coverage limits that do not appear in the retrieved passages and answers that drift to unrelated subjects. The company wants such responses blocked before users see them. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Add a denied topic named fabricated coverage information with sample phrases of invented limits, and raise the prompt attack filter strength to High so misleading prompts are rejected
Enable the contextual grounding check in the guardrail with grounding and relevance thresholds, passing the retrieved passages as the grounding source and the user question as the query
Set temperature to 0 and a low top-p for every request, and add a word filter that lists every coverage limit value that the policy documents actually contain
Raise the misconduct and violence content filters on outputs to their maximum strength, and attach a second guardrail version to the knowledge base retrieval call
quiz.explain: The contextual grounding check scores whether a response is supported by the retrieved passages and whether it answers the question, and blocks those below the thresholds. Choice D fails because content filters judge harmful categories; an invented coverage limit contains no violence or misconduct, so stricter filters change nothing.

quiz.q: A company lets a generative AI agent propose remediation plans for AWS Config findings, such as changing security group rules. Policy requires that a named on-call engineer approves every plan before it runs, that approvals may take up to 3 days, that rejections are recorded, and that the flow is auditable. Which design meets these requirements?
choices: Write each plan to an Amazon SQS queue with a 3-day delivery delay so that engineers can review it in the console, and have a Lambda function apply the plan when the message becomes visible
Run a Step Functions Express workflow that emails the plan to the engineer and uses a 3-day Wait state, followed by a Choice state that reads the decision from a DynamoDB item
Run a Step Functions Standard workflow with a .waitForTaskToken task that sends the plan and token to the engineer, resumed by SendTaskSuccess or SendTaskFailure
Have a Lambda function send the plan to the engineer and poll a DynamoDB table every minute until a decision is recorded, then apply or discard the plan from the same invocation
quiz.explain: A Standard workflow can wait days on a task token, records both approval and rejection in its execution history, and only proceeds after an explicit decision. Choice B fails because Express workflows run for at most 5 minutes and do not support the task token callback pattern.

days.recap: Use versioned Bedrock guardrails (denied topics, content and prompt attack filters, masking, contextual grounding) for model-independent safety, AgentCore Identity and per-tool least privilege to bound what agents can reach, and Step Functions Standard callbacks so humans approve high-risk AI actions.

days.title: Domain 2 Review: Security, Compliance, and Governance

concepts.heading: Identity: Federation, App Auth, and Least Privilege
concepts.body: Task 2.1 is about who can do what. Workforce access across accounts goes through IAM Identity Center federated over SAML 2.0 with SCIM provisioning; external pipelines federate with OIDC and AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; customer apps use Cognito user pools for tokens and identity pools for AWS credentials; pods get their own roles with EKS Pod Identity. Least privilege then layers controls that each answer a different question: trust policies and external IDs decide who may assume a role, session policies narrow one session, permissions boundaries cap roles that teams create, ABAC with session tags scales one policy across tenants, and source identity keeps chained sessions attributable. Workloads outside AWS use IAM Roles Anywhere certificates instead of keys. When options look similar, ask whether the requirement is about authentication, the ceiling for a principal, or a condition on attributes, because distractors swap these tools.

concepts.heading: Perimeters and Organization Guardrails
concepts.body: Data perimeters and organization policies stop mistakes from becoming exposures. SCPs cap what principals in member accounts can do (Region deny, protected security services, approved Bedrock models); RCPs cap what anyone can do to resources in member accounts (an organization-only identity perimeter for S3, KMS, STS, SQS and Secrets Manager, with an AWS service principal exemption). VPC endpoint policies with aws:ResourceOrgID keep traffic from private subnets inside the organization's resources, and Verified Access evaluates every request to private applications against identity and device posture. IAM Access Analyzer validates the result by finding external and unused access and by checking policies in pipelines. Control Tower turns these into managed preventive, detective and proactive controls per OU, Account Factory vends accounts with them already applied, and AWS RAM shares Transit Gateways and subnets so networks are not duplicated.

concepts.heading: Encryption Choices at a Glance
concepts.body: Task 2.2 decisions follow a short ladder. Customer managed KMS keys with automatic rotation are the default for data at rest; imported material, a CloudHSM key store or an external key store change where the key material lives, with XKS the only option that keeps it outside AWS. CloudHSM itself is the answer for single-tenant FIPS 140 Level 3 HSMs under exclusive customer control or PKCS#11, JCE and OpenSSL applications, with two HSMs in different AZs and backups copied to another Region. In transit, ACM supplies renewing public certificates, AWS Private CA supplies private ones (short-lived mode for high volume), and the load balancer listener security policy sets TLS 1.3. For post-quantum readiness, protect long-lived traffic with hybrid ML-KEM key exchange offered by the client, sign with ML-DSA keys in KMS, and build crypto agility with an inventory and KMS aliases.

concepts.heading: Logging, Monitoring, and Compliance Evidence
concepts.body: Tasks 2.3 and 2.4 reward knowing which record answers which question. Who called which API is CloudTrail, collected by an organization trail into a log archive account with log file validation and Object Lock. What a resource looked like on a date, and whether it was compliant, is AWS Config history delivered to a central bucket, with organization rules and SSM Automation remediation. Threats come from GuardDuty, posture checks and aggregation from Security Hub CSPM, and long-term security data from Security Lake. Vulnerabilities come from Inspector and are fixed by Patch Manager patch policies. What a model was asked and answered is Bedrock model invocation logging, configured per Region. Evidence of AWS's own controls and agreements such as a BAA comes from AWS Artifact. Residency requires checking every copy, including replicas, backups, multi-Region keys and cross-Region inference destinations.

concepts.heading: Responsible AI Controls
concepts.body: Task 2.5 combines three ideas. Content control: Bedrock Guardrails with denied topics, content and prompt attack filters, PII masking or blocking, and contextual grounding for RAG, released as immutable versions and applied to non-Bedrock models with ApplyGuardrail. Access control: AgentCore Identity for inbound authentication and outbound credential providers, one execution role per agent, one minimal role per tool, and deterministic authorization in tool backends using the authenticated user rather than model-supplied values. Human oversight: Step Functions Standard workflows with .waitForTaskToken, a timeout with escalation, and a deterministic Choice state so only high-risk actions wait for an authenticated reviewer. A recurring trap offers a system prompt instruction as the control; instructions reduce probability but never enforce a limit, so the correct answer puts the control outside the model.

examPoints: When a Domain 2 question lists several plausible security services, first decide whether it asks about identity, a policy ceiling, encryption, evidence, or AI safety, because each maps to a different family of controls.

Be suspicious of answers that rely on instructions, conventions or manual reviews (system prompts, session name runbooks, quarterly exports) when the requirement says must never or cannot be bypassed; the correct answer is usually a preventive control enforced by AWS.

quiz.q: A SaaS company runs one AI agent for hundreds of tenants. Its tools read a shared DynamoDB table whose partition key begins with the tenant ID, and tenants sign in with Amazon Cognito, which places the tenant ID in the access token. The company must guarantee that a tool call for one tenant can never read another tenant's items, even if the model is manipulated into supplying a different tenant ID, without creating per-tenant infrastructure. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Have the tool backend assume a role with a TenantId session tag from the validated token, under a policy that requires dynamodb:LeadingKeys to match that tag
Place the tenant ID in the agent's system prompt for each session and instruct the model to always pass it to the tools, then add a guardrail denied topic that covers other tenants' data
Filter query results in the tool code by comparing each item's tenant attribute with the tenant ID argument that the model passes to the tool, and log any mismatches for review
Deploy a separate agent runtime, tool set and DynamoDB table per tenant in its own AWS account through Account Factory, and route each request to the tenant's account by subdomain
quiz.explain: Session tags from the verified token scope the credentials themselves, so DynamoDB rejects any request for another tenant's partition key no matter what the model asks. Choice C fails because the filter trusts the tenant ID that the model supplies, which is exactly the value an injection can change, and the credentials can still read every tenant.

quiz.q: A financial company has 300 accounts in AWS Organizations. Auditors pick a date each quarter and ask whether any security group allowed inbound SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 on that date, which resource it was, and when it was fixed. Evidence older than 90 days is often missing. Which solution provides this evidence with the LEAST ongoing manual effort?
choices: Enable Security Hub CSPM with central configuration and export the failed control findings to a spreadsheet at the end of each quarter for the auditors to review
Enable VPC Flow Logs in every VPC to a central bucket and use Amazon Athena to search for accepted connections on port 22 from public addresses on each requested date
Search CloudTrail event history in each account for AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress calls each quarter and record the results in a central evidence register
Record security groups and their compliance with AWS Config, deploy restricted-ssh as an organization rule, and query the central history files with Athena
quiz.explain: Config records each security group's configuration and compliance changes with timestamps, so any date can be answered from the central history files. Choice B fails because flow logs record traffic, not configuration; an open rule with no SSH traffic that day leaves no trace in the flow logs.

days.recap: Domain 2 asks you to combine federated identity and least privilege, organization-wide perimeters and guardrails, the right encryption and key placement, complete and tamper-resistant evidence, and AI controls that live outside the model.

days.title: Purchase Options and Rightsizing: On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot, Capacity Reservations, Graviton, and Compute Optimizer

concepts.heading: Matching Purchase Options to the Usage Curve
concepts.body: Cost-optimized purchasing starts with the shape of the workload. Draw the hourly usage curve and split it into layers. The steady floor that runs around the clock for a year or more belongs on a commitment (Savings Plans or Reserved Instances). Predictable but variable usage above the floor is covered by On-Demand, ideally reduced with scheduled or target tracking scaling so idle capacity disappears. Fault-tolerant, interruptible work such as batch processing, CI builds, rendering or stateless web tiers behind a load balancer can run on Spot Instances at a deep discount, with the understanding that EC2 can reclaim them with a two-minute interruption notice. For example, a fleet that never drops below 40 instances, peaks at 120 on weekdays, and runs nightly batch jobs would commit for about 40, scale On-Demand for the daytime peak, and run the batch on Spot. Committing to the peak is the classic over-purchase trap.

concepts.heading: Savings Plans Versus Reserved Instances
concepts.body: Both trade a one- or three-year commitment for a lower rate, with No Upfront, Partial Upfront or All Upfront payment. Compute Savings Plans commit to a dollar amount per hour and apply automatically to EC2 in any family, size, operating system or Region, plus AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda, which makes them the safest choice when the architecture may change. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give a deeper discount for one instance family in one Region while still allowing size and OS changes. Standard Reserved Instances offer similar savings for a specific instance type, and Convertible RIs can be exchanged for other types. Regional RIs apply discounts flexibly across AZs, while zonal RIs also reserve capacity in one AZ. SageMaker AI usage is covered only by SageMaker AI Savings Plans, not EC2 plans or RIs. When a scenario mentions migrating from EC2 to containers or serverless during the term, Compute Savings Plans keep the discount.

concepts.heading: Capacity-Based Options and Spot Strategy
concepts.body: Discounts and guaranteed capacity are different things. On-Demand Capacity Reservations reserve instances in a specific AZ for as long as you need, billed at the On-Demand rate whether used or not; they carry no discount by themselves, but a Savings Plan or regional RI applies to them, so you can combine guaranteed capacity with a discount for events such as a product launch or DR readiness. EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML reserve GPU instances for a defined future period for training jobs. Spot is the opposite trade: lowest price, no guarantee. To make Spot reliable, diversify across many instance types and AZs with an Auto Scaling group using a mixed instances policy and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy, keep a base of On-Demand instances, react to interruption notices or rebalance recommendations, and checkpoint long jobs. A Spot fleet pinned to one instance type in one AZ is a reliability anti-pattern.

concepts.heading: Architecture Choices That Change the Bill
concepts.body: Some cost decisions are architectural. AWS Graviton (Arm) instances, available for EC2, Lambda, Fargate, RDS, Aurora and ElastiCache, typically deliver up to about 40% better price-performance than comparable x86 instances, provided the code and container images build for arm64; managed services often need only a configuration change. Lambda is cheapest for spiky or low-utilization work because idle time costs nothing, while containers or EC2 win for steady, high-utilization services where per-request pricing would add up. Step Functions has two price models: Standard workflows bill per state transition and suit long-running, auditable, exactly-once processes, while Express workflows bill per request and by duration and memory, which is far cheaper for high-volume, short event processing that finishes within 5 minutes. For example, millions of IoT messages per day transformed in a few seconds each belong in Express workflows.

concepts.heading: Rightsizing with AWS Compute Optimizer
concepts.body: Rightsizing means matching resources to measured demand before or alongside buying commitments; committing first locks in waste. AWS Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics and recommends better configurations for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, Lambda functions, ECS services on Fargate and more, labeling resources as over-provisioned, under-provisioned or optimized and estimating savings, including moves to Graviton. Memory utilization is not a default EC2 metric, so install the CloudWatch agent to get memory-aware recommendations. The default lookback is 14 days; enhanced infrastructure metrics extend it to three months to capture monthly cycles, at extra cost. Enable it for the whole organization from the management account or a delegated administrator. Cost Explorer's rightsizing recommendations and Savings Plans recommendations then help size the commitment on the rightsized baseline. A question that asks for data-driven sizing with minimal effort points to Compute Optimizer.

concepts.heading: Scaling Policies and Fargate Spot
concepts.body: Elastic scaling turns idle capacity into savings. Target tracking keeps a metric near a target, such as average CPU at 50% or ALB requests per target at 1,000, and adds or removes capacity automatically. Scheduled scaling handles known patterns, for example scaling a development environment to zero at 20:00 and back up at 07:00 on weekdays, or raising minimum capacity before a daily batch window. Predictive scaling forecasts recurring daily and weekly cycles to launch capacity ahead of demand. For containers, Amazon ECS capacity provider strategies can mix FARGATE and FARGATE_SPOT: a base of tasks on regular Fargate guarantees the minimum, and a weight sends most additional tasks to Fargate Spot at a deep discount, which suits interruption-tolerant workers and queue consumers. Fargate Spot tasks receive a two-minute warning (SIGTERM) before interruption, so applications should drain gracefully. Scaling plus rightsizing comes first, commitments second.

examPoints: A question with a steady baseline, a changing compute mix, or a planned move to Fargate or Lambda is testing Compute Savings Plans over EC2 Instance Savings Plans or Reserved Instances.

A question that needs guaranteed capacity in one AZ for an event is testing On-Demand Capacity Reservations (combined with a Savings Plan for the discount), while one about interruption-tolerant work is testing Spot or Fargate Spot with diversification.
A question about high-volume, short workflows costing too much on Step Functions is testing a move from Standard to Express workflows.

quiz.q: A company runs a web platform on EC2 in two Regions with a steady baseline of about 80 vCPUs around the clock. Over the next three years it plans to move several services to Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate and some event processing to AWS Lambda, and it may change instance families as it adopts Graviton. Which purchase option gives the largest commitment discount that will keep applying through these changes?
choices: Three-year Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance types in each Region, sold on the Reserved Instance Marketplace when services move to containers
Three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the current instance family in each Region, which allow changes of size and operating system within that family
A three-year Compute Savings Plan sized to the steady hourly baseline, which applies across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda
On-Demand Capacity Reservations for the baseline in each Region, which lock in a lower hourly rate for as long as the reservations remain active
quiz.explain: A Compute Savings Plan applies to EC2 in any family or Region and to Fargate and Lambda, so the discount follows the workload as it changes. Choice B fails because EC2 Instance Savings Plans are tied to one instance family in one Region and do not cover Fargate or Lambda.

quiz.q: A media company runs video thumbnail workers as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate that pull jobs from an Amazon SQS queue. Jobs can be retried, and the queue depth varies widely during the day. At least four workers must always be running, and the company wants to cut compute cost without managing instances. What should a solutions architect do?
choices: Move the workers to EC2 Spot Instances in a single instance type and AZ with an ECS capacity provider, and set the Auto Scaling group minimum to four instances
Use a capacity provider strategy with a base of four tasks on FARGATE and a higher weight on FARGATE_SPOT, scale the service on queue depth, and handle SIGTERM to finish or release jobs
Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the Fargate vCPU and memory used by the workers, and keep the service at a fixed size that covers the busiest hour of the day
Run all workers on FARGATE_SPOT only with a desired count of four, and add a scheduled scaling action that doubles the count during business hours
quiz.explain: The FARGATE base guarantees four workers, Fargate Spot carries the variable extra tasks at a discount, and queue-based scaling removes idle tasks; retryable jobs tolerate interruptions. Choice C fails because EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not apply to Fargate, and sizing for the busiest hour leaves most capacity idle.

days.recap: Commit only to the rightsized steady baseline (Compute Savings Plans for flexibility), cover peaks with scaled On-Demand, run interruptible work on Spot or Fargate Spot, reserve capacity only when it must be guaranteed, and use Graviton, Lambda versus containers, and Express versus Standard workflows as architectural cost levers.

days.title: AI/ML Cost Optimization: Bedrock Pricing Modes, Service Tiers, Prompt Caching, Model Choice, SageMaker AI Endpoints, and Cross-Region Inference

concepts.heading: Bedrock Pricing Modes: On-Demand, Batch, and Provisioned Throughput
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock bills foundation model inference in three main ways. On-demand charges per input and output token with no commitment; every call is synchronous and the account's requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute quotas cap how fast a large job can run. Batch inference takes prompts as JSONL records in Amazon S3, runs them asynchronously with CreateModelInvocationJob, writes results to an S3 output prefix, and is priced lower than on-demand for supported models. It suits catalog enrichment, document summaries and nightly classification where no user waits and the deadline is hours. Provisioned Throughput buys model units billed every hour, with or without a term commitment, whether used or not, so it suits steady, predictable traffic or models that require it, such as some custom models. A common trap sizes Provisioned Throughput for a few hours of nightly peak and pays for it all day; a large latency-tolerant job belongs in batch.

concepts.heading: Bedrock Service Tiers: Standard, Priority, Flex, and Reserved
concepts.body: For supported models, Bedrock lets you choose a service tier per request with the optional service_tier parameter. Standard is the default with normal on-demand pricing. Priority gives preferential processing for latency-critical traffic at a premium. Flex gives a discounted price for work that can accept longer processing times, such as evaluations, summarization or agent steps that are not user-facing. Reserved is a capacity reservation of tokens per minute for one or three months, arranged through the account team and billed monthly. Because the tier is set on each call, one application can use Flex for a back-office agent while its chat feature stays on Standard. Know the difference between Flex and batch: Flex is still a synchronous call that returns each result, so a multi-step agent can chain steps; batch returns all results when the job finishes, which only fits independent records. Priority never lowers cost.

concepts.heading: Prompt Caching and Response Caching
concepts.body: Many applications send the same long prefix with every request: instructions, a policy handbook, tool definitions or few-shot examples. Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, on supported models, lets you mark a cache checkpoint, for example a cachePoint block in the Converse API, after that static prefix. Later requests that start with exactly the same prefix read it from the cache at a reduced rate and skip reprocessing, so cost and time to first token both drop. Order matters: static content first, the changing user question last, because any change before the checkpoint breaks the match. The cache expires a short time after its last use and each model has a minimum prefix length. For example, a 30,000-token handbook sent with every adjuster question becomes a cached prefix. Separately, applications can cache complete answers to frequent identical questions in a store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB, so no model call is made at all.

concepts.heading: Choosing the Right Model Size
concepts.body: The biggest AI cost lever is often the model itself. Larger models in a family cost more per token and respond more slowly, yet many requests are simple. Evaluate smaller models on your own prompts before defaulting to the largest one. When traffic mixes simple and complex prompts, Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing sends each request to the cheaper of two models in the same family when it predicts similar quality, and to the stronger model otherwise; the application calls the router ARN instead of a model ID and the response reports which model answered. Token discipline adds up too: trim conversation history, retrieve fewer and better chunks in RAG instead of stuffing the context, set sensible maximum output tokens, and ask for concise structured output. For example, a help desk where most questions are how-to requests can route most traffic to the small model without hand-written classification rules.

concepts.heading: SageMaker AI Inference Cost Options
concepts.body: Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint types differ sharply in cost. Real-time endpoints bill per instance-hour for every instance behind them and suit steady, low-latency traffic; serverless inference bills per request and duration with no idle cost, runs without GPUs and suits intermittent traffic that tolerates cold starts; asynchronous inference queues large or long requests and can scale to zero instances when the queue is empty; batch transform runs a job over a dataset in S3 with no persistent endpoint. For steady real-time endpoints, two levers stand out. A SageMaker AI Savings Plan commits to hourly SageMaker spend for one or three years and applies across instance families and Regions; EC2 plans and RIs do not cover SageMaker instances. AWS Inferentia2 instances (ml.inf2), with models compiled by the AWS Neuron SDK, often lower the cost per inference after benchmarking. Multi-model endpoints and inference components let several models share instances. Managed Spot is a training feature, not an endpoint option.

concepts.heading: Cross-Region Inference and AI Data Transfer
concepts.body: A cross-Region inference profile lets Bedrock serve a request in another Region of the profile when the source Region is busy, which raises on-demand throughput without paying for reserved capacity. Geographic profiles (for example the US or EU profile) stay within a geography; global profiles can use supported Regions worldwide. Billing is at the source Region's token price with no additional routing or inter-Region transfer charge, and data at rest such as invocation logs stays in the source Region, but inference runs in the destination, so residency rules decide between geographic and global. The application still calls only its source Region, so one interface VPC endpoint for bedrock-runtime there is enough; no endpoints or peering are needed in destination Regions. Interface endpoints also avoid NAT gateway per-GB processing for large payloads such as scanned documents. Region-restriction SCPs and IAM must allow the Bedrock invoke actions in every destination Region.

examPoints: A question about millions of latency-tolerant prompts with a deadline of hours is testing Bedrock batch inference, while one about a synchronous agent that tolerates slower answers is testing the Flex service tier.

A question in which every request repeats a long, stable document or instruction block is testing prompt caching with the static prefix first, and one about a mix of easy and hard prompts is testing Intelligent Prompt Routing or a smaller model.

A question about bursts beyond on-demand quotas without idle capacity is testing cross-Region inference profiles (geographic when processing must stay in a geography), and one about steady SageMaker AI endpoints is testing SageMaker AI Savings Plans and Inferentia2.

quiz.q: An insurer's claims assistant calls an Amazon Bedrock model through the Converse API. Every request sends the same 30,000-token policy handbook and fixed instructions, followed by a short question from an adjuster. Token costs and time to first response are higher than planned, and the handbook changes once a quarter. What should a solutions architect recommend?
choices: Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the model, because model units are not billed per input token and so the repeated handbook would no longer add cost to each request
Move the adjuster's question to the start of each prompt and append the handbook after it, so the model reads the relevant text first and processes less of the handbook
Raise the maxTokens inference parameter and lower the temperature, so that each answer is complete in one pass and adjusters send fewer follow-up questions
Place the handbook and instructions first in each prompt with a cache checkpoint after them, so Bedrock prompt caching reuses the prefix and only the question is processed fresh
quiz.explain: Prompt caching turns the identical 30,000-token prefix into a cached read at a reduced rate and skips reprocessing, which lowers both cost and latency. Choice A fails because Provisioned Throughput charges for reserved model units every hour and the model still reprocesses the handbook on each request, so latency does not improve.

quiz.q: A company serves a fine-tuned model from a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on GPU instances. Traffic is steady around the clock and will remain so for at least three years, and the latency SLO must be kept. The finance team asks for the commitment-based discount that applies to this endpoint. What should a solutions architect recommend?
choices: Purchase a three-year SageMaker AI Savings Plan for the steady hourly SageMaker spend, which applies to real-time inference instances across instance families and Regions
Purchase three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plans for the GPU instance family, because SageMaker AI endpoint instances are billed as regular EC2 usage in the account
Purchase three-year Standard Reserved Instances for the GPU instance type in the endpoint's Region, and attach them to the endpoint configuration by instance type
Switch the endpoint to managed Spot capacity with checkpointing, and keep one On-Demand instance as a fallback so that the latency SLO is maintained during interruptions
quiz.explain: SageMaker AI Savings Plans are the commitment that covers SageMaker inference instances, and three steady years is the ideal case for them. Choice B fails because SageMaker instances are billed by SageMaker, not as EC2 usage, so EC2 Savings Plans and Reserved Instances give no discount.

days.recap: Match Bedrock spend to the workload with on-demand, batch, service tiers or Provisioned Throughput, cut tokens with prompt caching and right-sized models, commit to steady SageMaker AI endpoints with SageMaker AI Savings Plans and Inferentia2, and use cross-Region inference for burst capacity at the source Region's price.

days.title: Data Transfer and Network Costs: CloudFront and Origin Shield, VPC Endpoints Versus NAT, AZ-Aware Design, Replication, and Transit Gateway Versus PrivateLink

concepts.heading: The Data Transfer Price Map
concepts.body: Network cost questions are easier with a mental price map. Data coming into AWS from the internet is free, and data going out to the internet is charged per GB. Traffic between Availability Zones in the same Region is charged per GB in each direction, while traffic within one AZ over private IP addresses is free. Traffic between Regions is charged per GB by the sending side, so replication and cross-Region calls add up. On top of transfer, some services add a processing charge per GB: NAT gateways, Transit Gateway, interface VPC endpoints and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints. Data transferred from AWS origins such as S3, ALB or EC2 to CloudFront is not charged, and CloudFront's own delivery rates to viewers are generally lower than serving directly from the origin. When a scenario shows a surprising networking line in Cost Explorer, identify which of these boundaries the traffic crosses before choosing a fix.

concepts.heading: CloudFront Caching, Origin Shield, and Origin Failover
concepts.body: Amazon CloudFront lowers both latency and origin cost when the cache hit ratio is high. Cache policies decide the cache key: forward only the headers, cookies and query strings the origin really needs, because each extra value fragments the cache and sends more requests to the origin. Long TTLs with versioned file names avoid frequent invalidations. Origin Shield adds a centralized caching layer in one Region close to your origin, in front of the regional edge caches, so requests from many edge locations collapse into a single origin fetch; it raises the hit ratio and cuts origin load and egress for globally distributed traffic, live video or a multi-CDN setup, for an added per-request charge. For origin selection, serve S3 content through origin access control and keep dynamic paths on an ALB behind the same distribution. Origin groups provide failover to a secondary origin on chosen error codes, which suits a replicated bucket in a second Region.

concepts.heading: NAT Gateways Versus VPC Endpoints
concepts.body: A NAT gateway charges per hour and per GB processed, so private subnets that move a lot of data to AWS services through it pay for every gigabyte. Gateway VPC endpoints for Amazon S3 and DynamoDB have no charge at all and keep traffic private, so adding them to route tables is usually the first fix when NAT processing is dominated by S3 or DynamoDB traffic. Gateway endpoints work only for traffic that starts in their own VPC, so each VPC that moves bulk data needs its own. Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) exist for most other services, including Bedrock runtime, and charge per endpoint per AZ per hour plus a per-GB charge that is lower than NAT processing. When many spoke VPCs each hold lightly used interface endpoints, centralize them in a shared services VPC with Route 53 private hosted zones associated with the spokes; for example, 50 VPCs times 12 services times 3 AZs collapses to 36 endpoint-AZs.

concepts.heading: Availability Zone-Aware Architecture
concepts.body: Spreading across AZs is essential for resilience, but chatty traffic that crosses AZs pays per GB in both directions. Cost-aware designs keep high-volume conversations inside an AZ while keeping capacity in several AZs. Examples include sending application traffic to the database reader or cache node in the same AZ, using Kubernetes topology-aware routing so services prefer endpoints in their own zone, and configuring Kafka consumers on Amazon MSK to fetch from the closest replica. Load balancers differ: an Application Load Balancer balances across zones by default (cross-zone can be turned off only per target group) with no inter-AZ charge for that hop, while a Network Load Balancer has cross-zone load balancing off by default and charges inter-AZ transfer when you turn it on. Very large flows between two services can be co-located in one AZ only if the resilience requirement allows it. The exam usually rewards the answer that cuts inter-AZ bytes without giving up multi-AZ availability.

concepts.heading: Cost-Aware Multi-Region Replication
concepts.body: Every replicated byte pays inter-Region transfer plus storage and requests in the destination, so replicate deliberately. S3 Cross-Region Replication rules can filter by prefix or tag so only the data the DR or residency plan needs is copied, and they can write replicas into a cheaper storage class such as S3 Standard-IA or S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval in the destination. S3 Replication Time Control adds a 15-minute replication SLA for an extra charge, so use it only when an RPO demands it. DynamoDB global tables bill replicated writes in every replica Region plus inter-Region transfer, so put only tables that truly need multi-Region active writes into global tables, and keep large, rarely changed or Regional-only data elsewhere. AWS Backup copy actions should match the Regional RPO, for example one weekly copy kept 28 days rather than every daily backup. Cost-aware replication sizes copy scope and frequency to the requirement.

concepts.heading: Transit Gateway, VPC Peering, and PrivateLink Pricing
concepts.body: The three VPC-to-VPC options are billed differently. A Transit Gateway charges per attachment per hour plus a data processing charge per GB sent into it, so every byte between two attached VPCs pays processing. VPC peering has no hourly or processing charge; traffic within one AZ over peering is free and cross-AZ traffic pays the normal inter-AZ rate. AWS PrivateLink charges per interface endpoint per AZ per hour plus a per-GB charge, and the provider runs a Network Load Balancer, but it exposes only one service rather than whole networks. A common optimization keeps the Transit Gateway as the hub for most VPCs and adds peering for the few pairs that move very large volumes, using more specific routes such as a /16 to the peering connection beside a 10.0.0.0/8 route to the Transit Gateway. Consolidating a heavy peering mesh onto a Transit Gateway can raise the bill even though routing becomes simpler.

examPoints: A question in which NAT gateway processing is dominated by S3 or DynamoDB traffic is testing free gateway endpoints in each VPC, while one about many idle interface endpoints across spokes is testing centralized endpoints with shared private hosted zones.
A question about one VPC pair moving hundreds of terabytes through a Transit Gateway is testing VPC peering with more specific routes, because peering has no per-GB processing charge.

A question about origin load and egress for global viewers is testing CloudFront cache policies and Origin Shield, and one about replication cost is testing filtered S3 replication into cheaper storage classes and global tables only where needed.

quiz.q: A company connects 35 VPCs in one Region through a Transit Gateway, and every VPC route table sends 10.0.0.0/8 to it. A data lake VPC (10.20.0.0/16) and an analytics VPC (10.30.0.0/16) exchange about 400 TB per month, mostly between subnets in the same Availability Zones, and this traffic is now the largest line on the network bill. All other VPC pairs must keep using the Transit Gateway. Which change reduces cost the most with the least redesign?
choices: Create a VPC peering connection between the two VPCs and add routes for each other's /16 CIDR to the peering connection, keeping the 10.0.0.0/8 route to the Transit Gateway
Enable appliance mode on both Transit Gateway VPC attachments so that the traffic between the two VPCs stays in one Availability Zone and avoids the data processing charge
Move both VPC attachments into a separate Transit Gateway route table that contains only each other's routes, so their traffic is billed as attachment hours instead of per GB
Expose the data lake through an endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer and consume it from the analytics VPC through an interface endpoint powered by PrivateLink
quiz.explain: Peering has no per-GB processing charge and same-AZ traffic over it is free, and the more specific /16 routes divert only this pair while every other destination still uses the Transit Gateway. Choice C fails because every GB sent into a Transit Gateway is billed for processing no matter which route table it uses.

quiz.q: Application servers in private subnets of a VPC download about 60 TB per month from Amazon S3 buckets in the same Region and write results back to DynamoDB. The NAT gateway data processing charge has become the largest item on the bill. Security wants this traffic kept off the internet path. What is the most cost-effective change?
choices: Create interface VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB in every Availability Zone with private DNS enabled, and remove the NAT gateway from the private route tables
Move the application servers to public subnets with public IP addresses and an internet gateway, so that S3 and DynamoDB traffic no longer passes through the NAT gateway
Create gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB and add them to the private subnet route tables, so this traffic bypasses the NAT gateway at no additional charge
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance on a Graviton-based EC2 instance, which has no per-GB processing charge, and scale it vertically as traffic grows
quiz.explain: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB carry the traffic privately with no hourly or per-GB charge, removing it from NAT processing. Choice A would also remove NAT processing but adds per-AZ hourly and per-GB endpoint charges that gateway endpoints avoid, so it is not the most cost-effective.

days.recap: Know which boundary each byte crosses, raise CloudFront hit ratios with lean cache keys and Origin Shield, replace NAT processing with free gateway endpoints and shared interface endpoints, keep chatty traffic in-AZ, replicate only what the RPO needs, and add peering beside a Transit Gateway for heavy pairs.

days.title: Cost Allocation and Visibility: Tagging Strategy and Enforcement, Cost Explorer, Data Exports, Cost Categories, Split Cost Allocation, Budgets, and Anomaly Detection

concepts.heading: Designing a Tagging Strategy for Cost Allocation
concepts.body: Cost allocation has two data sources. The account structure assigns every charge, including charges that cannot carry tags such as some data transfer and support fees, so dimensions that must be 100% complete, such as business unit and environment, belong in accounts and OUs (for example retail-prod under a Retail OU). Tags then give finer splits inside an account, such as Project, CostCenter, Owner and Application. Keep the mandatory set small, define exact key names and allowed values, and document them. A resource tag appears in billing data only after its key is activated as a cost allocation tag on the Billing console, which in an organization is done once in the management account; new keys can take up to 24 hours to appear and another 24 hours to activate, and earlier months are not tagged unless a backfill is requested. Tag dependent resources at creation: launch template tag specifications for volumes and Data Lifecycle Manager copy-tags for snapshots.

concepts.heading: Enforcing Tags with Policies
concepts.body: Tagging only works when it is enforced, and three controls work together. Tag policies in AWS Organizations standardize tag keys (including capitalization) and allowed values, report noncompliance, and, with enforcement enabled for chosen resource types, prevent tagging operations that use noncompliant values. They do not by themselves force a tag to exist. To require a tag at creation, use an SCP that denies create actions such as ec2:RunInstances when the request lacks the tag, with a Null condition on aws:RequestTag/CostCenter. To detect resources that slipped through, deploy the AWS Config required-tags managed rule as an organization rule, with remediation or a ticket. Infrastructure as code and Service Catalog TagOptions make the right tags the default. For example, CostCenter values limited by a tag policy, required by an SCP on RunInstances and CreateVolume, and audited by required-tags give preventive and detective coverage.

concepts.heading: Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report via Data Exports
concepts.body: AWS Cost Explorer is the interactive view: filter and group cost and usage by service, linked account, Region, usage type, cost allocation tag or cost category, look back over past months, and forecast future spend. It also offers Savings Plans and Reserved Instance coverage, utilization and purchase recommendations. For detailed analysis, AWS Data Exports delivers the Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) to an S3 bucket, with hourly or daily line items, resource IDs, tags, cost categories, and amortized and net costs, in Parquet for querying with Amazon Athena or loading into a BI tool such as Amazon Quick Sight; a FOCUS-format export is also available for multi-cloud reporting. Create the export in the management account to cover every member account. A finance team that needs per-resource, hourly data joined with its own business data should get a CUR export queried with Athena, not screenshots from Cost Explorer.

concepts.heading: Chargeback and Showback with Cost Categories and Split Cost Allocation
concepts.body: Showback reports costs to teams; chargeback actually bills them. Cost categories turn raw billing dimensions into business groups with rules on linked account, tag, service or another cost category, for example Retail equals the retail accounts plus anything tagged BusinessUnit=Retail. Split charge rules divide shared costs, such as a shared networking account or support fees, across categories proportionally, evenly or by fixed percentages. Cost categories appear in Cost Explorer, Budgets and the CUR. Shared container clusters need one more step: split cost allocation data for Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS allocates the cost of the underlying EC2 instances to individual tasks or pods based on their CPU and memory reservation or usage, and adds those amounts to the CUR, so namespaces, services or teams on one cluster can be charged without separate clusters. Enable it in the Billing preferences of the management account.

concepts.heading: Showback for Amazon Bedrock Token Usage
concepts.body: Generative AI costs need their own allocation design because many teams call the same model in one account, and the bill shows one line per model per Region. AWS-provided foundation models cannot be tagged, so create an application inference profile per team or application from the model, tag it with keys such as business-unit, and have each application invoke the profile ARN instead of the model ID. Once the tag key is activated as a cost allocation tag, Cost Explorer and the CUR split Bedrock cost by team. For in-month token showback, Bedrock publishes CloudWatch metrics such as InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount, and model invocation logging records the token counts for each call with the profile or model used and the caller identity, which CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena can sum per team. Account separation still works when teams have their own accounts. Tagged application inference profiles are the exam answer for shared models.

concepts.heading: Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection
concepts.body: Visibility is not enough without alerts. AWS Budgets tracks cost, usage, Savings Plans or RI coverage and utilization against a threshold for a month, quarter or year, filtered by account, tag or cost category, and alerts on actual or forecasted spend through email or Amazon SNS, for example at 80% actual and 100% forecasted. Budget actions can respond automatically by applying an IAM policy or an SCP that blocks new resource creation, or by stopping specific EC2 or RDS instances, optionally after an approval. AWS Cost Anomaly Detection uses machine learning to learn normal spending patterns per monitor (by AWS service, linked account, cost allocation tag or cost category), flags unusual spikes even when no fixed threshold is crossed, reports the likely root cause such as service, account, Region and usage type, and sends alerts individually or as daily or weekly summaries. Use Budgets for known limits and Anomaly Detection for surprises.

examPoints: A question in which tags exist on resources but not in Cost Explorer or the CUR is testing activation of cost allocation tags in the management account; one about requiring a tag at creation is testing an SCP with aws:RequestTag, while tag policies standardize values.

A question about charging teams for shared EKS or ECS clusters is testing split cost allocation data, and one about splitting shared Bedrock model costs is testing tagged application inference profiles plus invocation logs or token metrics.

A question about unexpected spend spikes without a predefined threshold is testing Cost Anomaly Detection, while one about stopping spend when a limit is reached is testing Budgets with budget actions.

quiz.q: A company uses AWS Organizations with consolidated billing. Two months ago, platform teams began tagging all resources in member accounts with a CostCenter key, and the tags are visible on the resources. The finance team in the management account still cannot group by CostCenter in Cost Explorer or see it as a column in the CUR export. What should the company do?
choices: Attach a tag policy for CostCenter to the organization root with enforcement turned on, which publishes the tag key into the billing data of every member account
Activate CostCenter as a user-defined cost allocation tag in the management account's Billing console and allow time for the activation to take effect
Deploy the AWS Config required-tags rule in every member account, so that billing reads the recorded tag values from the configuration items of each resource
Create a CUR export in each member account with resource IDs, and join the exports with tag values listed by the Resource Groups Tagging API in Athena
quiz.explain: Billing tools use only tag keys that have been activated as cost allocation tags, and the management account activates them for the whole organization. Choice A fails because tag policies standardize keys and values and can block noncompliant tagging, but they do not activate a key for cost allocation.

quiz.q: Five product teams run their services in separate Kubernetes namespaces on one shared Amazon EKS cluster with EC2 worker nodes. Finance wants each team's monthly share of the cluster's compute cost in the Cost and Usage Report, based on what each team's pods actually request, without splitting the cluster. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST effort?
choices: Tag each worker node with the name of the team whose pods run on it most often, activate the tag for cost allocation, and add a pod affinity rule that keeps teams on their own nodes
Create a cost category with a split charge rule that divides the cluster's EC2 cost evenly across the five teams, and publish the result as a monthly showback report
Install an open-source cost tool in the cluster, export its namespace estimates to Amazon S3 each day, and have finance join them with the CUR in Athena every month
Enable split cost allocation data for Amazon EKS in the management account's Billing preferences, and report each team's pod costs by namespace from the CUR export
quiz.explain: Split cost allocation data allocates the EC2 instance cost to pods by their CPU and memory and writes it into the CUR, so namespaces can be charged without separate clusters. Choice B fails because an even split ignores how much each team's pods actually request, so it is an estimate, not an allocation.

days.recap: Put must-complete dimensions in accounts and finer splits in enforced, activated tags; analyze with Cost Explorer and CUR 2.0 from Data Exports; allocate shared costs with cost categories, split cost allocation data and tagged Bedrock application inference profiles; and alert with Budgets and Cost Anomaly Detection.

days.title: Storage, Database, and Observability Costs: S3 Tiering, EFS Lifecycle, EBS Volume Types, DynamoDB and Aurora Pricing, Backup Retention, and Log Costs

concepts.heading: S3 Intelligent-Tiering and Lifecycle Policies
concepts.body: Amazon S3 storage cost depends on matching the storage class to access. When access patterns are unknown or change, S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object automatically between frequent, infrequent and archive instant access tiers based on its own access history, with no retrieval fees, for a small monthly monitoring charge per object; objects smaller than 128 KB are not monitored and stay in the frequent tier, and optional Archive Access and Deep Archive Access tiers can be enabled for data that may wait hours. When the pattern is known, lifecycle rules are cheaper: transition logs to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for rarely read data that still needs millisecond access, to Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive for archives, and expire them when retention ends. Remember minimum storage durations (30 days for Standard-IA, 90 for Glacier Instant and Flexible, 180 for Deep Archive), expire noncurrent versions and abort incomplete multipart uploads.

concepts.heading: Glacier Classes and EFS Lifecycle Management
concepts.body: The S3 Glacier storage classes trade retrieval speed for price. Glacier Instant Retrieval returns data in milliseconds for archives read about once a quarter. Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, with free bulk retrievals, for backups and archives read once or twice a year. Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest, with retrievals within 12 hours (bulk up to 48), for data kept for compliance and almost never read. Pick the class from the realistic restore deadline: a three-day audit window tolerates Deep Archive, an incident investigation that needs files today does not. Amazon EFS has the same idea for file systems: lifecycle management moves files that have not been accessed for a set period, such as 30 days, from EFS Standard to EFS Infrequent Access and then to EFS Archive, and can move a file back to Standard on its first access. EFS One Zone classes cost less when single-AZ resilience is acceptable.

concepts.heading: EBS Volume Types: gp3, gp2, and io2
concepts.body: On gp2 volumes, performance is tied to size at 3 IOPS per GiB with burst credits for small volumes, so teams often over-provision capacity just to get IOPS. gp3 decouples them: every volume gets a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, you can provision more IOPS and throughput independently, and the price per GB is lower than gp2. For example, a 200 GiB gp2 volume has a 600 IOPS baseline; reaching 6,000 IOPS on gp2 would need about 2,000 GiB, while gp3 delivers 6,000 IOPS on the 200 GiB volume. Migrating gp2 to gp3 is done in place with Elastic Volumes and no downtime. io2 Block Express is for databases that need sub-millisecond latency, very high IOPS and higher durability, at a higher price, so reserve it for workloads that measurably need it. Throughput-optimized st1 and cold sc1 HDD volumes suit large sequential data. Compute Optimizer flags over-provisioned volumes.

concepts.heading: DynamoDB Capacity Modes and Table Classes
concepts.body: DynamoDB has two capacity modes. On-demand bills per read and write request with no capacity planning and suits new, spiky or unpredictable tables, including tables that are idle much of the time. Provisioned capacity bills per hour for the read and write capacity units you set, with auto scaling following target utilization, and is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic; reserved capacity, a one- or three-year commitment available in provisioned mode, lowers the rate further for the stable floor. You can switch between modes, with limits on how often. Table classes add a storage lever: DynamoDB Standard-IA has much cheaper storage but higher request prices, so it suits large tables that are read rarely, such as old orders kept for customer service. TTL deletes expired items at no write cost, which shrinks storage. For example, a steady 2,000 writes per second table belongs in provisioned mode with reserved capacity, a seasonal campaign table on-demand.

concepts.heading: RDS and Aurora: Reserved Instances, Serverless v2, I/O-Optimized, and Database Savings Plans
concepts.body: For steady relational databases, RDS reserved DB instances trade a one- or three-year term for a lower rate, often with size flexibility within an instance family. Aurora Serverless v2 scales in Aurora capacity units (ACUs) between a minimum and maximum you set, which suits variable or intermittent databases, and on supported versions can scale to 0 ACUs, pausing when idle so no compute is billed; a steady, busy database is usually cheaper on provisioned instances. Aurora storage has two configurations: Aurora Standard bills I/O per request, while Aurora I/O-Optimized has no I/O charges but higher instance and storage prices, and is the better choice when I/O is 25% or more of Aurora spend. Database Savings Plans commit to hourly spend across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache and other database services, regardless of engine, instance family, size or Region and including serverless usage, so the discount follows a move such as RDS for Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL.

concepts.heading: Backup Retention and Observability Spend
concepts.body: Backups and logs grow silently, so retention is a cost design. In AWS Backup, cold storage is cheaper but requires retention at least 90 days beyond the transition, so keep short operational backups (for example 35 days) warm and move long compliance copies (for example monthly for 7 years) to cold storage after 30 days. Match cross-Region copy frequency to the Regional RPO rather than copying every daily backup. For EBS, Data Lifecycle Manager can keep daily snapshots incremental in the standard tier and move quarterly snapshots to the EBS Snapshots Archive, which stores full copies cheaply but needs 24 to 72 hours to restore. For observability, CloudWatch Logs groups never expire by default, so set retention, filter debug noise at the source, use the Infrequent Access log class for logs rarely queried, export long-term logs to S3, and avoid high-cardinality custom metric dimensions by aggregating before publishing.

examPoints: A question about unknown or changing access patterns is testing S3 Intelligent-Tiering, while one with a known age-based pattern is testing lifecycle transitions, minimum storage durations and the Glacier class that matches the restore deadline.
A question about paying for capacity to get IOPS is testing gp2 to gp3 migration, and one about Aurora bills dominated by I/O is testing Aurora I/O-Optimized.

A question about long-term backups or logs costing too much is testing AWS Backup cold storage rules (retention at least transition plus 90 days), EBS Snapshots Archive through Data Lifecycle Manager, and CloudWatch Logs retention and filtering.

quiz.q: A team runs a database on a 200 GiB EBS gp2 volume. It needs a sustained 6,000 IOPS, so the team grew the volume to 2,000 GiB even though only 150 GiB of data is stored. Latency requirements are in the single-digit milliseconds. Which change lowers cost while meeting the performance requirement?
choices: Change the volume to io2 Block Express with 6,000 provisioned IOPS at the same 2,000 GiB size, because Provisioned IOPS volumes cost less per IOPS than gp2
Take a snapshot of the volume, restore it to a new 200 GiB gp2 volume, and enable fast snapshot restore so that the smaller volume reaches full IOPS immediately
Move the data to a new gp3 volume of about 200 GiB with 6,000 provisioned IOPS, because gp3 provides its IOPS independently of the volume size
Replace the volume with a throughput-optimized st1 volume of 2,000 GiB, which offers a lower price per GB while still sustaining the required random IOPS
quiz.explain: gp3 provides IOPS independently of size, so a small gp3 volume with 6,000 provisioned IOPS replaces 2,000 GiB of capacity bought only for performance, at a lower per-GB price. Choice A keeps the oversized volume and moves it to a more expensive volume type whose sub-millisecond performance the workload does not need.

quiz.q: A company protects Amazon EFS file systems and DynamoDB tables (with advanced DynamoDB backup features enabled) with AWS Backup. It needs daily backups kept 35 days for operational restores and monthly backups kept 7 years for compliance; monthly backups are restored less than once a year. Which backup plan configuration gives the lowest storage cost that meets the rules?
choices: A daily rule that keeps recovery points in warm storage for 35 days, and a monthly rule that moves recovery points to cold storage after 30 days and keeps them for 7 years
A daily rule that moves recovery points to cold storage after 7 days and deletes them after 35 days, and a monthly rule that keeps recovery points in warm storage for 7 years
A daily rule kept 35 days and a monthly rule kept 90 days in a vault with Vault Lock in compliance mode set to 7 years, so that the lock extends retention at the cold storage price
A daily rule kept 35 days in warm storage, and a monthly rule with a vault lifecycle rule that exports recovery points to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days
quiz.explain: The 35-day daily backups cannot meet the 90-day cold storage minimum, so they stay warm, while the rarely restored monthly copies spend almost 7 years at the cold storage price. Choice B fails because a recovery point moved to cold storage must be retained at least 90 days after the transition, so AWS Backup rejects a 7-day transition with 35-day deletion.

days.recap: Tier S3 and EFS data by access, pick Glacier classes by restore deadline, move gp2 to gp3, choose DynamoDB capacity modes and table classes by traffic shape, use reserved instances, Serverless v2, I/O-Optimized or Database Savings Plans for relational spend, and design backup and log retention deliberately.

days.title: Domain 3 Review: Cost-Optimized Architecture Design

concepts.heading: Pricing Models: Commit to the Floor, Flex the Rest
concepts.body: Task 3.1 questions reward a layered purchase plan. Rightsize first with Compute Optimizer and scaling (target tracking, scheduled, predictive), then commit to the steady floor with Compute Savings Plans when the compute mix may change, EC2 Instance Savings Plans or RIs when it will not, and SageMaker AI Savings Plans for SageMaker instances. Use On-Demand for variable peaks, Spot or Fargate Spot for interruptible work with diversification and a guaranteed On-Demand base, and On-Demand Capacity Reservations only when capacity itself must be guaranteed. Architecture choices change the bill as much as purchase options: Graviton for price-performance, Lambda for spiky low-utilization work versus containers for steady load, and Step Functions Express for high-volume short workflows. Watch for the traps of committing to the peak, buying a commitment that does not cover the target service, and paying a premium tier that a latency-tolerant workload does not need.

concepts.heading: AI/ML Cost Levers
concepts.body: For Bedrock, choose the pricing path from the latency need: on-demand Standard for interactive traffic, Flex for synchronous work that tolerates slower answers, batch inference for large independent jobs with deadlines in hours, Priority only for latency-critical paths, and Provisioned Throughput or Reserved only for steady, predictable volume. Reduce tokens with prompt caching of a static prefix, response caching for repeated questions, trimmed context and smaller models, letting Intelligent Prompt Routing choose between two models of a family. Cross-Region inference profiles add burst capacity at the source Region's price with no routing fee; pick a geographic profile when processing must stay in a geography, and reach Bedrock through an interface endpoint in the source Region instead of NAT. For SageMaker AI, match endpoint type to traffic (real-time, serverless, asynchronous, batch transform) and test Inferentia2 with the Neuron SDK for steady inference.

concepts.heading: Network and Data Transfer Costs
concepts.body: Task 3.2 is about knowing which boundary traffic crosses and which component adds a per-GB charge. Inter-AZ and inter-Region traffic is billed per GB; NAT gateways, Transit Gateways, interface endpoints and PrivateLink add processing charges; gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB and same-AZ peering traffic are free. So replace NAT paths to S3 and DynamoDB with gateway endpoints in each VPC, centralize lightly used interface endpoints, add peering beside a Transit Gateway for heavy pairs, and keep chatty traffic in one AZ without giving up multi-AZ capacity. CloudFront reduces egress and origin load when cache keys are lean, and Origin Shield collapses requests from many edge caches into one origin fetch. Replication should be scoped: filtered S3 replication into cheaper classes, global tables only for tables that need multi-Region writes, and backup copies sized to the Regional RPO.

concepts.heading: Allocation, Visibility, and Alerts
