concepts.body: Task 3.3 combines structure, data and alerts. Accounts and OUs carry the dimensions that must cover every dollar, and a small set of tags carries finer splits; tags must be activated as cost allocation tags in the management account before billing tools use them. Enforcement layers tag policies for standard values, SCPs with aws:RequestTag conditions to require tags at creation, and the Config required-tags rule to find gaps. Cost Explorer gives interactive views and recommendations, while CUR 2.0 through Data Exports, queried with Athena, gives line-item detail. Cost categories and split charge rules build chargeback groups, split cost allocation data divides shared ECS and EKS clusters by task or pod, and tagged Bedrock application inference profiles plus invocation logs split shared model costs. Budgets alert on thresholds and can act, and Cost Anomaly Detection catches unexpected spikes.

concepts.heading: Storage, Database, and Observability Costs
concepts.body: Task 3.4 asks you to match data to price. S3 Intelligent-Tiering handles unknown access patterns; lifecycle rules handle known ones, respecting minimum storage durations and choosing the Glacier class from the restore deadline. EFS lifecycle moves cold files to Infrequent Access and Archive. On EBS, gp3 decouples IOPS from size, io2 is for workloads that need its latency and durability, and Data Lifecycle Manager archives long-lived snapshots. DynamoDB on-demand fits spiky tables, provisioned with auto scaling and reserved capacity fits steady ones, and Standard-IA fits large, rarely read tables. Relational spend drops with reserved DB instances, Aurora Serverless v2 for variable load, Aurora I/O-Optimized when I/O dominates, and Database Savings Plans across engines. AWS Backup cold storage needs retention of at least transition plus 90 days, and CloudWatch Logs needs explicit retention, filtering and the Infrequent Access class for rarely queried logs.

examPoints: In a Domain 3 question, identify the usage shape first (steady, spiky, interruptible, latency-tolerant, rarely accessed), because the cheapest option almost always follows from that shape rather than from the service name.

Eliminate answers that buy capacity for a peak, add a processing hop such as a Transit Gateway, NAT gateway or extra endpoint that the traffic does not need, or rely on manual estimates when a native allocation feature exists.

quiz.q: A retailer must regenerate marketing descriptions for about two million catalog items every night with an Amazon Bedrock model. Results are needed in the product database by the next evening and nobody waits on an individual item. Daytime traffic is a few thousand interactive requests. Finance wants the lowest inference cost without capacity that sits idle during the day. Which design meets these requirements?
choices: Purchase a six-month Provisioned Throughput commitment sized for the nightly peak, and route the daytime interactive requests to the same provisioned model to keep it busy
Send all two million prompts on demand with the Priority service tier from a Step Functions Map state so that the catalog is finished as early in the night as possible
Host an open-weight model on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint with GPU instances and target tracking scaling, and send each catalog item as a separate synchronous request
Write the prompts as JSONL records to Amazon S3 each evening, submit Bedrock batch inference jobs, and load the generated descriptions from the S3 output prefix
quiz.explain: Batch inference fits large, asynchronous jobs with a deadline of hours, costs less per token than on-demand for supported models, and needs no reserved capacity. Choice A pays for model units around the clock for the whole term, while a few thousand daytime requests cannot keep that capacity busy.

quiz.q: A company has 50 spoke VPCs connected through a Transit Gateway. Each spoke has its own interface endpoints for 12 AWS services in three Availability Zones, and the endpoint hourly charges are significant although API traffic to those services is light. The spokes also read several terabytes per day from Amazon S3 in the same Region. Which TWO-part change lowers network cost while keeping traffic private?
choices: Deploy a single S3 gateway endpoint in a shared services VPC and route spoke S3 traffic to it through the Transit Gateway, and keep the interface endpoints in every spoke
Centralize the interface endpoints in a shared services VPC with Route 53 private hosted zones shared to every spoke, and add an S3 gateway endpoint in each spoke
Remove all interface endpoints and send AWS API traffic and S3 traffic through centralized NAT gateways in an egress VPC that already serves internet-bound traffic from the spokes
Keep interface endpoints in every spoke but deploy each in a single Availability Zone, and send S3 traffic to the shared services VPC through the Transit Gateway
quiz.explain: Centralizing lightly used interface endpoints collapses 1,800 endpoint-AZs to 36, and free gateway endpoints in each spoke keep the heavy S3 traffic off the Transit Gateway. Choice A fails because a gateway endpoint serves only traffic that originates in its own VPC, so spoke traffic arriving through the Transit Gateway cannot use it.

days.recap: Domain 3 rewards matching each workload's shape to the cheapest option that still meets its requirements: commitments for the floor, the right Bedrock and SageMaker AI pricing path, fewer processing hops for data, complete allocation with alerts, and storage and retention tuned to access.

days.title: Migration Assessment and Rehosting: Discovery, Wave Planning, the 7 Rs, and AWS Transform MGN

concepts.heading: Discovery and Portfolio Assessment
concepts.body: A large migration starts by measuring what exists: server inventory (CPU, memory, disks, OS), utilization over time, and which servers talk to each other. Inventory and sizing can come from the hypervisor, for example vCenter, through an agentless collector, while process-level data (which program opened which connection) is only visible from inside the operating system, so it needs an agent on each server. Collection should run for several weeks so that monthly batch jobs also appear. AWS Transform is the recommended AWS service for discovery and assessment today; AWS Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub stopped accepting new customers on 2025-11-07, so treat them as legacy names in older questions. For example, a team uses agentless collection for 850 low-risk VMs and agents on 50 critical servers. A scenario that asks what to do before planning hundreds of servers is testing discovery and assessment.

concepts.heading: Building the Business Case with AWS Transform Assessments
concepts.body: Leadership usually wants a cost comparison before funding a migration. AWS Transform migration assessments turn a server inventory, from its discovery tool or exports of existing tools, into a data-driven total cost of ownership (TCO) business case: each server is right-sized to a best-fit AWS service from measured utilization, pricing options and licensing are analyzed, and the team can add on-premises costs such as hardware, licenses, data center space and support that never appear on a server invoice. A business value assessment adds benefits beyond run-rate cost, such as staff productivity. For example, 1,200 VMs averaging 15 percent CPU are modeled on smaller instances, so the case reflects measured use rather than nameplate size. Older questions may name AWS Migration Evaluator for this job. If a question asks for a data-driven TCO or business case from real utilization, the answer is a migration assessment, not discovery dependency maps or the Pricing Calculator alone.

concepts.heading: Dependency Mapping and Wave Planning
concepts.body: Servers that communicate constantly are grouped into one application (a dependency group) and normally move in the same wave, because splitting them forces chatty traffic across the hybrid link. If a web tier makes 200 queries per page to a database, a 30 ms round trip over VPN would add seconds to every page. Waves are then ordered by risk: early pilot waves hold simple, low-criticality applications with few dependencies, which lets the team refine the runbook (DNS cutover steps, firewall rules, launch settings), and later waves carry the critical, highly connected systems. Blackout periods, team availability and license dates also shape the schedule. When an exam scenario shows two dependent applications scheduled in different waves, the expected fix is to move them together or plan a tested hybrid interim state.

concepts.heading: Choosing One of the 7 Rs for Each Application
concepts.body: Every application gets a strategy. Retire switches it off; Retain leaves it where it is for now, often for latency to local hardware or vendor support terms; Rehost lifts and shifts servers to EC2 unchanged; Relocate moves a whole platform such as VMware without converting VMs; Replatform makes a targeted swap such as a self-managed database to Amazon RDS while the application stays the same; Repurchase replaces it with a different product, often SaaS; Refactor re-architects the code for cloud-native services. The deciding question is what happens to the existing code: thrown away for a bought product is repurchase, kept but with one managed component is replatform, rewritten is refactor. Refactoring pays off for high-value, frequently changed applications whose architecture limits scaling. Expect questions that describe a migration plan and ask which R it is.

concepts.heading: Rehosting at Scale with AWS Transform MGN
concepts.body: AWS Transform MGN (previously AWS Application Migration Service) is the main AWS service for rehosting physical, virtual and cloud servers onto Amazon EC2. A replication agent on each source server (or agentless replication from vCenter) continuously copies disks at the block level to lightweight replication servers in a staging subnet, while the source keeps running. Test launches start instances from the replicated data so the team can check boot, networking and the application without touching the source. At cutover the source stops, the final changes replicate, and production instances launch, so downtime is minutes. Launch templates and post-launch actions standardize settings across hundreds of servers. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery uses a similar replication engine but keeps replicating indefinitely for DR, while MGN stops after cutover. The exam signal is many servers, no code changes, minimal downtime and repeatable test launches.

examPoints: A question that describes hundreds of servers with unknown dependencies and asks what to do before scheduling waves is testing discovery and dependency mapping (AWS Transform today), not an immediate rehost.
A question that asks for minimal-downtime lift-and-shift of many Windows and Linux servers with isolated test launches is testing AWS Transform MGN and its replicate, test, cutover workflow.
A question that describes a migration plan in words (managed database swap, SaaS replacement, platform move) is testing whether you can name the matching R among the 7 Rs.

quiz.q: A company is moving a .NET application from Windows VMs to EC2 largely unchanged, but will move its self-managed SQL Server database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server to cut patching and backup work. The application keeps the same queries and drivers. Which migration strategy describes this plan?
choices: Rehost, because the application servers move to EC2 with no code changes at all
Replatform, because one component is swapped for a managed service without redesign
Refactor, because moving the database to RDS requires the application to be re-architected
Repurchase, because Amazon RDS replaces the existing database product with a new one
quiz.explain: Keeping the application and its SQL dialect while swapping the self-managed database for a managed service is the textbook replatform. Choice A (rehost) would move the database server unchanged to EC2 as well, so it misses the managed-service swap.

quiz.q: Discovery data shows that a web application scheduled for wave 2 makes about 200 database queries per page to a database scheduled for wave 6. Both teams want to keep their original dates. What should the migration team do before finalizing the wave plan?
choices: Keep both waves as planned, because AWS Transform MGN replicates the database continuously in the meantime
Move the database first in wave 2 and leave the web tier on premises until wave 6 to reduce risk
Raise the Site-to-Site VPN bandwidth so that the database traffic fits during the months between the two waves
Group the web tier and its database into one dependency group and migrate them together in the same wave
quiz.explain: Tightly coupled components move together so chatty traffic never crosses the hybrid link. Choice C adds bandwidth, but the problem is latency on 200 sequential queries per page, which more bandwidth does not remove.

days.recap: Discover and assess first (AWS Transform, including its migration assessment for the TCO business case), group servers by dependencies into risk-ordered waves, pick one of the 7 Rs per application, and rehost at scale with AWS Transform MGN's replicate, test, cutover workflow.

days.title: Data and Database Migration: DMS Full Load and CDC, Schema Conversion, DataSync, and Offline Transfer

concepts.heading: AWS DMS: Full Load Plus Change Data Capture
concepts.body: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) copies data from a source database to a target while the source stays online. A task of type full load and CDC first copies the existing rows, then change data capture reads the source transaction log (for Oracle through LogMiner or Binary Reader with supplemental logging, for SQL Server through MS-CDC or MS-Replication) and applies inserts, updates and deletes to the target until cutover. DMS data validation compares rows between source and target and reports mismatches. At cutover the team stops writes, lets CDC drain the last changes, checks validation and points the application at the new endpoint, so downtime is minutes even for a 5 TB database. Keep the source intact until the target is proven so rollback stays possible. A question with a large production database and a downtime window of minutes is testing full load plus CDC.

concepts.heading: Homogeneous Versus Heterogeneous: DMS Schema Conversion and AWS SCT
concepts.body: In a homogeneous migration, such as SQL Server to RDS for SQL Server or MySQL to Aurora MySQL, the engine stays the same, so DMS (or native tools) moves the data without schema conversion. In a heterogeneous migration, such as Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL, tables, views, sequences and procedural code like PL/SQL packages must be rewritten for the new engine first. AWS Schema Conversion Tool (a desktop application) and DMS Schema Conversion (the same capability inside the DMS console) analyze the source, convert what they can automatically and produce an assessment report of items that need manual work. Order matters: convert the schema first so DMS has target tables to load, then run full load plus CDC. A scenario that mentions different engines plus stored procedures is testing schema conversion before data movement; DMS alone never converts code.

concepts.heading: AWS DataSync for File and Object Data
concepts.body: AWS DataSync moves file and object data over the network between on-premises storage (NFS, SMB, HDFS, object stores) and Amazon S3, Amazon EFS or Amazon FSx. An agent VM near the source reads the data, and a task defines source, destination, filters, bandwidth limit and schedule. Runs after the first one copy only new and changed files, DataSync preserves metadata such as POSIX permissions and timestamps, and it verifies integrity with checksums. A typical cutover copies 80 TB over Direct Connect for several days while users keep working, runs hourly incremental tasks, then a short final task after writes stop, and clients remount the new file system. DataSync is the answer for a one-time or recurring online file migration with verification; Storage Gateway, by contrast, gives ongoing hybrid access through a local cache.

concepts.heading: Online or Offline: Doing the Bandwidth Math
concepts.body: Before choosing a tool, compute the transfer time. 100 TB over a fully used 1 Gbps link is about 800,000 seconds, roughly nine to ten days, and real links rarely run at full rate while production traffic shares them. When the online time breaks the deadline, move data physically. Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers, so for new customers AWS points to AWS Data Transfer Terminal, a secure AWS facility where the company brings its own storage devices and uploads data to AWS over a high-speed connection, or to partner solutions. When the network is adequate, DataSync over Direct Connect remains simpler. The exam signal is a large data set, a slow or busy uplink and a hard deadline: compute days first, then pick online DataSync or offline transfer.

concepts.heading: Sequencing a Data Cutover
concepts.body: Data migrations fail at cutover more often than during the copy. A sound plan converts and tests the schema, runs the full load, lets CDC or incremental DataSync runs catch up, and rehearses the cutover in a test window with the real runbook. On cutover day writes stop at the source, the last changes drain, validation results are checked, connection strings or DNS names change, and smoke tests run before users return. The source is kept read-only for a defined period so the team can fall back if the target misbehaves. For example, a 4 TB Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL move replicates for days, and the actual switch takes under 30 minutes. Questions that ask which TWO actions reduce cutover risk usually want data validation plus a rehearsed cutover with the source kept for rollback.

examPoints: A question that pairs a different target engine with stored procedures and a short downtime window is testing schema conversion (AWS SCT or DMS Schema Conversion) followed by a DMS full load and CDC task.
A question about moving NFS or SMB shares to EFS, FSx or S3 with incremental runs, preserved permissions and integrity checks is testing AWS DataSync.
A question that gives data volume, link speed and a deadline is testing whether you compute the online transfer time before choosing an offline option such as AWS Data Transfer Terminal.

quiz.q: A company must migrate a 4 TB Oracle database with hundreds of PL/SQL procedures to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The application may be unavailable for at most 30 minutes. Which approach meets these requirements?
choices: Convert the schema and PL/SQL with DMS Schema Conversion, then run a DMS full load and CDC task until a short cutover
Run a DMS full load task only during a weekend window, then convert the PL/SQL procedures on Aurora afterwards
Use AWS DataSync to copy the Oracle data files to Amazon S3 and restore them into the Aurora PostgreSQL cluster
Export the database with Oracle Data Pump, copy the dump with AWS Transfer Family, and import it into Aurora
quiz.explain: Schema conversion gives DMS target tables, and full load plus CDC keeps Aurora in sync so the outage is only the final switch. Choice C fails because Oracle data files cannot be restored into a PostgreSQL engine; DataSync copies files, not database contents.

quiz.q: A company must move 400 TB of archive data to Amazon S3 within 3 weeks. Its only uplink is a 1 Gbps internet connection that production traffic already uses at about 50 percent. The company is not an existing Snowball Edge customer. What should the solutions architect recommend?
choices: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and upload the archive in parallel from several servers
Copy the data to its own storage devices and upload it at an AWS Data Transfer Terminal facility
Run AWS DataSync tasks with a bandwidth limit of 500 Mbps so that production traffic is protected
Order Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices and fill several of them in parallel in the data center
quiz.explain: At about 500 Mbps free, 400 TB needs roughly 74 days online, so a physical transfer is required, and Data Transfer Terminal is the offline option for new customers. Choice D fails because Snowball Edge is no longer available to new customers.

days.recap: Use DMS full load plus CDC (with validation) for minimal-downtime database moves, convert schemas first with AWS SCT or DMS Schema Conversion when the engine changes, use DataSync for verified file migrations, and do the bandwidth math before choosing an offline path such as Data Transfer Terminal.

days.title: Replatform, Refactor, and Legacy Modernization: Managed Targets, the Strangler Fig, and AWS Transform

concepts.heading: Replatforming onto Managed Services
concepts.body: Replatforming keeps the application and its architecture but hands undifferentiated work to AWS. A self-managed MySQL on EC2 becomes Amazon RDS for MySQL or Aurora MySQL-Compatible, which take over patching, automated backups, point-in-time recovery and Multi-AZ failover, and the application usually changes only its connection endpoint. A self-managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ broker becomes Amazon MQ, so existing JMS, AMQP or MQTT clients keep working; moving to SQS or SNS instead would be a refactor because the API changes. A cron server becomes an EventBridge Scheduler schedule that invokes Lambda or an ECS task. When a feature RDS does not support is mandatory, such as a custom storage engine plugin, the database stays self-managed on EC2. The exam signal for replatform is reduce operational overhead with minimal code change.

concepts.heading: Containers or Serverless as the Target
concepts.body: AWS Lambda suits short, event-driven work: each invocation runs at most 15 minutes with up to 10,240 MB of memory, billed per millisecond. Containers on Amazon ECS or EKS with AWS Fargate suit long-running or heavy work: tasks have no maximum run time and can request up to 16 vCPU and 120 GB of memory, and you pay for requested vCPU and memory only while tasks run. Amazon EKS keeps Kubernetes tooling such as Helm charts, operators and GitOps controllers, while ECS is simpler for teams without Kubernetes experience. Multi-step jobs that outgrow one Lambda invocation can be split into a Step Functions workflow. For example, a two-hour reconciliation job needing 30 GB runs as a Fargate task started by EventBridge Scheduler. Exam stems usually hide a duration or memory number that rules Lambda in or out.

concepts.heading: The Strangler Fig Pattern
concepts.body: The strangler fig pattern replaces a monolith piece by piece instead of in one risky rewrite. A routing layer, such as an Application Load Balancer listener or Amazon API Gateway, sits in front of the application. When a new service is ready, one rule sends its paths, for example /orders/*, to the new ECS service or Lambda function, while the default rule still sends everything else to the monolith. Users keep one domain, each step is a routing change that can be reverted, and weighted target groups can shift a small share of traffic first. Over time the monolith shrinks until it can be retired. For example, /catalog/* moves next quarter and /checkout/* the quarter after. Questions that say incremental, no big-bang cutover, and the same endpoint for clients are testing the strangler fig with a routing facade.

concepts.heading: Decomposing into Microservices
concepts.body: Good decomposition follows business capabilities, also called bounded contexts, such as orders, inventory and customer accounts, rather than technical layers. Each service owns its data store; services that keep sharing one database stay coupled at the data layer, so one lock or schema change still affects all of them. Synchronous call chains are replaced with asynchronous messages where possible: an order service publishes an OrderPlaced event to Amazon EventBridge or writes to an SQS queue, and payment and email services consume it at their own pace, so a slow payment provider no longer times out the web tier. For example, a flash sale of 20,000 orders per minute becomes a queue backlog instead of failed requests. Exam distractors often keep a shared database or a five-hop synchronous chain; both undermine the point of decomposition.

concepts.heading: Modernizing Legacy Applications with AWS Transform
concepts.body: AWS Transform uses AI agents to speed up modernization work that used to be manual. For .NET, classic .NET Framework runs only on Windows, so every server carries a Windows license; AWS Transform for .NET analyzes the code and ports it to cross-platform .NET, which can then run in Linux containers on ECS or EKS, often on Fargate, one application or component at a time. For mainframes, AWS Transform helps analyze the COBOL code base, document business logic, decompose it into domains and refactor it toward modern languages, while teams test each piece. For VMware estates, AWS Transform supports discovery and migration planning. For example, a team ports one .NET Framework service per sprint and retires its Windows hosts. A question about high Windows licensing and gradual modernization is testing porting to modern .NET on Linux containers, not a full rewrite.

concepts.heading: Modernizing Databases and Reporting
concepts.body: Database modernization often means leaving commercial engines and splitting workloads by access pattern. Oracle or SQL Server can move to Aurora PostgreSQL with DMS Schema Conversion and DMS to cut license costs. Heavy reporting queries that slow the transactional database can be offloaded: DMS CDC or Aurora zero-ETL integration streams changes into Amazon Redshift or an S3 data lake queried with Athena, and the reporting feature becomes a separate component. Key-value access at extreme scale, such as a shopping cart read by cartId, fits Amazon DynamoDB, and repeated catalog reads fit an ElastiCache cache-aside layer in front of the existing engine. For example, moving reports to Redshift removes long scans from the OLTP database at month-end. Exam questions reward choosing the purpose-built store that matches the access pattern rather than scaling one relational instance.

examPoints: A question that asks to cut operational overhead with minimal code change (managed database, managed broker, scheduled tasks) is testing replatforming, not refactoring.
A question about replacing a monolith gradually behind one stable endpoint is testing the strangler fig pattern with an ALB or API Gateway routing facade.
A question about expensive Windows licensing for a .NET Framework estate is testing porting to cross-platform .NET in Linux containers, for example with AWS Transform for .NET.

quiz.q: A company wants to modernize a monolithic web application into microservices over two years. Each new service must take over specific URL paths while the monolith keeps serving the rest, clients must keep one domain, and each step must be easy to reverse. Which approach meets these requirements?
choices: Rewrite the whole application as microservices and switch DNS to the new environment in one planned weekend
Run the monolith and the new services in separate VPCs and give clients a different hostname for each service
Put an ALB in front whose path rules send migrated paths to new ECS services and all other paths to the monolith
Deploy the monolith to AWS Lambda first and then split the single function into smaller functions one by one
quiz.explain: Path-based rules implement the strangler fig: each migrated path moves by a reversible routing change behind one domain. Choice A is the big-bang rewrite the requirements rule out, with no easy way to reverse a single step.

quiz.q: A company runs a self-managed ActiveMQ broker on EC2 that dozens of Java applications use through JMS. The operations team wants to stop patching and failing over the broker but cannot change the producer and consumer code this year. What should the solutions architect recommend?
choices: Move to Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ with an active/standby broker and update the endpoint in configuration
Replace the broker with Amazon SQS standard queues and change each application to call the SQS API instead of JMS
Replace the broker with Amazon EventBridge rules that route each message type to the matching consumer application
Rehost the broker with AWS Transform MGN onto a larger EC2 instance in an Auto Scaling group of one
quiz.explain: Amazon MQ runs the same broker engine, so JMS clients keep working with only a configuration change while AWS handles patching and failover. Choice B requires code changes to every producer and consumer, which the company cannot make.

days.recap: Replatform to managed services when code must barely change, choose Lambda or Fargate containers by duration and size, refactor gradually with the strangler fig and domain-aligned services, and use AWS Transform and purpose-built databases to modernize .NET, mainframe and database estates.

days.title: Disaster Recovery Architectures: RTO and RPO, Elastic Disaster Recovery, Resilience Hub, and Multi-Region Failover

concepts.heading: RTO, RPO, and the Four DR Patterns
concepts.body: Recovery time objective (RTO) is how long the business can be down; recovery point objective (RPO) is how much data, measured in time, it can lose. Both come from the business, and cost rises as they shrink. Backup and restore keeps only backups in the recovery Region and rebuilds everything after a disaster, giving RTO in hours. Pilot light keeps the data tier replicating and the rest defined as infrastructure as code, giving RTO in tens of minutes. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but complete copy that scales up on failover. Multi-site active-active serves traffic from two or more Regions at once for near-zero RTO and RPO. For example, RPO of seconds with RTO of 15 minutes rules out backup and restore. Read the two numbers and the cost sentence in every DR stem before looking at the choices.

concepts.heading: Continuous Replication with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
concepts.body: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) protects physical servers, VMware VMs and cloud instances by installing an agent that sends continuous block-level replication to a low-cost staging area subnet in AWS. Because every write is replicated, the RPO is typically seconds, and on failover DRS launches recovery instances from the latest state or a chosen point in time, typically within minutes, with no application changes. Drills launch recovery instances without stopping replication or touching the source, and after the outage DRS supports failback to the original environment. You pay mostly for the light staging resources until you actually recover. AWS Transform MGN uses a similar engine but ends at a one-time cutover. The exam signal for DRS is an on-premises or cross-Region server workload that needs an RPO of seconds and an RTO of minutes without running a full standby site.

concepts.heading: Assessing and Recovering with Resilience Hub and Runbooks
concepts.body: AWS Resilience Hub defines an application from a CloudFormation stack, Terraform state, an AppRegistry application or an EKS cluster, and attaches a resiliency policy with target RTO and RPO for application, infrastructure, Availability Zone and Region disruptions. An assessment estimates what the current architecture can achieve, reports whether the policy is met or breached, and recommends fixes such as enabling Multi-AZ on an RDS instance or adding cross-Region backups, plus suggested alarms, standard operating procedures and AWS FIS experiments. Rerunning assessments in a pipeline catches resilience drift after changes. Recovery steps themselves belong in Systems Manager Automation runbooks, for example promote the replica, scale the standby, run health checks, then switch traffic, so a 2 a.m. failover is not improvised. A question that asks whether an application can meet its stated RTO and RPO, and what to change, is testing Resilience Hub.

concepts.heading: Moving Traffic Between Regions
concepts.body: Route 53 failover routing pairs a primary and a secondary record; when the primary health check fails, Route 53 answers with the secondary, and short TTLs such as 60 seconds limit how long resolvers keep the old answer. AWS Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IP addresses, puts each Region's load balancer in an endpoint group, and shifts traffic away from an unhealthy Region within seconds without depending on DNS caching; traffic dials can also drain a Region on purpose. Amazon Application Recovery Controller adds deliberate control: routing controls are highly available on/off switches tied to Route 53 health checks, zonal shift moves load balancer traffic away from one Availability Zone, and Region switch runs a recovery plan across Regions. For example, a trading API uses Global Accelerator for one-minute failover. Watch for the phrase without relying on DNS TTLs, which points to Global Accelerator.

concepts.heading: Multi-Cluster Container Strategies
concepts.body: An EKS cluster's control plane lives in one Region, and an ECS cluster with its services and capacity providers is Regional too, so container DR means a second cluster in another Region. Backup and restore with a tool such as Velero is cheap but rebuilds the cluster, add-ons and workloads during the outage, which can take hours. For short RTOs, keep a warm or active second cluster: GitOps tools such as Argo CD or Flux apply the same manifests to both clusters from one repository, ECR replication copies images so the DR cluster never pulls from the failed Region, data replicates through Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB global tables, and Route 53 or Global Accelerator moves users. Inside one Region, several identical clusters behind weighted routing contain cluster-wide faults such as a bad admission webhook and allow blue/green cluster upgrades.

concepts.heading: Testing and Validating DR Plans
concepts.body: A DR plan that is never exercised is a guess. Teams schedule regular drills that actually fail over: DRS recovery drills, promoting a database replica in a test environment, or switching a routing control during a game day, and they record the real time from declaring the disaster to serving customers again. That measured time, not the estimate in a document, is compared with the RTO. Resilience Hub assessments and recommended FIS experiments give a repeatable starting point, and runbooks are updated after every drill because expired credentials, renamed resources or changed dependencies are typical findings. For example, a drill shows that DNS cutover plus cache warm-up took 42 minutes against a 30-minute RTO, so the team pre-warms the cache in the standby Region. Exam answers favor regular, measured exercises over documentation reviews or one-off tests.

examPoints: A question that gives RTO and RPO values plus a cost constraint is testing which of the four DR patterns is the cheapest one that still meets both numbers.
A question that needs Regional failover in seconds with static IP addresses and no dependence on DNS caching is testing AWS Global Accelerator rather than Route 53 alone.
A question that asks whether an application can meet its resilience targets and what to fix is testing AWS Resilience Hub assessments and resiliency policies.

quiz.q: A company runs 40 on-premises VMware servers for an order system. The business requires an RPO of seconds and an RTO under 30 minutes for a data center failure, but will not pay for a fully running standby environment in AWS. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: Take nightly AWS Backup snapshots of the VMs and restore them into EC2 with CloudFormation during a disaster
Replicate the servers continuously with AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery and launch recovery instances on failover
Run a full-size copy of the order system on EC2 in active-active mode behind AWS Global Accelerator
Rehost the servers with AWS Transform MGN now and keep the on-premises servers as the disaster recovery site
quiz.explain: DRS replicates block changes continuously for an RPO of seconds and launches recovery instances in minutes, while only light staging resources run day to day. Choice A gives an RPO of up to a day, which breaks the seconds requirement.

quiz.q: A customer-facing API that mostly receives POST and PUT requests runs on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer in two Regions, with data in DynamoDB global tables. Clients cache DNS answers far longer than the record TTL, and failover must finish within one minute. Which solution meets the failover requirement?
choices: Use Route 53 latency-based records with health checks and lower the record TTL to 10 seconds
Create a CloudFront distribution with an origin group that fails over between the two load balancers
Configure the ECS deployment circuit breaker so failed tasks are relaunched in the healthy Region
Add both load balancers as endpoints of AWS Global Accelerator in two Regional endpoint groups
quiz.explain: Global Accelerator keeps the same anycast IPs and moves traffic between endpoint groups within seconds, so client DNS caching does not matter. Choice A still depends on clients honoring the TTL, which these clients do not; CloudFront origin failover in choice B applies only to GET, HEAD and OPTIONS requests.

days.recap: Pick the DR pattern from RTO, RPO and cost; use Elastic Disaster Recovery for continuous server replication, Resilience Hub and Systems Manager runbooks to assess and recover, Route 53, Global Accelerator and Application Recovery Controller to move traffic, a second cluster for container DR, and measured drills to prove the RTO.

days.title: Business Continuity: Backup Governance, Ransomware Protection, Failover Tests, and Chaos Engineering with FIS

concepts.heading: Centralized Backup Governance with AWS Backup
concepts.body: AWS Backup manages backups for EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS and other services through backup plans that set schedule, retention, lifecycle and copy rules, with resources selected by tags. With AWS Organizations, backup policies attached to OUs push the same plans into every member account, including accounts added later, so no team has to remember to configure backups. Copy actions send recovery points to a vault in a dedicated backup account and, if required, another Region; cross-account copies require both accounts to be in the same organization, and encrypted RDS snapshots need a customer managed KMS key shared with the destination, because the default aws/rds key cannot be shared. For example, a policy on the Prod OU backs up everything tagged backup=daily. Questions about consistent backups across many accounts and services are testing organization backup policies.

concepts.heading: Making Backups Immutable Against Ransomware
concepts.body: Attackers who gain administrator access often delete backups before encrypting data, so recovery copies must be both isolated and immutable. AWS Backup Vault Lock enforces write once, read many on a vault: governance mode can still be changed by users with special permissions, while compliance mode, after its grace period, stops anyone, including the root user, from deleting recovery points early, shortening retention or removing the lock. Amazon S3 Object Lock does the same for object versions in a versioned bucket, again with governance and compliance modes. EBS snapshot lock keeps individual snapshots in WORM state for a set duration or until a date, again in governance or compliance mode, while the Recycle Bin only recovers snapshots that were already deleted. For example, a compliance-mode lock with seven-year retention sits on the vault in a separate backup account. The exam answer for ransomware is cross-account copies plus a compliance-mode lock, not more frequent backups.

concepts.heading: FIS Experiment Templates and Blast Radius
concepts.body: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs controlled experiments defined in an experiment template. Actions say what to do, such as aws:ec2:stop-instances or aws:network:disrupt-connectivity, with durations and order. Targets choose resources by ARN, tags or filters, with a selection mode of ALL, COUNT(n) or PERCENT(n), so a first production experiment can touch only 10 percent of instances. Stop conditions are CloudWatch alarms: if one enters ALARM, FIS halts the experiment. An IAM role gives FIS permission to act. A multi-account template run from an orchestrator account uses target account configurations with roles in each account, so one experiment, one set of stop conditions and one record cover every tier. AWS also provides scenarios such as an Availability Zone power interruption. Questions about safe, scoped fault injection with automatic stopping are testing FIS templates and stop conditions.

concepts.heading: The Steady-State Hypothesis
concepts.body: Chaos engineering starts with a steady state: the normal, measurable output customers care about, such as orders per minute, success rate and latency. The hypothesis states that this steady state holds within stated limits while a specific fault is injected, for example: during an AZ power interruption, order success stays at or above 99.5 percent and p99 latency stays below 400 ms. It is written before the run, with numbers, and based on customer metrics rather than infrastructure events such as instance replacement. The same limits become CloudWatch alarms used as FIS stop conditions, and metrics during the fault are compared with a baseline period before it. A short dip to 98 percent success is then a clear fail and a finding to fix. If a question says engineers argued about whether an experiment passed, the missing piece is a numeric steady-state hypothesis.

concepts.heading: Failover Tests and Measuring Recovery Time
concepts.body: Resilience claims become facts only when recovery time is measured. A failover test injects the failure, for example FIS stops the primary database instance or disrupts one AZ, and records timestamps for detection (a Route 53 health check or CloudWatch alarm changes state), decision, traffic shift and full customer recovery (a Synthetics canary or the success-rate metric returns to normal). The difference between fault start and recovery is the measured RTO, compared with the target. Route 53 health check settings, such as request interval and failure threshold, directly add to detection time, so they belong in the analysis. For example, a test shows 90 seconds to detect and 4 minutes to promote a replica, which fits a 10-minute RTO with margin. Exam answers that measure real recovery during controlled tests beat answers that rely on vendor estimates or architecture diagrams.

concepts.heading: Designing for Self-Healing
concepts.body: Self-healing systems detect failure and replace the failed part without people. Redundancy comes first: spread instances across at least two Availability Zones, use one NAT gateway per AZ, and use Multi-AZ databases. Detection and replacement follow: load balancer health checks stop sending requests to a failed target, Auto Scaling groups with ELB health checks terminate and replace unhealthy instances, ECS services replace stopped tasks to keep the desired count, and Multi-AZ RDS fails over to the standby automatically. Static stability means the system keeps working during an AZ loss without needing to launch new capacity, for example by running enough instances in the remaining AZs. Fault tolerance at the application level adds timeouts, retries with backoff and queues. FIS experiments then prove the chain actually works. A stem describing a single shared component taking everything down is testing redundancy per failure domain.

examPoints: A question about backups surviving a compromised production account is testing cross-account copies to a vault with AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode, with S3 Object Lock or EBS snapshot lock for the matching data types.
A question about a first chaos experiment in production is testing a small COUNT or PERCENT target selection and CloudWatch alarms on customer metrics as FIS stop conditions.
A question in which nobody can agree whether a resilience test passed is testing the need for a numeric steady-state hypothesis written before the run.

quiz.q: A company plans its first AWS Fault Injection Service experiment in production: a network disruption on the EC2 instances of a checkout service in three Availability Zones. Leadership requires that only a small share of capacity is affected at first and that the experiment stops by itself if customers are affected. Which template configuration meets these requirements?
choices: Target instances by tag with selection mode ALL and have an on-call engineer stop the experiment manually
Target instances by tag with selection mode COUNT(1) and a stop condition on the CPU alarm of those instances
Target instances by tag with selection mode PERCENT(10) and a stop condition on checkout error-rate and latency alarms
Target instances by tag with selection mode PERCENT(10) and an EventBridge rule that deletes the template on alarm
quiz.explain: PERCENT(10) limits the blast radius and an alarm on customer-facing metrics as a stop condition halts FIS automatically. Choice D fails because deleting a template does not stop an experiment that is already running.

quiz.q: After a ransomware incident deleted backups held in the production account, a company with 60 accounts in AWS Organizations wants every RDS, EBS and DynamoDB resource backed up daily, with copies that no one, including administrators of any account, can delete before 35 days. Which solution meets these requirements?
choices: AWS Backup policies on the OUs that copy recovery points to a compliance-mode Vault Lock vault in a separate backup account
AWS Backup plans in each account with a cross-Region copy rule and an IAM policy that denies backup deletion to developers
Native automated backups for each service with 35-day retention and an SCP that denies snapshot deletion in member accounts
Nightly AWS DataSync tasks that copy exports of every database to an S3 bucket with a lifecycle rule to Glacier Deep Archive
quiz.explain: Organization backup policies apply the plan everywhere, and a compliance-mode Vault Lock in an isolated account stops even administrators from deleting copies. Choice B keeps copies in the same accounts, where an administrator who bypasses or changes the IAM policy can still delete them.

days.recap: Govern backups across accounts with AWS Backup policies and cross-account copies, make them immutable with Vault Lock, S3 Object Lock and EBS snapshot lock, run scoped FIS experiments against a numeric steady-state hypothesis, measure real recovery time in failover tests, and design every tier to detect and replace failures automatically.

days.title: Domain 4 Review: Resilience, Migration, and Business Continuity

concepts.heading: Migration Strategy: From Discovery to the Right R
concepts.body: Every migration answer starts from measured data. Discover servers, utilization and network dependencies (AWS Transform today, with older questions naming Application Discovery Service), build the TCO business case from utilization with an AWS Transform migration assessment, group dependent servers into the same wave, and order waves from simple pilots to critical systems. Then pick one of the 7 Rs per application: retire what nobody uses, retain what must stay near local hardware, rehost with AWS Transform MGN when speed and no code change matter, relocate VMware platforms, replatform with one managed swap, repurchase SaaS, and refactor high-value applications whose architecture limits the business. A useful self-test: for each stem, say aloud what happens to the existing code and servers; that sentence usually names the strategy and eliminates two choices immediately.

concepts.heading: Data Movement: Choosing the Tool by Data Type and Deadline
concepts.body: Databases move with AWS DMS: a full load plus CDC task keeps the target current, data validation checks rows, and cutover takes minutes. If the engine changes, convert schema and procedural code first with AWS SCT or DMS Schema Conversion. Files and objects move with AWS DataSync, which copies incrementally, preserves metadata and verifies checksums. Servers move with AWS Transform MGN, which replicates whole disks. When volume divided by usable bandwidth breaks the deadline, transfer offline through AWS Data Transfer Terminal or a partner, because Snowball Edge is limited to existing customers. For example, 200 TB over a 1 Gbps link at half utilization needs about 37 days. Distractors in this area often offer the right category of tool for the wrong data type, such as DataSync for a live database or DMS for an NFS share.

concepts.heading: Modernization: Replatform, Refactor, and Legacy Estates
concepts.body: Replatform when the goal is less operational work with minimal code change: RDS or Aurora for self-managed databases, Amazon MQ for existing ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ clients, EventBridge Scheduler with Lambda or Fargate for cron servers. Refactor when the architecture itself is the problem: apply the strangler fig with an ALB or API Gateway routing facade, decompose by business capability with a data store per service, and replace synchronous chains with queues and events. Use Lambda for short event-driven work under 15 minutes and Fargate containers for long or memory-heavy jobs. For legacy estates, AWS Transform helps port .NET Framework to cross-platform .NET on Linux containers and analyze and refactor mainframe code, and database modernization moves commercial engines to Aurora PostgreSQL and reporting to Redshift. The exam rewards gradual, reversible steps over big-bang rewrites.

concepts.heading: Disaster Recovery: Patterns and Failover Tools
concepts.body: Map RTO, RPO and budget to a pattern: backup and restore (hours), pilot light (tens of minutes), warm standby (minutes), active-active (near zero). Elastic Disaster Recovery gives seconds of RPO and minutes of RTO for servers without a full standby. Resilience Hub checks an application against a resiliency policy and recommends fixes; Systems Manager Automation runbooks make the recovery steps repeatable. For traffic, Route 53 failover records with health checks are DNS-based, Global Accelerator fails over within seconds on static anycast IPs, and Application Recovery Controller offers routing controls, zonal shift and Region switch for deliberate failover. Containers need a second cluster per Region, kept identical by GitOps and fed by ECR replication. When two answers both meet the RTO, the cheaper pattern is usually correct unless the stem says cost is secondary.

concepts.heading: Business Continuity: Immutable Backups and Proven Resilience
concepts.body: Continuity combines protected data with tested behavior. AWS Backup policies in Organizations apply plans to every account, copy actions send recovery points to an isolated backup account and Region, and compliance-mode Vault Lock, S3 Object Lock and EBS snapshot lock stop deletion even by administrators. Resilience is proven with AWS Fault Injection Service: templates with tag-based targets, small COUNT or PERCENT selections, and stop conditions on customer-facing alarms; multi-account templates for applications that span accounts; and a numeric steady-state hypothesis written before the run. Failover tests record detection and recovery timestamps so the measured RTO can be compared with the target. Self-healing designs rely on multiple AZs, load balancer and Auto Scaling health checks, ECS task replacement and static stability. Be suspicious of any answer that replaces an automatic mechanism with a person watching a dashboard.

examPoints: When a Domain 4 stem mentions a migration, first classify the payload (servers, databases, files, whole platforms) and the deadline, because each maps to a different AWS service.
When a Domain 4 stem gives RTO and RPO numbers, choose the cheapest design that meets both, and look for a test or drill that proves it.
When a stem mentions ransomware or a compromised account, the answer needs both isolation (another account) and immutability (a compliance-mode lock).

quiz.q: A company is migrating 300 servers, a 6 TB SQL Server database that must keep accepting writes until a 15-minute cutover, and 90 TB of NFS file shares that change daily. Which combination of services fits these three workloads?
choices: AWS Transform MGN for the servers, AWS DataSync for the database, and AWS DMS for the NFS file shares
AWS Transform MGN for the servers, AWS DMS full load and CDC for the database, and AWS DataSync for the file shares
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery for the servers, AWS DMS full load only for the database, and S3 Transfer Acceleration for the shares
AWS DataSync for the servers, AWS Transform MGN for the database, and AWS DMS with CDC for the file shares
quiz.explain: Each tool matches its payload: MGN replicates server disks, DMS full load plus CDC keeps the database current until a short cutover, and DataSync syncs changing file shares incrementally. Choice A swaps the database and file tools, and DMS cannot read an NFS share.

quiz.q: An e-commerce company has an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 2 hours for its main application. The CFO asks for the lowest-cost DR design that meets these targets. The database is Aurora MySQL and the application tier is defined in CloudFormation. Which design should the solutions architect choose?
choices: Multi-site active-active with full capacity serving traffic in two Regions behind Global Accelerator
Warm standby with a scaled-down copy of every tier running in the recovery Region at all times
Backup and restore with daily AWS Backup snapshots copied to the recovery Region
Pilot light with an Aurora Global Database secondary and the application tier launched from CloudFormation on failover
quiz.explain: A replicated Aurora secondary keeps RPO near seconds, and launching the stack from CloudFormation fits a 2-hour RTO at the lowest standing cost. Choice C fails the 5-minute RPO because daily snapshots can lose up to a day of data.

days.recap: Domain 4 joins migration (discover, choose an R, move servers, data and files with the right tool, modernize gradually), disaster recovery (pattern from RTO, RPO and cost, plus the right failover tool) and business continuity (immutable cross-account backups and FIS experiments that prove resilience).

days.title: Infrastructure as Code and Policy as Code: CloudFormation, CDK, Hooks, Config Rules, and StackSets

concepts.heading: Declarative CloudFormation Versus Imperative CDK
concepts.body: AWS CloudFormation is declarative: a YAML or JSON template states the desired resources, and CloudFormation works out the order of creation, updates and deletion, tracks every resource in a stack, and rolls back on failure. The AWS CDK is imperative in style: you write TypeScript, Python, Java or another language with loops, conditions and reusable constructs, and cdk synth turns the code into a CloudFormation template that cdk deploy hands to CloudFormation. cdk bootstrap prepares each account and Region with an S3 bucket, an ECR repository and IAM roles for deployments. Because the CDK synthesizes templates, stack events, change sets, drift detection and rollback still come from CloudFormation. For example, a construct library gives every team a compliant VPC in five lines of code. Questions that stress reusable abstractions and programming languages point to the CDK; questions about a plain reviewed template point to CloudFormation.

concepts.heading: Safe Changes: Change Sets, Rollback, and Drift Detection
concepts.body: Infrastructure as code is only safe when changes are previewed and the code stays the source of truth. A change set lists which resources will be added, modified, replaced or removed before an update runs, so replacement of a database or a load balancer is visible in advance. Stack policies and DeletionPolicy Retain or Snapshot protect stateful resources. If an update fails, CloudFormation rolls the stack back to its last known good state. Drift detection compares live resources with the template and flags changes made outside CloudFormation, such as a security group rule opened in the console. For example, a nightly job runs drift detection on all production stacks and opens a ticket for any drifted resource. On the exam, preview equals change set, manual out-of-band change equals drift detection, and protecting a resource from replacement equals stack policy or deletion policy.

concepts.heading: Proactive Policy as Code: Hooks, Guard, and CDK Aspects
concepts.body: Proactive controls check a resource definition before it is created. CloudFormation Hooks are registered in an account and Region and run before CloudFormation provisions resources of the targeted types: Guard hooks evaluate AWS CloudFormation Guard rules, for example that every AWS::RDS::DBInstance has StorageEncrypted and DeletionProtection set to true, and Lambda hooks run custom logic; the failure mode decides whether a violation fails the operation or only warns. Control Tower proactive controls are built on hooks. Earlier still, a pipeline stage can run cfn-guard validate against templates. In CDK code, an Aspect visits every construct during synthesis and can add an error annotation, so cdk synth fails with the construct path before any template exists; tools such as cdk-nag are built on Aspects. The exam signal is stop non-compliant resources before they are provisioned.

concepts.heading: Preventive and Detective Controls with SCPs and Config
concepts.body: Proactive checks cover only the CloudFormation path, so they are layered with other controls. Service control policies are preventive: they block API calls in member accounts regardless of tool, such as denying unapproved Regions or the disabling of CloudTrail, but they cannot inspect a template. AWS Config rules are detective: they evaluate resources after they exist, record compliance over time and can trigger automatic remediation through Systems Manager Automation, for example re-enabling S3 Block Public Access. Organization conformance packs deploy a versioned set of Config rules and remediations to every account, including future ones, and report a compliance score per account. Config also offers proactive evaluation for supported rules. For example, a 30-rule baseline pack shows 96 percent compliance in one account and 71 percent in another. Good answers combine layers: hook or aspect to prevent, SCP to block, Config to detect drift and remediate.

concepts.heading: Keeping Secrets Out of Templates
concepts.body: Anything written into a template, a parameter default or an output can be read by everyone with access to the stack or the repository. CloudFormation dynamic references resolve values only during a stack operation: {{resolve:secretsmanager:prod/db:SecretString:password}} reads a Secrets Manager secret, {{resolve:ssm-secure:name}} reads a Parameter Store SecureString for supported properties, and {{resolve:ssm:name}} reads plain parameters such as an AMI ID. The template, change sets and events show only the reference string. For a new RDS or Aurora database, ManageMasterUserPassword lets the service create and rotate its own secret in Secrets Manager, so no password passes through the template at all. In the CDK, the same references are produced by constructs instead of literal strings. A question showing a password in a parameter default or a NoEcho parameter is testing dynamic references or service-managed secrets.

concepts.heading: Multi-Account and Multi-Region Deployment with StackSets
concepts.body: CloudFormation StackSets deploy one template as stacks into many accounts and Regions from an administrator account. With service-managed permissions, StackSets uses trusted access with AWS Organizations, targets whole OUs, and can automatically deploy to accounts that join those OUs later, optionally removing stacks from accounts that leave. Self-managed permissions require an administration role and an execution role created in every target account. Operation preferences control maximum concurrent accounts, failure tolerance and Region order, so a bad baseline stops after a few failures instead of reaching every account. A delegated administrator account can manage StackSets so the management account is not used day to day. For example, a logging and Config baseline is deployed to every account in the Workloads OU across three Regions. Questions about rolling one baseline to all current and future accounts are testing service-managed StackSets with automatic deployment.

examPoints: A question that must block non-compliant resources before CloudFormation creates them is testing CloudFormation Hooks (or CDK Aspects for CDK code), not AWS Config rules, which act after creation.
A question that shows a database password in a template parameter or default value is testing dynamic references to Secrets Manager or SecureString parameters, or a service-managed master password.
A question about deploying a baseline to every current and future account in an OU is testing service-managed StackSets with automatic deployment.

quiz.q: A platform team deploys all infrastructure with CloudFormation. Security requires that any RDS instance without encryption or deletion protection be rejected before it is created, in every pipeline and for console-launched stacks alike. Which solution meets this requirement?
choices: An AWS Config rule with automatic remediation that enables encryption on unencrypted RDS instances after they are created
A CloudFormation Guard hook activated in each account and Region that fails stack operations creating non-compliant RDS instances
A service control policy that denies rds:CreateDBInstance in all member accounts unless the request comes from the pipeline role
A weekly CloudFormation drift detection run on all stacks that reports RDS instances whose settings differ from the template
quiz.explain: A Guard hook evaluates each RDS resource before CloudFormation provisions it, for pipelines and console stacks alike, and fails the operation on a violation. Choice A acts only after creation, and encryption cannot simply be switched on for an existing unencrypted RDS instance.

quiz.q: A company manages 120 accounts in AWS Organizations and adds new accounts every month. It must deploy the same IAM roles and Config rules to every account in two OUs across three Regions, including future accounts, with the least ongoing effort. What should the solutions architect use?
choices: A CloudFormation StackSet with self-managed permissions and execution roles created by hand in each new account
A CDK app that a scheduled CodeBuild job deploys separately into every account listed in an exported spreadsheet
A CloudFormation StackSet with service-managed permissions targeting the two OUs with automatic deployment enabled
An AWS Config conformance pack deployed from the management account that also creates the IAM roles in each account
quiz.explain: Service-managed StackSets target OUs through Organizations and deploy automatically to accounts that join later. Choice A works, but someone must create execution roles in every new account, which is the ongoing effort the company wants to avoid.

days.recap: Write infrastructure declaratively in CloudFormation or imperatively in the CDK, preview and protect changes with change sets and drift detection, enforce policy as code in layers (Hooks and Aspects before creation, SCPs to block, Config rules to detect and remediate), keep secrets out of templates with dynamic references, and roll baselines out with service-managed StackSets.

days.title: CI/CD and DevSecOps Pipelines: Cross-Account Promotion, Scanning, Signing, and Deployments with Rollback

concepts.heading: Pipeline Building Blocks
concepts.body: AWS CodePipeline orchestrates stages: source, build, test, approval and deploy. Source actions start the pipeline from AWS CodeCommit, from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket through an AWS CodeConnections connection, or from an S3 object or an ECR image push. AWS CodeBuild runs a buildspec in a managed, ephemeral environment to compile, run unit tests, scan and package artifacts. Deploy actions call CloudFormation, AWS CodeDeploy, Amazon ECS or other targets, and a manual approval action can pause before production. A shared pipeline template, for example in the CDK, gives every service the same stages so quality and recovery do not depend on each team inventing its own process. For example, 40 microservices each get a pipeline stamped from one construct. Exam questions ask for automated, repeatable stages with gates rather than scripts run from a developer laptop.

concepts.heading: Cross-Account and Cross-Region Pipelines
concepts.body: A common design keeps pipelines in a tooling account and deploys into separate development, test and production accounts. Artifacts sit in an S3 artifact bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, because the AWS managed aws/s3 key cannot be shared across accounts; the key policy and bucket policy let the target accounts read artifacts. In each target account, a cross-account role trusts the pipeline role and has narrow permissions, and a separate CloudFormation service role holds the permissions to create resources, so the pipeline can only ask CloudFormation to deploy with an approved role via a scoped iam:PassRole. For actions in other Regions, CodePipeline uses an artifact store in each Region. For example, PipelineDeployRole in 222233334444 may update app-prod and pass CfnExecRole. Questions about deploy failures across accounts often hinge on the KMS key or a missing trust policy.

concepts.heading: Build Once, Promote the Same Artifact
concepts.body: Artifact promotion means the exact artifact that passed tests is the one that reaches production, never a rebuild. A pipeline builds a container image once, pushes it to Amazon ECR with an immutable tag, and later stages deploy that image by digest (image@sha256:...) to test and production accounts, which pull it through repository policies or registry replication. Configuration differs per environment through parameters or AppConfig, not through different builds. Approvals and automated tests sit between environments, and promotion records show who approved what. ECR tag immutability stops anyone from pushing new content under an existing tag such as v1.4.2. For example, image digest 3f9a passes integration tests in test, a manual approval follows, and the same digest deploys to production. Questions where production behaves differently from test because it was rebuilt are testing build-once promotion.

concepts.heading: Security Scanning as a Pipeline Gate
concepts.body: DevSecOps moves security checks into the pipeline so vulnerable code never ships. Amazon Inspector enhanced scanning for Amazon ECR scans images on push and continuously afterwards, rescanning when new CVEs are published, and scores findings by risk. A CodeBuild stage can read the scan findings for the new image and fail when critical or high findings exceed a threshold, stopping promotion. Infrastructure templates get the same treatment: a stage runs cfn-guard or similar checks and fails on violations. Inspector also scans EC2 instances and Lambda functions, so drift after deployment is caught. For organization-wide coverage, Inspector is enabled from a delegated administrator account. For example, an image with a critical OpenSSL CVE is blocked at the scan stage with a link to the finding. The exam signal is assess vulnerabilities before deployment and automatically fail the pipeline.

concepts.heading: Signing Artifacts and Verifying at Deployment
concepts.body: Scanning shows what is inside an artifact; signing proves who built it and that it has not changed. In the pipeline, an approved image is signed after tests and scans pass, using AWS Signer with the open-source Notation client, and the signature is stored next to the image in Amazon ECR. At deployment, an admission controller in Kubernetes, such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper with Ratify, checks each pod's image against trusted signing profiles and rejects unsigned or wrongly signed images. Deploying by digest ensures the signed image is the one that runs. For Lambda, code signing configurations with AWS Signer profiles make the function reject code packages that are not signed by a trusted profile. For example, a developer pushes an unsigned test image and tries to deploy it to production; the admission webhook denies the pod. Questions about provenance or tampering point to signing, not to scanning.

concepts.heading: Deployment Strategies with Automatic Rollback
concepts.body: Blue/green runs the new version beside the old and switches traffic, so rollback is a traffic switch in seconds; CodeDeploy does this for ECS with two target groups, and ECS also offers native blue/green, canary and linear deployments. Canary shifts a small share first, for example ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes, then the rest; linear shifts in equal steps, for example 10 percent every minute. Rolling replaces instances or tasks in batches with no duplicate environment, but rollback means redeploying the old version, and old and new versions serve traffic together. CodeDeploy deployment groups list CloudWatch alarms such as 5xx rate or p99 latency; if one fires during the deployment, traffic returns to the previous version automatically. The ECS deployment circuit breaker rolls back failed rolling deployments. Exam stems say instant rollback for blue/green, small slice first for canary, and no extra capacity for rolling.

examPoints: A question about a pipeline in a tooling account that cannot deploy into a production account is often testing the customer managed KMS key for artifacts and the cross-account role trust.
A question that requires blocking images with critical vulnerabilities before deployment is testing Amazon Inspector scanning of ECR images used as a pipeline gate.
A question that needs proof that the deployed artifact is the one the pipeline built is testing artifact signing (AWS Signer with Notation) plus verification at deployment and promotion by digest.

quiz.q: A pipeline in a tooling account must deploy CloudFormation stacks into a production account. The deploy action fails because the production account cannot read the pipeline artifacts, which are encrypted with the AWS managed aws/s3 key. What should the solutions architect do?
choices: Disable encryption on the artifact bucket and restrict access to it with a bucket policy for the production account
Copy the artifacts to a bucket in the production account with S3 Same-Region Replication before each deployment
Grant the production account role kms:Decrypt on the aws/s3 key through an IAM policy in the tooling account
Encrypt the artifact store with a customer managed KMS key whose key policy allows the production account role to decrypt
quiz.explain: AWS managed keys cannot be shared across accounts, so the artifact store needs a customer managed key whose policy grants the production role decrypt access. Choice C fails because the key policy of an AWS managed key cannot be changed to trust another account.

quiz.q: A company deploys an ECS service on Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer. It wants each release to receive 10 percent of traffic for 5 minutes, to return all traffic to the previous version automatically if the 5xx rate alarm fires, and to avoid redeploying the old version during a rollback. Which deployment approach meets these requirements?
choices: A CodeDeploy blue/green deployment with a canary configuration and the 5xx alarm listed in the deployment group
An ECS rolling update with minimum healthy percent 100 and the deployment circuit breaker enabled with rollback
A Route 53 weighted record that sends 10 percent of traffic to a second ALB, adjusted by a scheduled Lambda function
An ECS rolling update with maximum percent 200 and a CloudWatch alarm that stops the service when 5xx errors rise
quiz.explain: CodeDeploy blue/green with a canary configuration shifts 10 percent first, keeps the old task set running, and rolls traffic back on the listed alarm. Choice B rolls back by launching tasks from the previous deployment again, which is the redeploy the company wants to avoid.

days.recap: Build pipelines from CodePipeline, CodeBuild and CodeDeploy stages, run them from a tooling account with a shared customer managed key and narrow cross-account roles, build once and promote by digest, gate on Inspector scans, sign and verify artifacts, and deploy with blue/green, canary, linear or rolling strategies that roll back on alarms.

days.title: Evaluating and Monitoring AI Workloads: Bedrock Evaluations, Inference Metrics, Agent Observability, and Model Drift

concepts.heading: Three Ways to Evaluate Models in Amazon Bedrock
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Evaluations scores model output with three styles. Programmatic (automatic) evaluation computes metrics such as accuracy, robustness and toxicity with algorithmic scorers on built-in or your own datasets; it is fast and cheap but weak at judging completeness or faithfulness. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation lets a generator model answer each prompt while a separate evaluator model scores the answers on built-in metrics such as correctness, completeness, faithfulness and helpfulness, responsible AI metrics, or custom metrics, and explains each score. Human-based evaluation uses your own private work team, rating with thumbs up or down, Likert scales or ranking, and can compare two models on the same prompts. Prompt datasets are JSONL files in S3, optionally with reference answers. For example, 800 contracts with lawyer-written summaries score three candidate models in days. Match the style to scale and to who must make the judgment.

concepts.heading: Evaluating RAG and Models Outside Bedrock
concepts.body: A retrieval-augmented generation answer can fail in retrieval or in generation, and Bedrock Evaluations separates the two for a knowledge base. A retrieve-only job scores the returned passages for context relevance and context coverage against expected answers; a retrieve-and-generate job scores the final answers for faithfulness (is the answer supported by the retrieved text), correctness and completeness. Low coverage points to chunking, embeddings or metadata filters; high coverage with low faithfulness points to the prompt or the model. With bring your own inference responses, each dataset record already contains the response produced by another system, such as a SageMaker AI endpoint, so the job only runs the judge. Keeping prompts, judge model and metrics identical gives a like-for-like comparison. A question about confidently wrong answers from a knowledge base is testing these two RAG evaluation types.

concepts.heading: Quality Gates and Output Validation
concepts.body: For generative AI, a new prompt template, model version or retrieval setting can keep every request successful while answers get worse, so error-rate gates are not enough. A pipeline stage, for example CodeBuild or a Step Functions workflow, calls CreateEvaluationJob on a versioned golden dataset, waits for completion, reads the scores from the S3 output and fails if a metric drops below the production baseline; with baseline correctness 0.86 and a candidate at 0.79, the release stops. At runtime, outputs are validated before use: Bedrock Guardrails contextual grounding checks flag answers not supported by the source or not relevant to the query, applications validate structured output against a JSON schema before acting on it, and high-impact actions can wait for human approval. Questions about a regression found only through customer complaints are testing an evaluation gate in the pipeline.

concepts.heading: Inference Latency and Model Metrics
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock publishes metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace with a ModelId dimension: InvocationLatency, Invocations, InvocationThrottles, InvocationClientErrors, InvocationServerErrors, InputTokenCount and OutputTokenCount. Averages hide slow tails: if 85 percent of calls take 1 second and 15 percent take 9 seconds, the average is 2.2 seconds while 15 percent of users wait 9 seconds. Alarm on a percentile such as p90 per ModelId to enforce a latency SLO. SageMaker AI endpoints split latency into ModelLatency (time in the container) and OverheadLatency (time SageMaker adds), and Serverless Inference adds ModelSetupTime for cold starts; spikes with flat ModelLatency and non-zero ModelSetupTime mean cold starts, fixed with Provisioned Concurrency. Model invocation logging is configured per Region and records prompts and responses for audit. Exam stems often show a healthy average beside unhappy users.

concepts.heading: Monitoring AI Agent Performance
concepts.body: One agent request is a chain of model calls and tool calls, so agent monitoring asks about the chain: end-to-end session latency, the slow step, tokens spent per session and tool-call error rates. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability is built on Amazon CloudWatch and OpenTelemetry. Agents on AgentCore Runtime emit runtime metrics automatically; for traces and spans, enable CloudWatch Transaction Search and instrument the agents with AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT). Common agent frameworks emit OpenTelemetry spans for model and tool calls, so the framework choice does not matter. The CloudWatch generative AI observability views compare agents and let an operator drill from a slow session to the span that caused it, and alarms work like any other metric. For example, twelve agents from different frameworks appear on one dashboard. CloudTrail shows who called an API, not the internal steps of a session.

concepts.heading: Detecting Drift with SageMaker AI Model Monitor
concepts.body: Models degrade when the world changes. Data drift means the inputs shift, such as new merchant types or different transaction amounts, and can be detected immediately; model quality drift means predictions get worse and needs ground truth, which may arrive weeks later. SageMaker AI Model Monitor works on data captured from an endpoint and runs on a schedule. A data quality monitor compares captured inputs with statistics and constraints computed from the training data (statistics.json and constraints.json) and reports violations. A model quality monitor merges captured predictions with ground-truth labels uploaded to S3 and computes accuracy, precision, recall or AUC against a baseline. Bias drift and feature attribution drift monitors use SageMaker Clarify. All monitors publish CloudWatch metrics for alarms or a retraining pipeline. For a fraud model with labels 30 days late, use both monitors.

examPoints: A question that needs scaled quality scores such as correctness and faithfulness on the company's own data is testing a Bedrock LLM-as-a-judge evaluation job; required expert sign-off points to a human-based job with a private work team.
A question in which average latency looks healthy while users complain is testing percentile alarms (for example p90 of InvocationLatency per ModelId).
A question about inputs shifting away from the training data, or accuracy measured once delayed labels arrive, is testing SageMaker AI Model Monitor data quality and model quality schedules.
